codes.sample: 64 participants (27 M, 37 F; age 13–81, mean 39.78) who came to the Audiology Unit of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, Nepal, with self-reported misophonia complaints (Apr 2025–Jul 2026). They were randomly drawn from a sampling frame of patients with misophonia complaints; 100 were invited and 64 completed the questionnaire.
codes.instruments: Nepali A-MISO-S (items 1–6 scored 0–24; severity bands subclinical 0–4, mild 5–9, moderate 10–14, severe 15–19, extreme 20–24)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S mild band (5–9); recorded for reference only, from a misophonia-selected sample
case_definitions.quote: 39 participants (60.9%) demonstrated subclinical misophonia symptoms, 18 (28.1%) showed mild symptoms, 4 (6.3%) showed moderate symptoms, and 3 (4.7%) exhibited severe misophonia symptoms

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S moderate band (10–14); recorded for reference only
case_definitions.quote: 4 (6.3%) showed moderate symptoms

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S severe band (15–19); recorded for reference only
case_definitions.quote: 3 (4.7%) exhibited severe misophonia symptoms

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Participants were picked because they had misophonia: "recruited from individuals who presented to the Audiology Unit ... with symptoms suggestive of misophonia" and "recruited based on their self-reported experience of the symptoms" (p.5). No unselected screened pool is reported, so this is E1. Severity-band counts are listed only for reference.

codes.sample: University students in Türkiye who were not selected for misophonia. Invitations went by email to about 2600 students; 294 completed the survey (11.3% response rate). Mean age 23.4 ± 5.0; 71.4% female (n = 210).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Scale (Wu et al., 2014): 17 items in the Turkish version by Deniz Sakarya & Çakmak (2022), with emotion, behavior and total scores. Also the CTQ and the DERS.
codes.possible_duplicate: None known. The authors state: "No data from this sample have been used or published in any prior studies."
codes.note: Eligible sample and misophonia-specific scale, but only correlations and mediation results are given (Tables 2-3). There are no score distributions. p. 8: "This study did not examine whether participants' misophonia Scale scores exceeded clinical cutoff points." No count can be derived; the authors say data are available on request.

codes.sample: 144 adults with tinnitus, referred by GPs to an ENT clinic in Norway (Møre og Romsdal Hospital Trust), analysed at baseline before digital TRT+CBT treatment. Excluded: THI <16 (n=29) and patients missing questionnaires (n=121) out of 294 who consented (424 referred). Split by THI into mild (47), moderate (59) and severe+ (38). Recruited for tinnitus, not misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Norwegian MQ-NOR, 17 items rated 0–4), using a cut-off of 14 taken from earlier studies (ref 36, Jakubovski et al. 2022). Also measured: THI, HQ, PHQ-9, GAD-7.

case_definitions.definition: MQ score above cut-off (14), at pre-treatment baseline, total sample
case_definitions.location: Page 5 Results; Table 1 p.3; Page 7-8 Discussion
case_definitions.quote: Indications of hyperacusis was present in 16.67% of the sample, and 62.50% for misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: MQ above cut-off, mild tinnitus group (THI 18-36)
MQ above cut-off, moderate tinnitus group (THI 38-56)
MQ above cut-off, severe+ tinnitus group (THI 58-100)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This appears to be a single Norwegian clinical cohort (possibly also reported in a student thesis by the first two authors, NTNU).
codes.note: Tinnitus clinical sample, so it meets I1. The MQ cut-off is unclear: Methods give a 0–68 range and "a score of 14 as a cut-off". Table 1 note says 15–68. Discussion says "62.5% ... scored above cutoff on the MQ"; whether that means >14 or ≥14 is not stated. The total of 90 is derived from Table 1; only 62.50% is printed. Sample is a completer subset (144 of 294 who consented).

codes.sample: 108 adults with DSM-5 OCD from the OCD outpatient clinic at Çukurova University (133 screened) and 81 healthy controls drawn from hospital staff and their relatives, aged 18–65, Turkey, August–October 2025. Neither group was recruited because of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Symptom List (MSL), symptom-severity subscale only (50 items rated 1–4, total 50–200). Also ASI-3, MAAS, Y-BOCS and BAI.
codes.note: The sample is eligible (OCD patients and controls). Misophonia is reported only as MSL means (OCD 104.10 ± 33.00 vs control 87.56 ± 20.07), plus correlations, regressions and mediation results. No cut-off, severity band or case count is given. The tables appear only as text, but they report means and statistics. A reviewer may want to check the published Table 2 for frequency data.

codes.sample: 227 general-population adults from Mumbai, India (students linked to a tertiary teaching hospital plus their relatives and friends; snowball sampling). 96 male, 131 female, aged 18–77 (mean 34.29). Excluded: hearing problems, self-reported psychiatric history, anyone on medication. Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Marathi translation of the A-MISO-S (6 items, score 0–24), given in face-to-face structured interviews by an audiologist. Bands: 0–4 subclinical, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 severe, 20–24 extreme.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥10 (moderate or higher; 'clinically significant')
case_definitions.quote: 21(9.25%) moderate, and 4(1.76%) severe misophonic symptoms... approximately 10.9% of the population exhibited clinically significant misophonic symptoms (moderate or higher severity)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥5 (mild or higher)
A-MISO-S 5–9 (mild band)
case_definitions.quote: Among the 227 participants, 65(28.63%) exhibited mild

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 10–14 (moderate band)
A-MISO-S ≥15 (severe or higher)
case_definitions.quote: 15–19 4(1.76%) Severe 20–24 0 Extreme

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: There are internal inconsistencies to check. Table 2 says clinically significant is 10.96%, but 25/227 = 11.0%. In Table 4, the age-group totals add to 141+73+12=226, not 227. Group 2's bands add to 72, not 73. The mild counts by age add to 79, but Table 2 gives 65. Use Table 2 for the main estimate. Psychiatric and medication exclusions may bias the estimate downward.

codes.sample: The thesis recruited 113 adults with misophonia (self-diagnosed or professionally diagnosed) from the Reddit r/misophonia community and from a misophonia research mailing list. After cleaning, 89 valid responses remained (63 female, 19 male, 5 non-binary, 2 prefer not to say; age 18–77). Chapter I is a literature review of misophonia treatments.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Activation Scale (Dozier, 2016), self-rated. Also slider ratings (1–100) of reactions to trigger, control and noise-cancelled sounds, plus Likert items on how often specific sounds trigger the participant.
codes.note: Sec 2.3.3 (p.38): "Participants for the study were selected from the population of people with misophonia, either self-diagnosed or with an official diagnosis... The misophonia community on Reddit." No unselected screened pool. Misophonia Activation Scale given only as mean ± SD (6.4 ± 1.9); the "at least 4" claim has no count. Chapter I is a review with no prevalence data.

codes.sample: Cross-sectional online survey (Google Forms) of university students in Türkiye, mainly from İzmir Bakırçay University, during COVID-19 distance education. 252 took part, 5 were excluded for hearing loss, leaving 247 analysed (67 M, 180 F). Mean age 21.47 (SD 4.91). Students were not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Decreased Sound Tolerance Scale-Screening (ASTÖ-T/DSTS-S; Allusoglu & Aksoy 2022): 31 items, including a 14-item misophonia subscale scored 0-42. The highest subscale score marks the primary DST symptom. Also used: the SSQ (KUİK) and a demographic form.
codes.possible_duplicate: Also presented as an oral presentation at the International Maldia Health Sciences Congress, Malatya, 14-16 October 2022 (p.1).
codes.note: Misophonia subscale results appear only as p values (Table 2), box plots and Spearman correlations (Table 3). No count of misophonia-primary or above-cut-off cases. Table 1 has 65/247 (26.3%) reporting disturbance by sounds before the pandemic, but this is general, not misophonia-specific.

codes.sample: Conference abstract ID-6897 (IPAC 2025, J Hear Sci 15(1), p. 69–70). 48 adults aged 18–45 (mean age 31.54 ± 7.25) with normal hearing. They were split into misophonia, ASMR and control groups, but the abstract does not give the size of any group, the size of the screened pool or how participants were recruited.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ) and ASMR-15, used to identify group membership. Also MOCI, EMO-CHeQ, and auditory and video-based emotion recognition tests.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The same issue includes a related case-control abstract by the same Bezmialem group (ID-6898, Eroğlu & Çetinkaya: 31 misophonia vs 31 controls), but it appears to be a different sample.
codes.note: Group comparison. The MQ was used "initially to identify participants", but the abstract gives no misophonia group n, no screened-pool size and no MQ cut-off, so prevalence cannot be derived. If recruitment targeted people with misophonia or ASMR, E1 may also apply. A full paper, if one exists, should be checked for screening data.

codes.sample: 28 people with a professional ASD diagnosis (aged 2-55; 19 male, 9 female), or their guardians, from João Pessoa, Brazil. Recruited for autism, not for misophonia. Online Google Forms survey; undergraduate thesis (TCC), UFPB, 2023.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc 22-item questionnaire (Anexo A) on general auditory hypersensitivity: presence of hypersensitivity, bother from loud sounds and from soft/low sounds, agitation, symptoms, coping strategies and music acceptance. It has no misophonia-specific items or case definition.
codes.note: Misophonia appears only in the introduction. Results cover only general auditory hypersensitivity (24/28, 85.71%), loud-sound bother (23/24) and soft-sound bother (21/24; 'sons baixos' means low intensity, not misophonic triggers). No trigger-sound items and no misophonia case definition. Reviewer may check whether the soft-sound item could count as a proxy.

codes.sample: 67 older adults aged 65-84 (mean 72.27, SD 5.4; 34 women, 33 men), Türkiye, Dec 2024-Jun 2025. Excluded: middle ear dysfunction, neurological or psychiatric diagnosis. Not recruited for sound sensitivity. 77.6% had hearing loss and 49.3% had tinnitus. The recruitment setting is not described.
codes.instruments: Decreased Sound Tolerance Scale-Screening (DSTS-S), misophonia subscale (14 items, scored 0-3), given in face-to-face interviews. Also used: Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) and audiometry.

case_definitions.definition: DSTS-S misophonia subscale score >=4 (clinically significant, per Allusoglu & Aksoy 2022)
case_definitions.location: Page 4, Results text and Table 2; criterion on Page 3
case_definitions.quote: Hyperacusis symptoms were observed in 42 (62.7%) participants, phonophobia in 31 (46.3%) participants, and misophonia in 29 (43.3%) participants.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The cut-off is on page 3: "4 or higher for misophonia were considered clinically significant." Table 2 gives Misophonia Absent 38 (56.7%) and Present 29 (43.3%). The recruitment source is not reported (convenience sample, possibly from an audiology clinic), so a reviewer may want to check it. The sample is small.

codes.sample: 369 Turkish adults (aged 20–55, 72.1% female) recruited online via WhatsApp/Instagram with purposive sampling. Inclusion required at least 3 trigger sounds and meeting all of the Schröder et al. (2013) misophonia criteria on a pre-screening form. The number of people screened is not reported.
codes.instruments: Pre-screening form based on Schröder et al. (2013) diagnostic criteria; Misophonia Scale (Koroglu & Durat, 2024; 30 items, cut-off 60.5); ACE Scale; Cognitive and Emotional Empathy Scale
codes.note: All participants were recruited because they had misophonia: they answered a study announcement and had to meet the Schröder criteria on pre-screening, and those who failed were automatically excluded. The screened pool size is not reported, so there is no denominator. No count below the 60.5 cut-off is given either; results are correlations and SEM only.

codes.sample: 772 UK adults recruited via Prolific, stratified by sex, age and ethnicity to be representative of the UK general population. Interview subsample: 29 Prolific participants invited from every S-Five decile. A separate self-identified misophonia sample (n=26) was interviewed for the ROC analysis and is not eligible.
codes.instruments: S-Five (25 items, total 0-250) and S-Five-T trigger checklist; Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ); A-MISO-S used as self-report; Pre-OK-SCIM semi-structured clinical interview (preliminary version of the Oxford King's Structured Clinical Interview for Misophonia)

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total >=87 (cut-off from ROC against Pre-OK-SCIM 'significant misophonia')
case_definitions.quote: With 87 as the cut-off point on the S-Five, we found that 142 individuals out of 772 met the threshold for significant misophonia in our UK representative sample. Therefore, we estimated that a percentage of 18.4% of the UK population

case_definitions.definition: Pre-OK-SCIM interview outcome 'significant misophonia' in general-population interview subsample (sampled across S-Five deciles)
case_definitions.quote: The Pre-OK-SCIM classified 14% (4 participants) of the general population sample and 81% (21 participants) of the misophonia sample as having 'significant misophonia'.

codes.possible_duplicate: This appears to be the preprint/manuscript of Vitoratou et al.'s UK S-Five prevalence study, which was later published as a journal article (likely PLoS One, 2023). The same Prolific sample (n=772) may also appear in other S-Five papers by Vitoratou et al., such as the 2021a IRT study of triggers.
codes.note: The main estimate is 142/772. The interview subsample of 29 was deliberately spread across S-Five deciles, so it does not give an unbiased prevalence. The MQ severity item (>=7) is described, but no counts are reported for it. The 'significant misophonia' outcome is explicitly described as not a clinical disorder-level diagnosis. Gender split for the S-Five cut-off is not given (chi2 only).

codes.sample: 12 college students (Wichita State University, USA) recruited with inclusion criterion MQ severity score < 7 (minimal to mild misophonia); 2 excluded for hearing loss, leaving 10 analysed (9 female, mean age 22.7 ± 5.5).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014): symptoms + behaviours scales and single-item severity scale (1–15).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Trigger stimuli overlap with Kirby, Cunningham & Zant 2025 (JASA Express Lett.), but that appears to be a different sample.
codes.note: fNIRS experiment. Selected on MQ ("MQ severity score < 7", p.4), so all analysed were below cut-off by design. No unselected screening pool reported. Table 1 (p.5) gives only means (severity 2.6 ± 1.6), no counts for the minimal/mild bands, so I3 also fails. A reviewer may prefer "other" (selected for absence of misophonia).

codes.sample: Japanese university students taking psychology classes at a private university in Tokyo, surveyed Jul–Oct 2023. 440 responded; 439 with complete data were analysed (256 male, 183 female; mean age 19.57, SD 1.35). Non-clinical sample, not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Japanese version of the Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014; Tada et al., 2022), using the symptom scale cut-off of 14. Also the Japanese version of the Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ; Khalfa 2002; Kumagaya et al., 2013), cut-off 40.

case_definitions.definition: MQ symptom scale score above the cut-off of 14 (Wu et al., 2014). The text says 14 is the cut-off and reports the proportion 'exceeding' it.
case_definitions.location: Page 3, Results (音過敏症および音嫌悪症の保有率)
case_definitions.quote: 音嫌悪症尺度のカットオフ値を超える割合は40%（n=176）

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia plus hyperacusis: above the cut-off on both the MQ symptom scale (14) and the HQ (40)
case_definitions.quote: 音過敏症尺度と音嫌悪症尺度双方のカットオフ値を超える割合は7.3%（n=32）

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. Tada et al. (2022, same journal, 41.4%) is cited and used in the meta-analysis, but it is a separate sample (n=180).
codes.note: The abstract gives 7.2% for misophonia plus hyperacusis, but the Results and Discussion give 7.3% (n=32). 32/439 = 7.29%. The text does not say clearly whether the cut-off is ≥14 or >14; it says '14点がカットオフ値' and 'カットオフ値を超える'. The paper's own meta-analysis of MQ means (Table 2) also includes other studies; only the primary 439-student sample is relevant here.

codes.sample: Three unselected samples: Pilot, 2751 UBC psychology undergraduates from the subject pool (2028 F, 701 M); Study 1, 650 UBC undergraduates (514 F, 124 M); Study 2, 765 adult MTurk workers after attention checks (244 F, 516 M, 3 non-binary, 2 trans; age 18-93). None were recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Pilot and Study 2: an ad hoc yes/no misophonia question about strong negative reactions to specific or repetitive sounds. Studies 1 and 2: the MpAQ (Dozier), 21 items scored 0-3, with a sum score of 2 or more as the cut-off. The paper's main focus is misokinesia (MkAQ).

case_definitions.definition: Pilot: 'yes' to the ad hoc misophonia question
case_definitions.quote: for the misophonia question, a total of 1406 students (or 51.1%) responded yes.

case_definitions.definition: Pilot, females: 'yes' to the misophonia question
case_definitions.quote: a total of 1118 females (or 55.1%) and 280 males (or 39.9%) responded yes to the misophonia question.

case_definitions.definition: Pilot, males: 'yes' to the misophonia question
case_definitions.quote: a total of 1118 females (or 55.1%) and 280 males (or 39.9%) responded yes to the misophonia question.

case_definitions.definition: Study 1: MpAQ sum score of 2 or more (non-minimal misophonia sensitivity)
case_definitions.quote: in terms of misophonia rates, a total of 460 students (or 70.8%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ.

case_definitions.definition: Study 1, females: MpAQ sum score of 2 or more
case_definitions.quote: a total of 366 females (or 71.2%) and 83 males (or 66.9%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ.

case_definitions.definition: Study 1, males: MpAQ sum score of 2 or more
case_definitions.quote: a total of 366 females (or 71.2%) and 83 males (or 66.9%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ.

case_definitions.definition: Study 2 (MTurk): 'yes' to the ad hoc misophonia question
case_definitions.quote: for our misophonia question, a total of 325 participants (or 42.5%) responded yes.

case_definitions.definition: Study 2, by sex: 'yes' to the misophonia question
case_definitions.quote: a total of 120 females (or 49.2%) and 204 males (or 39.5%) responded yes to the misophonia question

case_definitions.definition: Study 2, by sex: MpAQ sum score of 2 or more
case_definitions.quote: a total of 188 females (or 77.1%) and 397 males (or 76.9%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ.

codes.possible_duplicate: This preprint probably matches the published article by Jaswal, De Blesser & Handy (2021, Scientific Reports), "Misokinesia is a sensitivity to seeing others fidget that is prevalent in the general population". The samples are likely the same.
codes.note: The main focus is misokinesia, but misophonia prevalence is reported in all three samples. The total Study 2 MpAQ ≥2 count is not printed; the sex counts add to 585/760, which leaves out 5 non-binary/trans participants. The MpAQ ≥2 cut-off is very lenient (≥2 of a possible 63). Sex denominators come from the participant descriptions.

codes.sample: 91 misophonics (24 M, 67 F; aged 25.1 ± 5.4) recruited during visits to psychiatrists/psychotherapists (42), ENTs (20), gynecologists (17) and urologists (12) in Ukraine. Also 91 opposite-sex partners "without misophonia" and 182 healthy controls without misophonia (91 M, 91 F).
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S; cut-off ≥1, with severity bands); psychiatric examination to confirm misophonia; IIEF, SQoL-M, SQoL-F, FSFI for sexual quality of life.
codes.possible_duplicate: These may be the same or overlapping misophonic patients as in the authors' earlier work: Banyra et al. 2021 Bulg J Psychiatr ("Impact of misophonia on the quality of sexual life"), 2022 Arch Psychiatry Res ("Misophonia in urological patients"), and 2023 Bulg J Psychiatr.
codes.note: All participants were enrolled because they had misophonia ("Individuals with misophonia were recruited during their visits..."). The severity bands on p.3 (22/46/18/3/2 of 91) are within this selected group. No screened clinic denominator is given. Partners and controls were chosen as being without misophonia (A-MISO-S = 0).

codes.sample: Turkish adults recruited online via social media: a validation sample of 548 (aged 18–63, 80% female) and a separate sample of 117 (122 before 5 exclusions) for anxiety and quality of life. People who self-reported psychiatric diagnoses or hearing problems were excluded. The authors call it a 'normal population' sample, not recruited because of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Turkish MisoQuest (14 items, total score 14–70), with a cut-off of 61 or above. STAI and SF-36 were also used, but they do not measure misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest total ≥61 (cut-off taken from Siepsiak et al. 2020b)
case_definitions.quote: In our study, misophonia was detected in 2% of the total sample (N = 665) according to this cut-off value.

codes.possible_duplicate: None found.
codes.note: Prevalence appears only in the Discussion, as a rounded 2% of the combined N = 665 (548 + 117). The case count is not printed; 2% of 665 is about 13, but rounding allows roughly 10–16. The exact count may be in the public figshare data (doi 10.6084/m9.figshare.24903288.v2). No separate figure for each subsample.

codes.sample: Experimental case-control study (US, UCSC). Misophonia group: 31 people recruited for misophonia from an earlier interview study; 5 excluded, 26 analysed (selected sample, not usable). Control pool: 38 unselected 'naive' participants from the UCSC psychology research pool. All completed the DMQ. 7/38 scored above the DMQ symptom-severity cut-off of 1.5 and were excluded, leaving 31.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ) symptom severity composite: affective, physiological and cognitive subscales, scored 0–4. Also A-MISO-S and Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ). Vividness/imagery scales (VVIQ, BAIS-V, CAIS) are not misophonia measures.

case_definitions.definition: DMQ symptom severity score >1.5 (0–4 composite) among unselected psychology research-pool participants recruited as controls
case_definitions.quote: We also recruited 38 naive participants from the psychology research pool at the University of California Santa Cruz (UCSC) as the control group. We excluded seven control participants who scored higher than 1.5 in the DMQ symptom severity scale

codes.possible_duplicate: The misophonia group came from Samermit et al. (2022, Front Psychol 13:890829) interview participants. The control research-pool sample is not obviously reported anywhere else.
codes.note: Eligible only via the control pool: 38 unselected students screened with the DMQ, 7 >1.5 excluded. The misophonia group was recruited for misophonia (E1). The 1.5 cut-off is the authors' own, not validated. 18.4% is derived, not printed. Reviewer: confirm that a post-hoc exclusion count from a control pool counts as screening an unselected pool. If not, mark not_eligible (E1).

codes.sample: Online longitudinal survey, adults aged 18+, international (mostly US/UK). Purposive two-arm recruitment: the misophonia arm came through a Misophonia Institute (US) mailing (over 5,000 contacts, mostly self-diagnosed misophonia). A 'general population' comparison arm came through social media and snowball sampling. Baseline N=994 (491 self-reported misophonia, 503 not). Follow-up N=222.
codes.instruments: Single yes/no self-report item, 'Misophonia (sensitivity to sensory stimuli)', used to form the groups. Misophonia Response Scale (MRS), reworded, with no cut-off and described as not diagnostic. Plus SF-36, BAAQ, DPSS-R, STAI-6, CES-D-10 and Rosenberg self-esteem scale.

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported 'Yes' to having misophonia (single item in the health-conditions list) — pooled purposive sample, not a prevalence estimate
case_definitions.quote: Of these 994 participants, 491 stated they did have misophonia (the misophonia group) and 503 stated they did not have misophonia (the general population group).

codes.possible_duplicate: Builds on Dibb et al. (2021), the MRS development study by the same group, which used a different sample. No duplicate of this sample is evident.
codes.note: 491/994 is set by design: recruitment targeted people with misophonia (Misophonia Institute) plus controls. Respondents from the general-public channel are not reported separately, so no proportion for an unselected subsample can be derived. If the reviewer sees that channel as unselected, the fallback reason is I3_no_counts. MRS results are only means.

codes.sample: A representative German general-population household survey (Dec 2020–Mar 2021), with participants aged 16–96 chosen by random route and the Kish grid. There were 2,519 valid assessments: 52.5% female, mean age 50.3 years.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ: Symptom, Emotions and Behaviors, and Severity scales) and the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale-Revised (AMISOS-R), German translations, completed as paper-and-pencil self-reports.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Severity Scale >7 (primary criterion for clinical misophonia symptoms)
case_definitions.location: Results, Prevalence estimate of clinical misophonia symptoms
case_definitions.quote: In our sample, 126 individuals, which corresponds to 5.0% of the total sample, had a MQ Severity of >7 and were considered as suffering from clinical misophonia symptoms.

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R total score >23 (secondary criterion; cut-off is mean minus 1 SD from an external misophonia sample, Jager et al.)
case_definitions.location: Results, Prevalence estimate of clinical misophonia symptoms
case_definitions.quote: The secondary cut-off criterion of an AMISOS-R rating of >23 was met for 148 individuals, which corresponded to 5.9% of the total sample.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Symptom Scale >14 (trigger sensitivity screen)
case_definitions.location: Results, Prevalence estimate of clinical misophonia symptoms
case_definitions.quote: As far as trigger sensitivity was concerned, 81 participants (3.2%) had an MQ Symptom scale score of >14.

case_definitions.definition: Both MQ Severity >7 and AMISOS-R >23
case_definitions.location: Results, Prevalence estimate of clinical misophonia symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Fifty-five individuals (2.2%) fulfilled both cut-off criterions.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified in the text. The same 2020–2021 German USUMA/Leipzig representative survey may have been used in other papers by the same authors (Jakubovski et al.); check for overlap.
codes.note: There are no page markers, so locations are given as section labels. The AMISOS-R cut-off was derived from an external clinical sample's distribution, not from this sample, so distribution_based is false. Table 2 confirms the 126 misophonia cases under MQ Severity >7. Note that the text says '>7' while the statistical analysis section mentions 'the cut-off of 7'.

codes.sample: 59 undergraduate students (Mage = 20.49, SD = 2.64, 45 female) recruited through the psychology department participant pool at the University of South Carolina, USA. This is an unselected non-clinical sample. Sub-ns vary by measure (n = 52 to 59).
codes.instruments: No misophonia instrument. Only the Bucknell Auditory Imagery Scale – Vividness subscale (BAIS-V), the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ), valence/arousal ratings of the stimuli, and physiological measures (EMG, EDA, HR, SKT).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Misophonia appears only as motivation (a "comparison baseline for the study of misophonia") and as the funder (Misophonia Research Fund). The "two behavioral questionnaires" (p.5) were BAIS-V and VVIQ (p.8). There is no misophonia questionnaire, interview or case definition, so no prevalence can be extracted. Could also be coded not_misophonia.

codes.sample: 40 adolescents aged 11–16 in the US (UC Davis): 18 autistic and 22 non-autistic comparison participants. They were recruited from community advertising, an autism research registry and a general-population participant pool. Recruitment was not based on misophonia, but the study ads mentioned 'how children on the autism spectrum experience sights and sounds'.
codes.instruments: Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ, self-report); MIST-A misophonia subscale; Core Discriminant Sounds (CDS) psychoacoustic misophonia score (CDSMiso). Other measures: MIST-A hyperacusis and other subscales, VADQ, BBCSS, SEQ-3.0, loudness discomfort levels (LDLs).
codes.possible_duplicate: Part of a larger project that included the same participants: Dwyer, Sillas, Saron & Rivera (2024), preprint on hyper-focus/monotropism (osf.io/4k9bg). That preprint probably reports no misophonia counts. A related PhD dissertation by Dwyer may describe the same sample.
codes.note: Eligible sample, but the main text gives only means/SDs, ranges, regressions and correlations (Tables 2–3), with no count meeting any cut-off. Number with CDSMiso above 0 (above controls' 75th percentile) is not reported. Supplementary Tables A.3 and A.12–A.15 were not retrieved; the reviewer may want to check them for counts.

codes.sample: 21 undergraduate students (mean age 18.5; 11 female, 8 male) from an Introduction to Psychology course at The Ohio State University, recruited for course credit for a pilot stimulus-rating experiment. The text does not say they were recruited because of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ); Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Scale (S-Five/S5), with a cut-off above 87 out of 250

codes.possible_duplicate: The pilot data come from a larger experiment (a dissertation by Hansen et al., n.d., under review). That experiment may report the same or overlapping participants.
codes.note: This is a very small convenience pilot sample inside a stimulus-database paper. The text does not say how participants were selected beyond course credit. Because the study warned that sounds could be unpleasant, self-selection is possible, but no misophonia-based recruitment is described. The percentage is derived from 4/21. DMQ scores were collected, but no DMQ case counts are reported.

codes.sample: 30 adults aged 23-54 from various occupations in Telangana, India (homemakers 5, ASLP 4, AWT 2, students 4, musicians 2, conductors 3, teachers 4, special educators 3, correspondents 3). Band counts were derived by adding up Table 2 (14/6/8/2, total 30), which matches the printed percentages. The percentages inside Table 2 are mislabelled (e.g., 0.40% for 40%). No one scored in the extreme band.

codes.sample: Convenience online survey of University of Mysore undergraduate and postgraduate students, India, aged 18-30 (mean 22). 172 responded and 2 declined consent, leaving N=170 (32 male, 138 female). Recruited as students, not for misophonia.

The most common trigger was chalk scratching, so construct validity is questionable.

codes.sample: Unselected participants from UNLV Music Lab studies: "N = 187: Ages 6–15" and "N = 178: Ages 18+" (total 365; Female N = 224, Male N = 141). The sample was not recruited for misophonia.

No case definition is given, and no number or proportion of cases can be worked out. The measure may also fail I2, since it is a behavioural task rather than a misophonia instrument.

codes.sample: 210 adult Turkish patients with misophonia complaints who came to the Hacettepe University Hospital Audiology Department or were referred by psychiatrists, and who met Schröder's criteria (77.6% female; mean age 27.85±9.49 years).

No unselected pool reported. MAQ severity bands (p.4: mild 49.5%, moderate 29.5%, etc.) are within this selected sample only.

codes.sample: Case-control ABR study. 30 Mysore University students with misophonia (invited from an earlier prevalence survey) and 15 controls who scored 0 on the RAMISO-S. Age 18–40. The text says 36 (90%) were female and 4 male, which adds up to 40, not 30. The size of the surveyed pool is not reported.

The number surveyed and the number screening positive are not given, so no prevalence can be derived. Severity bands (15 mild, 10 moderate-severe, 5 severe-extreme) are reported only among the 30 selected cases.

codes.sample: Cross-sectional study at Acibadem Maslak Hospital Neurology Clinic, Turkey (Sept 2022–May 2023). The MQ does not separate misophonia from hyperacusis or phonophobia.

codes.sample: Japanese online anonymous survey. No cut-off is applied and no number or proportion of controls meeting a misophonia definition is given. The 5–20% in the introduction comes from earlier studies.

codes.sample: Case-control psychophysiology study at the University of South Carolina, ages 18–45. Misophonia group: 107 people with self-identified misophonia were screened and 57 were analysed. The 10/52 (19.23%) is visual-only triggers within the misophonia group, not prevalence. 6 control candidates excluded for finding triggers "extremely annoying", but no screening denominator or case definition.

codes.sample: 90 Polish children aged 7–18 and their mothers (83 analysed: 45 misophonia, 38 controls; 44 vs 37 in the tables). Recruited through social media, radio and email adverts. Parents reported whether their child was over-responsive to sounds, then had a phone screening. Controls were chosen because they had no sound sensitivity.

The 54% family-history figure covers relatives of cases, so it is not a prevalence sample. The authors say prevalence was not checked because participants were not randomly chosen.

codes.sample: Nonclinical online sample of US adults aged 18-65 recruited via Amazon MTurk. Not selected for misophonia. 384 completed the study; 297 passed all three attention checks and were analysed (52.5% male, mean age 39.13). Data were collected in the first months of COVID-19.

However, the correlations in Table 2 report N = 265 and the regression df also imply 265, so some MQ data may be missing. codes.possible_duplicate: Related to Samermit et al. 2022 (stimuli reused), but the samples look different. Within this report, Expt 3C's 6 misophonics have the same demographics as Expt 3A's 6, so the 3C figures may be copied or may be the same people.
codes.note: Pooled figures don't add up: per-experiment counts for 3A+4+5A+5B give 26/154 (16.9%), but the pooled sentence gives 11.69% and 9.09% (~18+14=32), and what each refers to is unclear. Expts 1–2 are excluded as selected samples because misophonics were actively recruited (soQuiet, Reddit). No page markers, so locations are given by section.

codes.sample: 80 Turkish adults aged 19–64: 40 with misophonia, recruited from people who came to an audiology unit (Ankara University, Ibn-i Sina Hospital) complaining of sound sensitivity, and 40 healthy controls matched for age and gender. No unselected screened pool is reported.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Symptom List (MSL; used with the Kılıç et al. 2021 criteria for diagnosis), Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; severity only), Khalfa Hyperacusis Questionnaire, loudness discomfort levels (LDL), and the Hearing in Noise Test (HINT).
codes.possible_duplicate: Preliminary findings were presented orally at the 7th International Conference on Hyperacusis and Misophonia (ICHM7), 15–17 September 2024.
codes.note: This is a case-control experiment. The misophonia group was recruited because of sound-sensitivity complaints ("who presented with complaints of sound sensitivity"). The controls were chosen to have no misophonia. The paper does not give a screened pool or a denominator from which a prevalence could be derived. Twelve people were excluded for hyperacusis, but no pool size is given.

codes.sample: Validation study: 26 individuals with misophonia and 26 age-, sex-, handedness-matched controls without misophonia (University of South Carolina). Recruitment source and any screening pool are not described.
codes.instruments: S-Five (Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Scale), used to assess misophonia presence and severity. The DVMSQ is used only as a taxonomy for organising the stimulus categories.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same participant data probably reported in O'Reilly C. et al., 'Examining Physiological Responses to Misophonic Triggers', ASPAI 2025 (ref. 11).
codes.note: Stimulus-database (data descriptor) preprint. Its validation is a case-control study with groups defined by misophonia status: 'The study included 26 individuals with misophonia ... and 26 control participants without misophonia' (p.7). No unselected screened pool is reported, so no prevalence can be derived. Only group mean S-Five scores are given. E4_design could also be argued.

codes.sample: 69 recruited at Ohio State, Fall 2022: 39 Intro Psych undergraduates (course credit) and 30 community members recruited via flyers, Reddit and word of mouth ($10). Final analysed n=65 (ages 18–37). Data collection continued "until we obtained at least 24 individuals with misophonia and 36 controls."
codes.instruments: S-Five (S5), cut-off 87/250; DVMSQ (screening item plus diagnostic criteria for clinically significant or sub-clinical misophonia); a single self-identification item ("Do you think you have misophonia?"). OCI-R and DASS-21 were also given.

case_definitions.definition: S5 total score above the 87 cut-off (a priori misophonia group)
case_definitions.quote: these 65 participants broke down into 26 individuals with misophonia ... and 39 controls

case_definitions.definition: Post hoc 'extreme' group: self-reported 'Yes' to having misophonia AND DVMSQ clinically significant misophonia AND S5 above 87
case_definitions.quote: Using this method, the extreme misophonia group included 18 participants

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Same lab (Ohio State) as the FOAMS and sound-discomfort papers (refs 9, 34), but those used different samples.
codes.note: Experiment. Community recruits came via Reddit and flyers, possibly misophonia-targeted. Recruitment continued until at least 24 cases were reached, so the sample was likely enriched. No separate counts for the undergraduates. The supplement (S1 Table: per-participant source and DVMSQ labels; Fig 1) was not retrieved.

codes.sample: 53 adolescents aged 12–18 with ADHD (K-SADS-PL/DSM-5) from two Turkish child psychiatry outpatient clinics, plus 50 age- and sex-matched outpatient controls with no psychiatric disorder. Neither group was recruited for misophonia, so the sample meets I1.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale–Revised (AMISOS-R; Turkish version; bands 0–10 normal/subclinical, 11–20 mild, 21–30 moderate, 31–40 severe), self-report, including yes/no trigger and emotion endorsement

case_definitions.definition: CANDIDATE ONLY, not a valid case definition: endorsed at least one AMISOS-R trigger sound type (i.e., did not tick 'None'); ADHD group
case_definitions.quote: Sound type | | None | 6 (11.3) | 6 (12.0)

case_definitions.definition: CANDIDATE ONLY, not a valid case definition: endorsed at least one AMISOS-R trigger sound type (i.e., did not tick 'None'); control group
case_definitions.quote: Sound type | | None | 6 (11.3) | 6 (12.0)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: AMISOS-R bands are defined but no counts per band are given. Only means are reported (ADHD 14.30±7.20, control 9.72±6.95; Table 3), plus correlations and regression results. Table 2 gives only any-trigger endorsement, which is not a case definition. The reviewer could count it as a frequency item, making the study eligible.

codes.sample: 72 people with self-reported misophonia were screened with the S-Five; 40 met criteria and were enrolled. 23 of them (20 F, 3 M; aged 14–32) were analysed in the MEG experiment. There was no non-misophonia control group.
codes.instruments: S-Five (Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Scale; Vitoratou et al 2021), used for screening; its RIRS score was used in correlations. Also KBIT-2, Edinburgh handedness inventory and an audiology battery.

case_definitions.definition: Met S-Five criteria for misophonia (exact cut-off not stated) among screened people who self-reported misophonia. The pool was not unselected.
case_definitions.quote: we began by recruiting participants with self-reported misophonia. Out of 72 screened participants, 40 (35 females, 3 males) met the criteria for misophonia as measured by the Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Scale, known as the S-Five

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. All 23 analysed participants are part of the same 40-person cohort (17 earlier datasets were excluded because of a sound-normalisation error).
codes.note: The screened pool (n=72) was recruited because of self-reported misophonia, so 40/72 is not a prevalence in an unselected sample. This is an experimental MEG study of people with misophonia. Also note: the text says 40 participants were '35 females, 3 males', which adds up to 38.

codes.sample: 30 students aged 19–31 (19 female, 11 male) recruited via social media and posters, Dublin City University, Ireland. People with neurological, clinical, visual or auditory conditions were excluded. Everyone completed the AMISOS and SMS first. Those scoring >14 were then excluded from the experiment (3 people), and 1 more was excluded for error rate >20%.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (AMISOS; 7 items, 0–28, with severity bands); Sussex Misophonia Scale (SMS) trigger checklist; a self-report item on whether the participant had misophonia / was more sensitive to common trigger sounds (no counts reported).

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS score above the sample median (median split at 5.5): 'misophonia group' (PwM)
case_definitions.quote: Group assignment was based on whether participants scored above or below the median split score of overall participants (M= 5.5). ... Overall, 30 individuals participated in the study, of which 15 were categorised in each group.

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS above moderate level (>14, i.e., severe/extreme); these participants were excluded
case_definitions.quote: The AMISOS scores ranged from 0 to 14, however, three participants who scored above moderate misophonia levels were excluded.

codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly a student thesis (DCU Psychology) that a later journal article may be based on; none is cited in the text.
codes.note: Borderline. Unclear if the study was advertised as a misophonia study. The median split gives 50% by design. Severe cases (>14) were removed, so the final n=30 is truncated and the screened denominator is unclear (30+3, maybe +1). 23/30 reported at least one SMS trigger, which is not a case definition. Table 2 prevalence figures come from Naylor et al. 2021, not this sample.

codes.sample: 341 adults aged 30–50 from across India (232 F, 109 M; 201 urban, 140 rural). They chose to join an online Google Forms survey and needed English up to 12th standard. They were not recruited for misophonia. 315 had no otological problems and 329 had no hearing loss.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ; Johnson, revised by Dozier 2015). 21 items scored 0–3, total 0–63. Bands as printed: subclinical 0-11, mild 12-14 [sic, probably 12-24], moderate 25-37, severe 38-50, highly severe 51-63.

case_definitions.definition: 'Misophonia' overall (MAQ). The cut-off is not stated, and the 107 cases include 87 classed as subclinical
case_definitions.quote: out of 341 subjects, the prevalence of misophonia was approximately 31.37% (N=107).

case_definitions.definition: MAQ subclinical band (0-11), among the 107 'misophonia' cases

case_definitions.definition: MAQ highly severe band (51-63)
case_definitions.quote: only one had a highly severe degree of misophonia (0.93%)

case_definitions.definition: Derived: MAQ mild or worse (mild+moderate+highly severe; no severe cases reported)

'Misophonia' overall, males

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. Same AIISH group as Patel et al. 2023 (college students), Aryal & Prabhu 2022 and Sujeeth et al. 2023 (high-school students), but those used different samples.
codes.note: The 31.37% figure has no stated cut-off, and 81% of its cases are 'subclinical' (MAQ 0-11). Mild or worse gives 20/341 (5.87%, derived). The Discussion gives conflicting numbers (9.34% moderate, 5.60% mild). The mild band is misprinted as 12-14. Urban/rural band percentages do not add up and look copied from the gender rows. The online sample chose to take part.

codes.sample: 343 undergraduates from a psychology research pool at a large southwestern US university (69.7% female; ages 18–36, M = 18.96). Not recruited for misophonia. Complete cases after listwise deletion, taken from the larger dataset in Norris et al. (2022).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire items (MQ1–MQ20) and S-Five-style items (S5_1–S5_87). Binary outcome variable MQDX, described as a "self-report binary diagnosis variable" (probably from the MQ, but the text does not say how it was derived).

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported binary misophonia diagnosis (MQDX), used as the classification outcome
case_definitions.quote: The original data sample consisted of undergraduate students (N = 343) ... the group sizes are unbalanced (16.5% diagnosed, 83.5% not).

codes.possible_duplicate: The data are a subset (after listwise deletion) of the dataset in Norris, Kimball, Nemri & Ethridge (2022), Frontiers in Neuroscience, 'Toward a Multidimensional Understanding of Misophonia Using Cluster-Based Phenotyping'. The same sample may be reported there with a larger N.
codes.note: Methods tutorial, but it uses real survey data and reports a prevalence, so E4 likely does not apply; reviewer may disagree. Case count not printed: 16.5% of 343 is about 57. Page 22 says 'about 20%' instead. The text does not say how MQDX was derived. Check Norris et al. (2022) for the definition and full-sample count.

codes.sample: Carnegie Mellon University students, aged 18-22, recruited for course credit and not screened for any diagnosis. Exp 1: n=39 (21 M, 17 F, 1 other). Exp 2: n=21 (10 M, 10 F, 1 other; 11 of 32 excluded). Total analysed: 60. People with abnormal hearing were excluded.
codes.instruments: Two MisoQuest items (Siepsiak 2020) on a 5-point Likert scale, averaged into a 'Sound Intolerance' score: 'I find some sounds made by the human body unbearable'; 'Some sounds bother me so much that I have difficulty controlling my emotions'. A hyperacusis item was not scored.

case_definitions.definition: Mean score >=4.5 on the two MisoQuest items (labelled 'Sound Intolerance'; not explicitly called misophonia)
case_definitions.location: Results, Comparison Across Experiments 1 and 2, Sound Intolerance Self-Rating
case_definitions.quote: Only five of our 60 participants earned a score of 4.5 or greater.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Borderline. The sample is unselected and the items come from MisoQuest. But the authors call the score 'Sound Intolerance', and the >=4.5 cut-off is not a validated misophonia criterion; it is mentioned only in passing. The reviewer should decide if it counts as a case definition. Per-experiment counts are only in Suppl. Fig S1 (not retrieved). Small study (n=60).

codes.sample: 288 Polish-speaking adults aged 18 to 59, 80.2% women, recruited online Dec 2021 to Mar 2022 through misophonia-related social media groups: Facebook 'Mizofonicy', Reddit r/misophonia, and Twitter #misophonia/#mizofonia. 81.3% (n=234) self-identified as having misophonia. A test–retest subsample of 68 people.
codes.instruments: S-Five (Polish translation) and S-Five-T trigger checklist; MisoQuest; Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ: MSYS, MEBS, MSES); also PHQ-9, GAD-7, ASI-3. Self-identified misophonia was asked as a yes / no / not sure item.
codes.note: Psychometric validation study. Everyone was recruited from misophonia social media groups ('groups on social media sites relating to misophonia'), and no unselected screened pool is reported. Only self-identification counts are given (81.3%, n=234 yes; '13.1% (n = 13)' no, which doesn't add up). No counts are given for an S-Five cut-off or for MSES≥7.

codes.sample: 256 Chinese adults (aged 18+, fluent in Mandarin) recruited by snowball sampling on social media (WeChat Moment, Weibo, Douban, Twitter, Reddit) and the KCL recruitment circular, Jan–Sep 2021. The text gives no sign that recruitment targeted misophonia. 71% female, mean age 25, 63% students. Described as a non-clinical / general population sample.
codes.instruments: Mandarin S-Five and S-Five-T trigger checklist; A-MISO-S given as self-report (n=125); Misophonia Questionnaire, MQ (n=118); single survey items on awareness of the term misophonia and on self-identifying as having misophonia; PHQ-9; GAD-7.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identified as having misophonia (single ad hoc survey item)
case_definitions.quote: 85 participants (33%) stated they were aware of the term misophonia and 41 (16%) identified as having misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified for certain. The data may also appear in a King's College London student thesis by JW/QW, who collected the data. It is a separate sample from the UK S-Five studies (Vitoratou et al., 2021b, 2022).
codes.note: Only count: self-identified misophonia, 41/256 (16%). A smaller subset is used elsewhere (33 vs 159, n=192). No counts are given for the MQ cut-off (≥7, n=118) or any S-Five/A-MISO-S threshold; only means and correlations. The reviewer should decide whether a self-identification item meets I2/I3. If not, use I3_no_counts.

codes.sample: Case-control study (thesis), Istanbul: 30 participants with clinically significant misophonia symptoms, identified by the ENT and psychiatry departments of Seyrantepe Hamidiye Etfal Hospital, plus 40 healthy controls matched on age, sex and education, with no misophonia symptoms and no psychiatric history. Total N=70, aged 18-65.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Scale/Misophonia Questionnaire (Wu et al., 2014; Turkish version by Sakarya & Çakmak, 2022), cut-off ≥7 on the severity item; DASS-21; Digit Span; Verbal Fluency; Stroop; Öktem Verbal Memory Processes Test.
codes.possible_duplicate: This full text is the 2024 Üsküdar University master's thesis by Davut Aslan (supervisor Hasan Demirci). The 2025 Neuropsychiatric Investigation article with the same title probably reports the same sample.
codes.note: Cases had to have clinically significant misophonia; controls were chosen for having none. No unselected screened pool is reported. The 30/70 (42.9%) and severity bands (moderate 19, severe 11; Table 3) come from the study design, not prevalence. Controls' Misophonia Scale scores appear only as means (Table 6), with no counts meeting the cut-off.

codes.sample: Doctoral thesis made up of 4 articles. The eligible part is Article 2: 94 analysed inpatients with a current depression diagnosis (100 enrolled) from psychiatric wards in Kraków and Warsaw, Poland, aged 18–79. OCD, psychosis, addiction, bipolar episode and cognitive impairment were excluded. Patients were recruited because of depression, not misophonia.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, 14–70; cut-off 61), plus a face-to-face semi-structured interview based on the Schröder et al. (2013) criteria.

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia on both the face-to-face interview (Schröder criteria) and MisoQuest ≥61
case_definitions.quote: Eight out of 94 subjects were diagnosed with misophonia (8.5%), meeting criteria for misophonia in both face-to-face interview and MisoQuest.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest ≥61 of 70 (cut-off = mean − SD of misophonia group in validation study)
case_definitions.quote: According to the assumed cutoff in MisoQuest (61 out of 70 points), 11 patients should be classified as having misophonia (11.7%).

case_definitions.definition: Interview diagnosis incl. 4 mild cases (8 + 4)
case_definitions.quote: A total of 8.5% of patients met the criteria for misophonia. If we included the 4 cases with mild misophonia, with very limited impact on one's life, this would be 12.76%.

codes.possible_duplicate: Article 2 is Siepsiak, Sobczak, Bohaterewicz, Cichocki & Dragan (2020), 'Prevalence of Misophonia and Correlates of Its Symptoms among Inpatients with Depression', IJERPH 17:5464. This thesis reproduces it in full, so it is the same sample.
codes.note: No page markers, so locations are by section. Other articles are not usable: Article 1's online sample was partly from misophonia support groups (68/383, 63/322 self-report), with no unselected subsample reported. Articles 3 and 4 recruited sound-sensitive people through ads. The thesis summary gives the range inconsistently (9–12%, 9–13%, 8–12%); use the article figures.

codes.sample: Kansas State University undergraduates and Manhattan, KS community. A Sona screening survey (DMQ, HQ, demographics) was given to an unreported number of respondents. 88 were recruited and 57 analysed (30 controls, 27 misophonic). Only people with HQ <22, age ≥18 and normal hearing were invited. Pilots: 37 and 66 undergraduates, with no group counts.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ) 12-item Impairment subscale (cut-off ≥14 = at least moderate); Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ, cut-off ≥22, used to exclude); Self-Assessment Manikin for stimulus ratings.

case_definitions.definition: DMQ Impairment subscale score ≥14 (moderate or severe) in the analysed EEG sample
case_definitions.quote: I ended up with 30 controls and 27 misophonics, for a total N of 57

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The appendix pilot samples (37 and 66 undergraduates) may overlap with the Sona pool.
codes.note: EEG case-control experiment. The Sona screening pool size and how many scored ≥14 are not reported. Groups were targeted (30 per group), people with HQ ≥22 were excluded, and EEG dropouts removed. So 27/57 is a group allocation, not a count from an unselected pool. The reviewer may disagree, since p.34 says "57 participants were screened using the DMQ".

codes.sample: Case series of 6 patients with tic disorders (chronic tic disorder with ASD/OCD comorbidity, or functional tic disorder), aged 14-32, seen clinically; no screened denominator.
codes.instruments: None; misophonia was described clinically. No misophonia-specific instrument or explicit diagnostic criteria are reported.
codes.note: Short report describing 6 cases ("We present 6 cases illustrating the clinical spectrum of misophonia-associated tics"; "Informed consent was obtained for all cases in this case report"). No unselected pool or denominator is given, so no prevalence can be derived.

codes.sample: All 257 patients who attended the Tinnitus and Hyperacusis Therapy Specialist Clinic (Royal Surrey NHS Foundation Trust, Guildford, UK) in 2019–2020 for tinnitus and/or hyperacusis and answered the misophonia item. Retrospective cross-sectional design. Mean age 53 (SD 16, range 17–97); 54% (139/257) female.
codes.instruments: Item 4 of the Sound Sensitivity Symptoms Questionnaire (SSSQ4), a single ad hoc item asking how often in the last 2 weeks the patient felt angry or anxious at eating, lip-smacking, sniffling, breathing, clicking or tapping sounds. Responses: 0-1, 2-6, 7-10 or 11-14 days (scored 0–3).

case_definitions.definition: Miso Cat 1: SSSQ4 score 2 or 3 (symptoms on 7-14 of the last 14 days, i.e. more than half the days)
case_definitions.location: Results, Comparison of Miso Cat 0 and Miso Cat 1
case_definitions.quote: Overall, 23% of patients (59/257) were classified as Miso Cat 1.

case_definitions.definition: Any misophonia symptoms: SSSQ4 score ≥1 (2-14 days); derived as 49+21+38
case_definitions.location: Results, Audiological and Psychological Factors; Discussion
case_definitions.quote: Of 257 patients, SSSQ4 scores of 0, 1, 2, and 3 were obtained for 149 (58%), 49 (19%), 21 (8%) and 38 (15%), respectively.

case_definitions.definition: SSSQ4 score 3 (symptoms on 11-14 days)
case_definitions.quote: SSSQ4 scores of 0, 1, 2, and 3 were obtained for 149 (58%), 49 (19%), 21 (8%) and 38 (15%), respectively.

case_definitions.definition: SSSQ4 score 2 (symptoms on 7-10 days)
case_definitions.quote: SSSQ4 scores of 0, 1, 2, and 3 were obtained for 149 (58%), 49 (19%), 21 (8%) and 38 (15%), respectively.

codes.possible_duplicate: Other Aazh et al. papers may draw on the same clinic's 2019–2020 records, especially the SSSQ/HIQ development paper (Aazh et al., 2022a) and the TIQ paper (Aazh et al., 2022b). Check for overlapping patients.
codes.note: Recruited for tinnitus/hyperacusis, which counts as 'another condition' under I1. But hyperacusis is itself sound intolerance, so check this is not an E1 sample. The single item is unvalidated (authors agree). No page markers, so locations are section names. The 42% (score ≥1) is stated in the Discussion; the count of 108 is my own sum of the band counts.

codes.sample: 60 adults aged 18-45 from the South Carolina community: a misophonia group (N=35, 30 female) recruited because they had misophonic reactions, and a matched control group (N=25, 20 female) screened to ensure they did not have misophonia. The paper does not report the size of the screening pool.
codes.instruments: Screening interviews; Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ); Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Scale (S-Five)
codes.possible_duplicate: May share participants with other University of South Carolina publications from the Shinkareva lab on misophonia physiology (e.g., Oh et al. 2025, Biol Psychol, ref [8]). This is a conference paper from ASPAI 2025, deposited on PsyArXiv/Scholar Commons.
codes.note: Case-control physiology experiment. The misophonia group was recruited for misophonia, and controls were "screened to ensure they did not have misophonia". No unselected screened pool or proportion is reported. The 35/25 group sizes come from the design. The 'nearly 5%' figure is cited from other studies (refs 2, 3).

codes.sample: Participants were recruited for a misophonia diary study via Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and WhatsApp, and the text mentions members of misophonia self-help groups. 109 registered in the app; 54 analysed with MisoQuest ≥52 (mean age 33; 83.3% female; mostly from Germany).
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (screening; cut-off first set at 61, then lowered to 52); daily diary using AMISOS-R part 3 (burden items); SCI, STAI, ISI, PSQ, KSS.
codes.possible_duplicate: The author's earlier unpublished bachelor thesis (Först, 2019, Universität Wien) on misophonia and stress/coping appears to be a different study.
codes.note: The pool was self-selected: the cut-off was lowered because many 'trotz der Zugehörigkeit zu einer Misophonie-Selbsthilfegruppe' scored below 61 (p.33–34). Of 109 registrants, 17 were excluded for failing the criteria OR giving incomplete screening data (p.37), so no screening prevalence can be derived.

codes.sample: Polish adults recruited online in two phases (Phase 1 N=383; Phase 2 N=322, 315 analysed after excluding under-18s). Recruitment was mixed: misophonia support groups plus groups unrelated to misophonia, deliberately enriched "due to the limited number of people with misophonia". No unselected subsample is reported separately.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, in development); self-report questions based on the Schröder et al. 2013 diagnostic criteria (misophonia = meets all criteria)

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported symptoms meeting all Schröder et al. 2013 criteria (Phase 1)

codes.possible_duplicate: Part of the University of Warsaw project "Psychological and psychophysiological correlates of misophonia" (Siepsiak, Dragan). Other MisoQuest or Siepsiak papers may reuse these data.
codes.note: Borderline case. Participants were partly recruited from misophonia support groups to enrich the sample, and the unselected recruits are not reported separately, so I1 is not met. If the reviewer accepts mixed samples, the counts are 68/383 and 63/322. The authors say prevalence cannot be inferred from this study.

codes.sample: 74 adults pooled from two pupillometry experiments at the University of Amsterdam (Exp 1: 35 enrolled, 5 excluded; Exp 2: 44). Recruited through university student recruitment, (online) misophonia support groups, Dr. Rouw's misophonia research contacts, and word of mouth. The paper does not report the students separately.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), with severity bands: subclinical 1–4, mild 5–9, moderate 10–14, severe 15–19, extreme 20–24. Also a trial-wise 4-point aversiveness rating of the sounds, which is not a case definition.

case_definitions.quote: 27% was sub-clinical (scores 1–4), 43% experienced mild misophonia (scores 5–9)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S extreme misophonia (score 20–24)
case_definitions.quote: 1% experienced extreme misophonia (scores 20–24)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Exp 1 heart-rate and frisson data are said to be the focus of other reports, which may share participants.
codes.note: Recruitment mixed students with misophonia support groups and research contacts; no unselected subsample is reported. The authors say the results cannot be used to estimate prevalence. So I1 is doubtful but E1 does not strictly apply. Counts are derived from percentages of 74, which sum to 99%. The reviewer should decide between E1 and eligible.

codes.sample: Online study (UK, Goldsmiths). 64 self-reported ASMR responders recruited from an ASMR Facebook group (40F/24M, age 18–38) and 68 controls (52F/16M, age 18–66) recruited from students and acquaintances who said they do not experience ASMR. Neither group was recruited for misophonia or sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014): Misophonia Symptom Scale (MSS; cut-off ≥14), Misophonia Emotions and Behaviors Scale, Misophonia Severity Scale (cut-off ≥7).

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The same authors have an earlier ASMR study (Janik McErlean & Banissy, 2017), but this looks like a different sample.
codes.note: Only percentages are printed, so counts were worked out from group n's (female n=40/52, matching N=92). Controls are not fully unselected: people in the student pool who reported ASMR (47%) were excluded. A third group recruited outside social media and reporting ASMR is only in Supplement 2 (70.8% met MSS ≥14; n not in the main text).

codes.sample: 175 Polish community adults aged 18-40, recruited through social media and a CAWI survey panel. A screening pool of over 800 was used to set R-GPTS paranoia cut-offs. Participants were then assigned to extreme groups: 103 low-paranoia (LP, R-GPTS ≤1) and 72 high-paranoia (HP, R-GPTS ≥35). Selection was based on paranoia, not misophonia.
codes.instruments: A single ad hoc experience sampling (ESM) item rated 1-7: "Do you feel unpleasant emotions because of sounds made by other people (eg, smacking, chewing, sniffling, breathing, or others) right now?" Prompted 8 times a day for 7 days.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is part of a larger project at the Institute of Psychology, Polish Academy of Sciences (Sonata Bis grant 2019/34/E/HS6/00279; Bielawski & Gawęda). Other papers from the same project on misophonia and paranoia (e.g., ref 28/30) may use the same or an overlapping sample.
codes.note: Only means and SDs for the ESM item: total 1.53 (1.2); HP 1.97 (1.5); LP 1.22 (0.8) (Tables 2-3), plus network edges. No count or proportion meets any misophonia case definition. The 800+ screening pool was not assessed for misophonia. Supplementary tables S1-S4 were not retrieved; the text says they hold only network values.

codes.sample: 607 young adults aged 18-30 in Türkiye (mean age 21.48 ± 2.88; 450 female, 157 male), recruited face-to-face. Inclusion required normal hearing and no metabolic, neurological, psychological or psychiatric disorder. Not recruited on the basis of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Decreased Sound Tolerance Scale-Screening (DSTS-S), misophonia subscale (14 items, scored 0-3); also PSQI, SSQ and Beck Anxiety Inventory.
codes.note: Misophonia was measured with the DSTS-S misophonia subscale in an eligible unselected sample. Results are given only as mean ± SD (15.21 ± 11.45, range 0-42), subgroup medians/IQR (Table 4), correlations and regression coefficients. No cut-off, severity band or misophonia case count/percentage is reported or derivable. Prevalence is given only for poor sleep and anxiety bands.

codes.sample: Unselected US adults in a cross-sectional online survey: VCU undergraduate participant pool (N=451) and MTurk community adults (N=375); combined N=826 after data cleaning. The only inclusion criterion was age ≥18; nobody was recruited for misophonia or sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: MQ (severity cut-off ≥7); ad hoc screening item ('Compared to other people, are you sensitive to certain sounds made by other people?' Yes/Sometimes/No); A-MISO-S for screen-positive subset only (N=542); self-reported misophonia diagnosis (community only).

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a 2015 VCU doctoral dissertation (Cash, advisor Vrana). The same student and MTurk samples may also appear in later journal articles by Cash/Vrana or others; check for overlap.
codes.note: MQ cut-off is written two ways: '7 or higher' (pp.38, 52) vs 'greater than 7' (p.61). Counts don't fully match: 129/817 is 15.8%, but the report gives 15.6%. The A-MISO-S was given only to people who screened positive, so its denominator (542 = 314 students + 228 community) is that subset, not the full sample. Page numbers are the dissertation's printed page numbers.

codes.sample: 253 adults (≥18 y) in an online study, recruited through mailing lists and social networks. Named sources were mostly misophonia support Facebook groups (French and international), plus a tinnitus/hyperacusis group and an audiology group. 69% self-reported misophonia. Misophonics were n=78 and controls n=55.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, cut-off ≥61; French translation by the authors, not validated); a self-report yes/no/don't-know question about misophonia; a new psychoacoustic test (CDS score, cut-offs set by ROC on this sample).

case_definitions.quote: Subjects were labeled as misophonics (n = 78; median age = 32, MAD = 8) if they self-reported misophonia and if their MisoQuest score was above (or equal to) 61.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The ROC re-analysis of Siepsiak et al. MisoQuest data is a secondary analysis of another dataset, not this sample.
codes.note: Recruited mainly via misophonia support groups; no unselected screened pool reported, so counts are not prevalence. Generic mailing lists and an audiology group were also used, so the reviewer may see it as borderline. If kept, counts come from Table 2. CDS-score percentages (76.8% of n=168; 85.5% below cut-off of n=76) use a cut-off set on this same sample.

codes.sample: 1572 undergraduates from the Virginia Commonwealth University participant pool (1154 female, 412 male, 6 other; mean age 19.49). Cross-sectional online survey, Jan 2018–Dec 2019. Not recruited for misophonia; the author calls it 'an unselected student sample'.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ: symptom, emotions/behaviours and severity scales); Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ); DST Differential Diagnostic Scale (Cash, 2015); latent class analysis using MQ and HQ indicators.

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a VCU dissertation (Wallace, supervised by Vrana). The same 2018–2019 VCU sample may also appear in a journal article by Wallace/Vrana. Other Vrana-lab VCU student samples (Cash 2015; Cusack, Cash & Vrana 2018) come from earlier years and are probably separate.
codes.note: The page numbers are the dissertation's running-header pages, because the text has no '=== Page N ===' markers. The 13.1% figure for scores >=7 is printed in the text. The count of 207 is derived from the Table 1 bands and matches the 13.1% (207/1572 = 13.2%). The LCA classes use SD cut-offs based on this sample. A reviewer should choose the primary definition; the suggested one is MQ >=7.

codes.sample: German online survey, 2020–2021 (Bielefeld). 2,150 started; 1,881 adults analysed (82.7% female, mean age 33.1). Recruited through a clinic website, social networks, psychology-student mailing lists, lists of people interested in misophonia research, and misophonia media articles. Aimed at both affected and unaffected people; 87.5% self-identified with misophonia.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S, AMISOS-R, MAQ, MQ (including item 18 severity scale), MSL, Misophonia Trigger List; WSAS adapted for misophonia-related impairment; ad hoc self-identification item (0–100) after a misophonia description. All in German translation.

case_definitions.quote: 87.5% (n = 1,646) of the individuals indicated that the description applied to them with scores ≥50.

codes.possible_duplicate: Same Bielefeld survey (Sept 2020–May 2021, N=1,881) may appear in other reports by this group (e.g., German MQ/AMISOS-R translation or validation papers, or theses). Check before including.
codes.note: Counts are clearly reported; sampling is the issue. The survey was openly about misophonia and advertised via misophonia media and lists of people interested in misophonia research, plus psychology-student lists. No unselected subsample is reported separately, and the authors say prevalence cannot be inferred. Leans E1; a reviewer should decide whether this mixed recruitment meets I1.

codes.sample: 78 undergraduates from the UCSC Psychology research pool. Who could take part depended on a misophonia pre-questionnaire: people who answered "yes" were taken for the misophonia group and people who answered "no" for the control group. Groups were then reassigned by DMQ score: 29 misophonia, 49 control. Ages 18-24. They received course credit.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ). Symptom severity score = mean of the affective, physiological and cognitive subscale items, range 0-4. Cut-off >1.5, following Mahzouni et al. (2024). Also an unnamed yes/no misophonia pre-questionnaire, used only to screen people for the groups.

case_definitions.definition: DMQ symptom severity score >1.5 (misophonia group), within the quota-recruited sample
case_definitions.location: Ch. II Methods, Participants, pp. 22-23; Figure 1 caption, p. 24

case_definitions.definition: DMQ symptom severity score >2.5
case_definitions.quote: the average DMQ score for the misophonia group was 2.14, and the control group was 0.83, with only 6 participants having DMQ scores greater than 2.5.

codes.possible_duplicate: Same lab and same DMQ >1.5 criterion as Mahzouni et al. (2024), Multisensory Research 37(6-8):475-498. That paper appears to be a separate, earlier sample. This dissertation may later be published as a journal article.
codes.note: Borderline case. Students were recruited by quota on a self-reported misophonia pre-questionnaire ("yes" for the misophonia group, "no" for controls). This deliberately over-represents misophonia, so 29/78 is not a prevalence estimate. The size of the screened pool and the pre-screen results are not reported. Reviewer should confirm exclusion under E1.

codes.sample: US adults aged 18-65 recruited via MTurk/CloudResearch, May 2021 (N = 2550 initially recruited). Final analysed N = 377: 245 controls and 132 in the misophonia group, formed by MQ screening after the control group was filled.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ). The group cut-off was Symptom subscale ≥2, Emotions & Behaviors subscale ≥2 and Severity ≥7. Also used: IADS-2 sound ratings, PANAS and AIM.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Symptom ≥2, Emotions/Behaviors ≥2 and Severity ≥7 (screening only after controls were recruited); the denominator is not valid
case_definitions.quote: In total, 2550 participants were initially recruited, with the vast majority screened out by the narrowed MQ criteria after forming the control group. A total of 377 participants remained after screening and passing attention checks, including a control group of 245 participants and a misophonia group of 132 participants.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Unselected MTurk pool, but staged recruitment: controls (≥225) came first, then MQ cut-offs were applied to later participants. The 2550 includes attention-check failures. The number screened with the MQ and whether controls were below the cut-off are not reported, so no valid prevalence denominator can be derived. The reviewer may prefer 'unclear'.

codes.sample: 36 participants recruited through online ads, flyers and databases, mostly University of Florida undergraduates. They were "prescreened to include individuals scoring high on the Misophonia Symptom Scale". 34 were analysed (21 female, mean age 19.85).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (Wu et al., 2014), using only the Misophonia Symptom Scale (MSS) subscale (7 items, scored 0–28). Wu's cut-off of 14 or more is mentioned but not applied. Loudness discomfort levels were also measured.
codes.possible_duplicate: Preliminary subset of an ongoing preregistered study (OSF e26ad, University of Florida, funded by the Misophonia Research Fund). Later reports from the same project may describe an overlapping sample.
codes.note: Participants were prescreened for high MSS scores. The screened pool and how many met the criterion are not reported. No counts either: MSS is used as continuous ("ranging from 0 to 20 (M = 9.55, SE = 0.88)"), and the number scoring 14 or more is not given. The exploratory high/low groups ("10 per group") are an analytic split, not a case definition.

codes.sample: 101 tinnitus patients (54 women, 47 men, aged 19–72) at the Institute of Physiology and Pathology of Hearing, Poland. All were included because they reported additional problems with decreased sound tolerance: "zgłaszających dodatkowe problemy związane z obniżoną tolerancją na dźwięki" (p. 4).
codes.instruments: Ad hoc VAS item for misophonia (0–10/0–100), asking whether sounds people make while eating, chewing, swallowing, smacking or breathing are unpleasant; interview item on poorly tolerated sound types; Hyperacusis Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ/KNS); THI; UCL audiometry.

case_definitions.definition: Interview: patient reports poor tolerance of sounds made by people (smacking, sneezing, swallowing, etc.); not a validated cut-off
case_definitions.quote: Pacjenci zgłaszali, że źle tolerują: ... dźwięki wydawane przez ludzi, typu mlaskanie, kichanie, przełykanie itp. (26%)

codes.possible_duplicate: Probably overlaps with Raj-Koziak et al. 2023, J Clin Med 12(20):6622 (HAQ development in tinnitus patients), which may draw on the same patient pool.
codes.note: Excluded under E1: patients were recruited for tinnitus plus self-reported decreased sound tolerance, with no unselected screened pool. The misophonia VAS gives only a mean and median (M=36.86). If the reviewer accepts selection on decreased sound tolerance, the 26% (n=101) from the interview could make it eligible.

codes.sample: 1188 Turkish high school and university students (322 aged <18, 866 aged ≥18; 87% female; mean age 18.9). Online convenience sample recruited via social media pages used by students, December 2020.
codes.instruments: Turkish version of the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S; 0-24; bands 0-4 subclinical, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 severe, 20-24 extreme), plus a sociodemographic questionnaire.
