case_definitions.quote: 17.2% of adolescents and 12.6% of adults had moderate and severe misophonia symptoms.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Recruitment was not based on misophonia, but the survey was advertised as a misophonia study on social media. The authors say self-selection may have raised prevalence. Some printed % differ slightly from Table 5 derivations (57.2 vs 57.8; 17.2 vs 17.1). Table 1 swaps the sex percentages.

codes.sample: 60 normal-hearing university students aged 18-30 (AIISH, Mysuru, India). 30 were in the misophonia group, diagnosed using Schröder criteria, with mild or moderate MAQ severity. 30 were controls without misophonia symptoms. No screened pool was reported.
codes.instruments: Schröder et al. (2013) diagnostic criteria; Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ). Severity bands: 0-11 subclinical, 12-24 mild, 25-37 moderate, 38-50 severe, 51-63 extreme.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same group (Prabhu, AIISH Mysuru) published other case-control misophonia studies: Aryal & Prabhu 2023 on ABR (J Otol) and cortical functioning (Eur Arch ORL). The samples may overlap, but this does not affect the decision.
codes.note: Case-control design. Participants were described as "university students with misophonia" and grouped by diagnosis (30 vs 30). The report does not give the size of the pool screened or how many met criteria within it. Table 1 gives only mean MAQ scores for the mild and moderate subgroups, not their counts. No prevalence can be derived.

codes.sample: Two German online samples aged 16+: Study 1 N=639 (86.2% female, mean age 34.3); Study 2 N=235 (85.1% female, mean age 35.8). Recruited via social media and university mailing lists. Sources included misophonia self-identification groups, general groups and hearing-disorder groups (tinnitus, hyperacusis). Psychology students got course credit.
codes.instruments: German S-Five (case if total score is 87 or more); BMQ-R (Jager et al. 2020 diagnostic criteria, with a severe band); MisoQuest (means only). Also non-misophonia scales: AQ, BITe, STICSA, DERS, NAQ, BEAQ, WHODAS 2.0, IPQ-MH, DPSS-R, PHQ-9, ASI-3, DOCS.

case_definitions.definition: Study 1: meets Jager et al. (2020) diagnostic criteria as classified by BMQ-R
case_definitions.quote: About half of the sample (47.5%) fulfilled the diagnostic criteria by Jager et al. (2020) (with 24.6% having severe symptoms) as classified by the BMQ-R.

case_definitions.definition: Study 1: severe misophonia symptoms per BMQ-R (Jager criteria)
case_definitions.quote: (with 24.6% having severe symptoms) as classified by the BMQ-R.

case_definitions.definition: Study 1: S-Five total score of 87 or more (significant misophonia)
case_definitions.quote: According to the S-Five total score cut-off (i.e., total score of 87 or higher; cf. Vitoratou et al., 2022a), more than half of the sample (57.4%) had significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Study 2: S-Five total score of 87 or more (significant misophonia)
case_definitions.quote: Significant misophonia as indicated by the S-Five total cut-off was observed for 58.3% of the sample.

codes.possible_duplicate: Study 1 was part of a larger validation study of the BMQ-R, so its sample likely overlaps with Remmert et al. (2022), the BMQ-R validation paper.
codes.note: Recruitment was mixed and deliberately enriched for misophonia. Sources included groups 'with individuals identifying as having misophonia', and authors say 'we aimed at gathering data mainly from affected individuals'. No unselected subsample is reported. Reviewer to decide I1 vs E1. BMQ-R n may be about 609-616 (Table 4), not 639.

codes.sample: Two online adult samples (18+, English-fluent) from the Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Study, second wave. MS (N=613) was recruited from misophonia support groups, so it is selected. MNS (N=202) came from a general social-media call on the authors' personal and professional accounts. Only the MNS is potentially eligible.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc self-identification item: "Do you identify as having misophonia?" (yes/no/unsure). Also a 35-item trigger intensity list (FITS/TES). The S-Five, MQ and A-MISO-S were administered, but their case counts are not reported here.

case_definitions.quote: In the MNS, 106 (52.5%) individuals stated that they identified as having misophonia, 54 (26.7%) stated that they do not have misophonia, and 42 (20.8%) said they were unsure

codes.possible_duplicate: Same second-wave data as the S-Five validation study (Vitoratou et al. 2021, ref 22). The MNS may also appear in other S-Five or Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Study reports.
codes.note: Borderline on I1. The MNS was a convenience social-media call for a misophonia study, not misophonia groups, but self-selection is likely (52.5% self-identified). Reviewer should check whether this counts as recruitment based on interest. The only case definition is self-identification. The authors call the MNS "pilot data" and say it is not representative.

codes.sample: 62 Polish children aged 7–17, recruited through mass media, social media and a parent database: 32 with misophonia and 30 controls without sound-related issues. This is a case-control design, and no unselected screened pool or screening yield is reported.
codes.instruments: A psychologist with expertise in misophonia assessed children using the Jager et al. (2020) criteria (phone screening, then an in-person interview). Cognitive tests came from the IDS-2.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same pilot sample as Siepsiak, Turek, Michałowska, Gambin & Dragan (2025), "Misophonia in children and adolescents...", Child Psychiatry and Human Development 56:758–771 (text says 'part of it has already been published').
codes.note: The groups were set up by design: children with misophonia were recruited as cases, and the controls were chosen because they had no sound-related issues. The group sizes (32 vs 30) therefore say nothing about prevalence. P.3: "misophonia group (n = 32...) and the control group (n = 30...)". The report gives no count of how many people were screened.

codes.sample: ALSPAC birth cohort (Children of the 90s), Avon, UK. Screened at about age 28 ("Life at 28+" wave, Dec 2020–Feb 2021). Returned data from 4253 adults: 1452 male, 2798 female, 3 sex unknown. General-population cohort, not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Sussex Screener for Misophonia (SSfM): agrees with the misophonia characterization plus a severity rating of disruption to daily life (not at all to very severely).

case_definitions.definition: SSfM: agrees with the misophonia characterization AND rates its disruption to daily life as more than 'not at all'
case_definitions.quote: Our returned data were from 4253 adults... this group contained 333 adults with misophonia (77 male, 256 female) and 3920 without (1375 male, 2542 female, 3 unknown)

case_definitions.definition: Same SSfM definition, females only
case_definitions.quote: 2798 females‐at‐birth ... 333 adults with misophonia (77 male, 256 female)

case_definitions.definition: Same SSfM definition, males only
case_definitions.quote: 1452 males‐at‐birth ... 333 adults with misophonia (77 male, 256 female)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same ALSPAC age-28 SSfM screening as Rinaldi & Simner (ref 11, the screener validation paper) and probably other Simner/Rinaldi ALSPAC misophonia papers. The prevalence data likely overlap; use only one.
codes.note: The paper does not print percentages; all three are calculated from the counts. Table 1 also gives misophonia counts within subsamples that had data at earlier ages (e.g., age 16: 227/2948; age 24: 233/3125), but these are subsets of the same screening. The 4253 total includes 3 people with unknown sex.

codes.sample: 1050 autistic adults (610 female, 427 male, 13 other; aged 16–85, M=46.8) from the Netherlands Autism Register. All had a professional DSM-IV-TR/DSM-5 autism diagnosis. This is a clinical sample recruited for another condition (autism), not for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale-Revised (AMISOS-R); also AQ-28 and SPQ-Short (not misophonia measures)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R ≥21 (>20), moderate or greater symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Total 1050 784 (75%) 266 (25%) ... In total, 25.3% scored >20 on the AMISOS-R.

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R ≥24 (recalculated to compare with Jakubovski)
case_definitions.quote: For Jakobovski, we recalculated prevalences in the current data to scores of 24+ (141 cases)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R ≥21, female subgroup
AMISOS-R ≥21, male subgroup

codes.possible_duplicate: The text is the medRxiv preprint (posted 11 Jan 2026), but the listed venue is J Autism Dev Disord 2026, so the preprint and journal article are probably the same study. The NAR sample may also overlap with other NAR publications (e.g., Weiland et al. 2020, SPQ).
codes.note: The main estimate, 266/1050, is internally consistent. Some Table 1 subgroup cells are not: for ethnicity, the <21 and ≥21 columns look swapped (Dutch 302 vs 513). For no co-occurring diagnosis, 427+94=521, not 512. Check these before using subgroup data. The ≥24 denominator is not stated explicitly.

codes.sample: 119 undergraduate students aged 18-25 at Başkent University, Ankara, Turkey (education, law and dentistry faculties), described as chosen by simple random sampling. 66 women, 53 men. Students with diagnosed psychological or neurological problems or known hearing loss were excluded. Not recruited on the basis of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ), Turkish version 'Mizofoni Ölçeği' (Deniz Sakarya & Cakmak 2022). Clinically significant misophonia = MQ severity scale score ≥7 (0-15). State-Trait Anxiety Inventory.

case_definitions.definition: Clinically significant misophonia: MQ severity scale ≥7 (out of 15), whole sample
case_definitions.quote: Of 119 participants, 25 (21%) were found to have clinically significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Clinically significant misophonia (MQ severity ≥7), women
case_definitions.quote: Kadınlarda mizofonisi olmayan 52 kişi ve mizofonisi olan 14 kişi belirlenmiş

case_definitions.definition: Clinically significant misophonia (MQ severity ≥7), men
case_definitions.quote: Erkeklerde mizofonisi olmayan 42 kişi ve mizofonisi olan 11 kişi belirlenmiş

codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with Deniz Sakarya & Cakmak 2022, the Turkish MQ validation study (Psikoloji Çalışmaları 42(1):231-55). That study had the same first author, the same kind of population ('aynı popülasyonda') and reported 38%. Ethics approval for this study dates from 2018.
codes.note: The cut-off is the standard MQ severity cut-off of ≥7. Table 1 also gives item-level response percentages, e.g. eating sounds rated 'always true' by 31.1%. These are symptom items, not case definitions. Minor inconsistency: in Table 2 the household-size groups (83+37) add up to 120, not 119. Students with psychiatric or neurological diagnoses were excluded, which could lower prevalence.

codes.sample: Ch.2: 20 self-identified misophonic participants plus 20 age/gender-matched controls from UCSD students and the San Diego area. Ch.1 (reprint of Edelstein et al. 2013): misophonic interviewees and controls; the reprint pages (7–17) are blank in the retrieved text. Ch.3: 24 absolute-pitch musicians (not about misophonia).
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S, MAS-1 and MAQ given only to the self-identified misophonic participants. Controls filled in a short demographic form that screened for undiagnosed misophonic symptoms.
codes.possible_duplicate: Chapter 1 is a reprint of Edelstein, Brang, Rouw & Ramachandran (2013), Front Hum Neurosci 7:296. Chapter 2 was being prepared as a manuscript (Edelstein, Monk, Rouw, Ramachandran).
codes.note: Misophonics were recruited as self-identified; controls were recruited as matched controls, not an unselected screened pool. The only count is 0/20 controls with symptoms (p.26: "No control participants were found to experience misophonic symptoms"), which is not a prevalence estimate. Ch.1 reprint pages are missing, but that study also used self-identified misophonics.

codes.sample: 439 university students in Japan (256 male; mean age 19.57, SD 1.35), described as general adults. Recruitment was not based on sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: Japanese version of the Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2013; Japanese version by Tada et al., 2022), 17 items, 5-point scale, with a cut-off of 14 on the 'misophonia symptoms' factor. Also used: Japanese version of the Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ), cut-off 40.

case_definitions.definition: MQ misophonia symptoms factor score above the cut-off of 14
case_definitions.quote: MQ のカットオフ点を超える割合は40%（n=176）であった。

case_definitions.definition: Above both the MQ cut-off (symptoms ≥14) and the HQ cut-off (40), i.e., misophonia plus hyperacusis
case_definitions.quote: いずれのカットオフも超えた割合は7.3%（n=32）であった。

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a conference abstract (JPA 88th convention, 2024, 1D-035-PD). The same student sample (n=439) may also appear in a later full article or thesis by Yamazawa & Midorikawa (Chuo University). It is a different sample from Tada et al. (2022, n=180).
codes.note: The denominator of 439 is assumed to be the whole sample ('全対象者のうち'). The text says 'exceeding' (超える) the cut-off of 14, so it is unclear whether a score of exactly 14 counts as a case. The sex breakdown of cases is not reported; only a t-test is given.

codes.sample: 28 consecutive self-selected adults with bothersome tinnitus who completed an unguided internet CBT program for tinnitus (Oct–Dec 2020); aged 18–75, mean 52; 17 male. Recruited for tinnitus, not for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc single self-report item in the iCBT(T) assessment module: "Do you have misophonia? Misophonia is a strong emotional reaction to certain sounds, such as sounds created by chewing food, swallowing, tapping, breathing, lip smacking, nose sniffing, and other man-made noises."

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported 'yes' to the single ad hoc item 'Do you have misophonia?', which includes a definition
case_definitions.quote: Based on their responses to questions 10 and 11 listed in Table 1 , 12 participants reported experiencing hyperacusis and 5 reported misophonia. All participants who reported misophonia also reported hyperacusis.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: This is a clinical sample recruited for another condition (tinnitus). Misophonia was measured with one self-report yes/no item. The sample is small and includes only people who finished the program, so selection bias is possible. The percentage was derived as 5/28. All 5 people who reported misophonia also reported hyperacusis.

codes.sample: Secondary analysis of Cash (2015) data: VCU undergraduates (N=451) and US community adults recruited through MTurk (N=377), combined N=828, not recruited for misophonia. Online cross-sectional survey.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014): Symptom Scale, Emotions and Behaviors Scale, Severity Scale (cut-off ≥7 stated); misophonia screening items; Hyperacusis Questionnaire; OCI-R; ASI-3; MAI; HADS-A.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same sample as Cash, T. V. (2015), VCU doctoral dissertation, "Decreased sound tolerance (DST): Prevalence, clinical correlates, and development of a DST assessment instrument". That dissertation probably reports misophonia prevalence for this sample.
codes.note: MQ Severity cut-off ≥7 is stated, but only means are given (M=2.94, N=817), plus correlations and regressions. No count meets any cut-off. The Lit Review cites Cash (2015), "503 people that screened positive for misophonia", with no denominator. N=694 passed a general tinnitus/DST/misophonia screen, which is not misophonia-specific. Get Cash 2015.

codes.sample: 150 online adult participants (41 women, 107 men, 2 no answer; mean age 50.02), recruited online. The text gives no sign they were selected for misophonia; the discussion calls them a non-clinical group.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014; Japanese version by Tada et al., 2022); ratings of how unpleasant 6 MQ sounds are; HSP Scale; OCD scale; OCPD items
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified; this is a conference abstract (JPA 88th convention, 2A-054-PI), and a later full article on the same sample may exist.
codes.note: The MQ was given to an unselected online sample, but the abstract reports only correlations (MQ with HSP r=.628, OCD r=.394, OCPD r=.252) and mean unpleasantness ratings by sound source. It gives no MQ cut-off and no number or proportion of participants meeting any misophonia case definition. The full 1-page text was retrieved.

codes.sample: 92 young adults (18–25, UIUC students) recruited for task-based fMRI; 91 analysed (1 excluded for motion). Groups: misophonia only n=29, hyperacusis only n=14, comorbid n=24, controls n=25. They were chosen from a larger online student survey based on MQ/HQ scores suggesting possible misophonia/hyperacusis, plus controls.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ); structured clinical interview based on Lewin et al. (2015) criteria; Khalfa Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ >22 for hyperacusis).
codes.possible_duplicate: Comes from the same online student survey as Brennan et al. (2024), which may report prevalence in the unselected pool. Same participants as Ajmera et al. (2025, resting-state fMRI).
codes.note: Case-control fMRI study. Participants were picked because their survey scores "suggested possible hyperacusis and/or misophonia", and controls were added to the design. The size of the screened pool and the number meeting each criterion are not given; the text points to Brennan et al. (2024). Group counts (e.g., 53/92 diagnosed) reflect the design, not prevalence.

codes.sample: About 1,200 college students at a public US East Coast university (VCU, Spit for Science cohort). They were surveyed as freshmen, and the sound-tolerance questions were asked in follow-up surveys in their sophomore and junior years. This is an unselected student sample.
codes.instruments: A single ad hoc screening item for misophonia: "Compared to other people, are you sensitive to certain sounds made by other people?" There were also single items for tinnitus and hyperacusis, and 4 SCL-90 anxiety items.
codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with other publications that use the VCU Spit for Science sound-tolerance data (Wallace, Vrana and colleagues).
codes.note: This is a poster. The retrieved text has no numbers for the misophonia item (no n or % endorsing it) and no follow-up-wave denominators. Results appear only in figures (e.g., 'Figure 5'), which were not extracted. Check the poster image: if the figures give the n or % endorsing the item, it is eligible; if not, it is I3_no_counts.

codes.sample: N=703 adults online (UK, King's College London): 396 recruited via Prolific (general population) and 307 recruited from misophonia support groups on social media. Results are not split by recruitment source.
codes.instruments: S-Five (5 factors, no cut-off used); self-identification item "Do you identify with having misophonia?" (yes/no/unsure); also ASI-3, BCQ, DPSS-R, GAD-7, LESS-II, PHQ-9.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identifies as having misophonia (answered 'yes'). Mixed sample: Prolific plus misophonia support groups, not split by source
case_definitions.quote: A sample of 703 individuals, 315 of whom identified with having misophonia ... 396 were recruited from the sampling service Prolific, and 307 were recruited from misophonia groups on social media.

codes.possible_duplicate: Part of a wider King's College London misophonia project (Vitoratou, Uglik-Marucha, Gregory). The Prolific general-population subsample may overlap with other Vitoratou et al. S-Five / UK general-population publications.
codes.note: The Prolific subsample (n=396) is unselected, but the paper never says how many of these 396 self-identified with misophonia. The 315/703 figure mixes in 307 people recruited from misophonia support groups, so it can't be used as a prevalence estimate. No S-Five cut-off was applied. The reviewer could ask the authors for counts by recruitment source.

codes.sample: fMRI case-control study with 39 adults: 19 with misophonia (15 F, 4 M, mean age 31) and 20 controls (15 F, 5 M, mean age 29). The misophonia participants were invited from an earlier behavioural sample of 232 individuals with misophonic complaints (Rouw & Erfanian, 2018).
codes.instruments: Misophonia symptoms severity (MSS) questionnaire, 15 items rated 1-5 with the score as the item mean. Interview to check controls for misophonia complaints.
codes.possible_duplicate: The pool the cases came from (N=232 with misophonic complaints) is the sample of Rouw & Erfanian 2018, J Clin Psychol, 'A Large-Scale Study of Misophonia'.
codes.note: Cases came from people already reporting misophonic complaints (p.4: "individuals with misophonic complaints (N=232)") and were invited for high MSS scores. Control recruitment is not described. No unselected screened pool. The 19/39 split is set by the design, so it is not a prevalence estimate.

codes.sample: A representative German general-population sample, aged 16–96, recruited by random route with Kish grid selection (USUMA, March–May 2022). N = 2522 respondents out of 6192 addresses (41.2%); 51.4% female; mean age 49.42. Participants were told only that the study was about psychological health and well-being.
codes.instruments: AMISOS-R (Amsterdam Misophonia Scale-Revised), self-completed. It has a trigger checklist and a 10-item severity total (0–40) with bands: 0–10 subclinical, 11–20 mild, 21–30 moderate to severe, 31–40 severe to extreme. PHQ-4 was also used.

case_definitions.definition: Reports sensitivity to at least one specific misophonic sound (AMISOS-R trigger checklist)
case_definitions.quote: Among those participants who reported at least one specific misophonic sound (33.5%, n = 844)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R 0–10 subthreshold/subclinical, among those reporting triggers
case_definitions.quote: In the total sample of N = 2522 participants, subthreshold symptoms were reported by 21.3% (n = 537)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R 11–20 mild misophonia
case_definitions.quote: mild symptoms were reported by 9.9% (n = 251)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R 21–30 moderate to severe misophonia
case_definitions.quote: moderate to severe symptoms were reported by 2.1% (n = 53)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R 31–40 severe to extreme misophonia
case_definitions.quote: severe to extreme symptoms were reported in 0.1% (n = 3) of participants

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R ≥21, moderate to extreme (clinically relevant)
case_definitions.quote: Moderate to extreme Misophonia(n = 56) ... only a very small rate of participants actually report clinically relevant symptoms (2.3%)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R ≥11, at least mild (derived: 251+53+3)
case_definitions.quote: mild symptoms were reported by 9.9% (n = 251), moderate to severe symptoms were reported by 2.1% (n = 53) and severe to extreme symptoms were reported in 0.1% (n = 3)

codes.possible_duplicate: This is not the same sample as Jakubovski et al. [ref 23], a separate German population survey from Dec 2020–Mar 2021. However, the 2022 Leipzig/USUMA omnibus survey may have been used in other publications, so check for overlapping reports.
codes.note: The severity bands apply only to the 844 who reported triggers (537+251+56 = 844). The 1678 who reported no triggers are not counted in any band, including subthreshold. The abstract gives 33.3% and the results give 33.5% (844/2522 = 33.5%). The text says the Likert scale is '4-point', but it lists five anchors (0–4). There are no page markers, so locations are section and table labels.

codes.sample: Convenience sample of students, faculty and staff at the Institute of Health Sciences, Universidade Federal da Bahia (Brazil). Of 809 emailed, 25% responded, leaving a final n=206. Online Google Forms survey, June–December 2022.
codes.instruments: Lista de Triagem para Misofonia (Misophonia Screening List, 5 items, based on Schröder et al. 2013), translated to Portuguese but not validated. Also HADS and self-reported auditory complaints.

case_definitions.definition: Positive response to at least 3 of the 5 items of the Misophonia Screening List
case_definitions.quote: A presença de misofonia foi definida pela resposta positiva a pelo menos três dos cinco itens... A amostra final foi composta por 206 indivíduos... Misofonia Sim (%) N= 47 Não (%) N= 159

codes.possible_duplicate: Part of the project "Misofonia em estudantes, professores e técnicos em uma universidade pública brasileira" (UFBA). A thesis or other paper from this project by Valente JSP et al. may report the same sample.
codes.note: The paper does not print an overall prevalence; 47/206 is derived from the group sizes in Tables 1 and 2 (47+159=206). The email invitation came from a project with misophonia in its title and only 25% responded, so self-selection is possible, but recruitment was not based on misophonia. The screening list is not validated in Portuguese.

codes.sample: Collection of conference abstracts (ICHM7). The only abstract that may qualify is Goebel et al. (Mini-HQ9), p.10: 216 tinnitus inpatients (47% women, age 49 ± 10), evaluated retrospectively. This is a clinical sample recruited for tinnitus, not for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Structured Tinnitus Interview (STI, Goebel & Hiller), a clinician interview with a combined 'phonophobia/misophonia' category. GÜF, HQ and Mini-HQ9 were also used, but they are hyperacusis measures.

case_definitions.definition: Phonophobia/misophonia category from the Structured Tinnitus Interview, in tinnitus inpatients
case_definitions.location: Page 10, Goebel et al., Material and method
case_definitions.quote: We retrospectively evaluated 216 tinnitus-inpatients (47% women, age 49 ± 10) with the evaluated Structured Tinnitus Interview (STI, Goebel and Hiller, 2002): 60% HC; 15% phonophobia/misophonia; 24.4% without HC.

codes.possible_duplicate: The Goebel et al. tinnitus inpatient data (Schön Klinik Roseneck, Prien) may overlap with the earlier Mini-HQ9 work (2014) or with later full articles by the same group.
codes.note: Tentative. The only count is a combined phonophobia/misophonia interview category (15% of 216), and the case count is not printed. The reviewer should decide whether it counts as a misophonia case definition. Other abstracts fail: misophonia-recruited samples (E1: Banyra, Siepsiak, Öztürk Özdeş, Campbell), correlations only, or hyperacusis only (Sanfins 8.3%).

codes.sample: 207 adults aged 18–65 (74.4% female, mean age 35.7). They enrolled through a link on the Duke Center for Misophonia and Emotion Regulation website, most likely after searching online for misophonia information or seeing misophonia media stories. The text calls them a "community sample" of "adults with misophonia".
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), reported only as means: total 38.6 (SD 13.3), severity scale 7.4 (SD 2.6). Also the SCID-5, the SCID-5-PD, a M.I.N.I. screen and an ad hoc medical history questionnaire.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same Duke Center for Misophonia recruitment as other Duke papers (e.g., Guetta et al., 2022a/b on the Duke Misophonia Interview, and Rosenthal et al., 2021 on the DMQ). The samples may overlap.
codes.note: Recruited "by accessing a link on the Duke Center for Misophonia and Emotion Regulation website" ("searching for information about misophonia"). No unselected screened pool is reported. Also, no misophonia case definition with counts is given (MQ means and correlations only), so I3 would fail too.

codes.sample: 59 patients with multiple sclerosis (2017 McDonald criteria) from an MS outpatient clinic in Ankara, Turkey, who volunteered to answer questionnaires, plus 63 age- and sex-matched healthy controls with no diagnosed neurological disorder. Neither group was recruited because of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Schröder et al. (2013) diagnostic criteria for misophonia, applied after participants were told about misophonia. The authors' own Turkish translation of the A-MISO-S (not validated) was used to rate severity, but only means are reported. BDI and BAI were also given.

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia present per Schröder et al. (2013) diagnostic criteria – MS patients
case_definitions.quote: the frequency of misophonia was significantly higher in the MS group (37.3%) compared to controls (19.4%)... MS (n=59) Misophonia Absent 37 (62.7) Present 22

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia present per Schröder et al. (2013) diagnostic criteria – healthy controls
case_definitions.quote: Control (n=63) ... Misophonia Absent 50 (80.6) ... Present 12

codes.note: Two eligible groups: MS patients (clinical, recruited for another condition) and healthy controls. Control numbers don't add up: the text says n=63, but 50/62 = 80.6%, 12/62 = 19.4% and the total 87/121 = 71.9% all point to 62 assessed. Reviewer should choose the denominator. MS sex counts in Table 1 add up to 63. A-MISO-S bands are defined, but no counts per band.

codes.sample: 400 adults aged 18–65 living in Konya, Türkiye, recruited online by convenience/snowball sampling (62.3% women; 23.3% students; 7.5% audiologists; 6.5% doctor-diagnosed hearing loss). Not recruited for misophonia or sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: Decreased Sound Tolerance Scale-Screening (DSTS-S / ASTÖ-T; Alluşoğlu & Aksoy 2022): misophonia subscale with 14 items scored 0–3 (two factors: 5 items and 9 items). The scale also has hyperacusis (12-item) and phonophobia (5-item) subscales.

case_definitions.definition: DSTS-S misophonia subscale total score ≥4 (author cut-off)
case_definitions.quote: Mizofoni Var 314 78,5 Yok 86 21,5 Toplam 400 100,0 ... Mizofoni ölçeğinden aldığı toplam puan 4 ve üzerinde ise kişinin Mizofonisinin olduğu kabul edilmektedir.

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia Factor 1 (labelled 'Duygusal Yakınmalar', 5 items), cases presumably scoring ≥4; cut-off not stated explicitly
case_definitions.quote: Faktör 1 (Duygusal Yakınmalar) ... Toplam n 231 169 400 % 57,8 42,3 100,0

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia Factor 2 (labelled 'Fonksiyonel/Sosyal Yakınmalar', 9 items), cases presumably scoring ≥4; cut-off not stated explicitly
case_definitions.quote: Faktör 2 (Fonksiyonel/Sosyal Yakınmalar) ... Toplam n 94 306 400 % 23,5 76,5 100,0

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a 2024 master's thesis (Sevde Çevik, KTO Karatay). The thesis compares its results with Alluşoğlu (2020) and Coşkun (2023), which used different samples.
codes.note: Very low cut-off (≥4 out of 42) gives 78.5%, far above Kılıç et al. 2021 (12.8%). Breakdowns by sex, age and other variables are in Tables 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 and 63 (women 208/249; men 106/151). Factor labels look swapped relative to item content. Factor cut-offs are not stated explicitly.

codes.sample: 451 UK adults in an online survey, May–July 2023. 314/451 (69.6%) were University of Surrey students and staff, an eligible unselected subsample. The other 137 (30.4%) were recruited through misophonia, tinnitus and hyperacusis charity groups and social media. 130 completed the 2-week retest.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Impact Questionnaire (MIQ, 8 items, total 0–24). Also the Tinnitus Impact Questionnaire (TIQ) and Hyperacusis Impact Questionnaire (HIQ).
codes.possible_duplicate: Acknowledgments: "This project was based on the data collected for FBK's PhD research at University of Surrey." The PhD thesis or other papers from the same survey may report misophonia prevalence in this sample.
codes.note: MIQ results are given only as means/SDs (e.g., 9.69 (6.38) at test, N=130), factor loadings, ICC and MDC. No cut-off and no number or proportion meeting any misophonia case definition is reported, overall or for the university subsample. The open data on Zenodo might allow cases to be derived, but nothing is reported in the text.

codes.sample: ALSPAC birth cohort (Avon, UK), 'Life at 28+' wave, Dec 2020–Feb 2021. 4253 adults aged about 28 returned data: 1452 male at birth, 2798 female at birth, 3 sex unknown. General-population sample, not recruited because of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Sussex Screener for Misophonia (SSfM), an ad hoc written screener with example triggers, agree/disagree with a description of misophonia, and how much it disrupts daily life. Childhood DAWBA and sMFQ were also used, but only as outcomes.

case_definitions.definition: SSfM: agrees with the misophonia description AND does not choose 'not at all' for disruption to daily life
case_definitions.quote: Our participants with returned data were 4253 adults aged 28 ... this group contained 333 adults with misophonia (77 male and 256 female) and 3920 without misophonia

case_definitions.definition: Same SSfM definition, males only
case_definitions.quote: comprising 1452 males-at-birth ... 333 adults with misophonia (77 male and 256 female)

case_definitions.definition: Same SSfM definition, females only
case_definitions.quote: 2798 female-at-birth ... 333 adults with misophonia (77 male and 256 female)

codes.possible_duplicate: Likely the same ALSPAC Life at 28+ SSfM screening as other Rinaldi & Simner ALSPAC misophonia papers, e.g. the screener validation paper cited as ref [40] and the auditory/sound-sensitivity ALSPAC papers. The counts (333/4253) may be repeated there.
codes.note: Case-control analysis inside an unselected screened cohort, so the screening counts are usable. No percentages are printed; the ones above are my calculations. The severity bands (mild to very severe) are described but not reported as counts. The text has no page markers, so locations are given by section.

codes.sample: 20 self-identified misophonic participants and 20 age- and gender-matched controls (5 M / 15 F each), recruited from UCSD students and the greater San Diego area. This is an experimental case-control study of aversiveness ratings for eating and non-eating sounds.
codes.instruments: Misophonic group only: A-MISO-S, MAS-1, MAQ (means and ranges only). Controls: a short demographic form that asked about prior knowledge of misophonia and possible undiagnosed symptoms (ad hoc, items not described).

case_definitions.definition: Control screening form: control participants found to have misophonic symptoms (ad hoc demographic form)
case_definitions.quote: Control participants filled out a short demographic form that also assessed any prior knowledge of misophonia and sought to determine whether they may suffer from the condition unknowingly. No control participants were found to experience misophonic symptoms.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The same research group published Edelstein et al. 2013 (a different study).
codes.note: Cases were self-identified as misophonic. Controls were recruited as matched controls, not as an unselected pool screened for misophonia; the 0/20 figure comes from checking the controls, and the form's items and criterion are not described. Wu 2014 and Zhou 2017 prevalence figures are only cited. Reviewer may check whether the 0/20 control screening counts.

codes.sample: 74 adult patients (35 women, 39 men, aged 18–72) at a tertiary referral centre for tinnitus, all of whom also reported decreased sound tolerance (DST). Inclusion required both tinnitus and DST, i.e. sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: Patient interview about the types of sounds causing discomfort; VAS item for misophonia ("Are human-produced sounds (e.g., while eating, breathing, chewing, sniffing) unpleasant for you?", 0–100); Hyperacusis Questionnaire; THI; ULL; audiometry.

case_definitions.definition: Predominant misophonia (VAS misophonia score higher than VAS hyperacusis-loudness score)
case_definitions.quote: (2) those with predominant misophonia; ... The first group consisted of 44 subjects (60%), the second group consisted of 5 subjects (7%), and the third group consisted of 24 subjects (33%).

case_definitions.definition: Hyperacusis and misophonia at a similar level on the VAS
case_definitions.quote: (3) those with hyperacusis and misophonia at a similar level. ... the third group consisted of 24 subjects (33%).

case_definitions.definition: Interview: reports that sounds produced by humans (chewing, swallowing, sneezing) cause discomfort
case_definitions.quote: Only two persons reported that sounds produced by humans (chewing, swallowing, sneezing, etc.) caused them discomfort.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Excluded under E1 because the sample was recruited on sound sensitivity: patients needed both tinnitus AND reported DST ("patients with tinnitus ... who had reported problems with decreased sound tolerance"). No unselected pool of tinnitus patients was screened. Reviewer could reconsider if DST-selected tinnitus patients are treated as a clinical tinnitus sample. The VAS groups sum to 73, not 74.

codes.sample: Non-clinical Japanese online survey, N = 552 (152 university students enrolled in a course plus 400 working adults randomly sampled by a research company; 248 M, 303 F, 1 other; age 18–60, mean 35.5). The MQ was given to all 552. The ASMR analyses used a subsample (n = 180).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), translated into Japanese: 7-item Symptom Scale plus 10-item Emotions and Behaviors Scale, scored 0–4. Also used: the ASMR questionnaire (Barratt & Davis, 2015) and the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ).

case_definitions.definition: MQ Symptom Scale score >=14 (mean item score >=2), used as the cut-off suggesting misophonia symptoms; whole sample
case_definitions.location: Page 1 (abstract); cut-off on Page 3; Page 4 says 'over 50%'
case_definitions.quote: We investigated ASMR, misophonia symptoms, and autistic traits in a non-clinical population (N = 552; 18－60 years)... The prevalence of misophonia, previously unknown in Japan, was estimated at 54 %.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Symptom Scale score >=14; university students only
case_definitions.quote: 本研究で分析対象を大学生に限定した場合，音嫌悪症の割合は41.4 % であった。 (Page 2: 大学生152 名と社会人400 名をあわせた合計552 名)

codes.possible_duplicate: Footnote 2 says part of these results was presented at the Acoustical Society of Japan hearing research meeting (2020). That conference report may describe the same sample.
codes.note: Cut-off is on p.3 (Symptom Scale >=14). Case counts aren't printed; derived from %: 0.54x552≈298, 0.414x152≈63. No separate figures for the 400 working adults. Abstract says 54%; p.4 says only 'over 50%'. Table 1 is n=180, but MQ prevalence uses n=552. Cut-off uses only the Symptom Scale, not the full Wu algorithm, so prevalence may be inflated.

codes.sample: 18 autistic and 22 comparison adolescents, recruited through research registries, social media, community groups and personal contacts (July 2022–August 2023). They were not recruited for misophonia. Caregivers also completed proxy questionnaires.
codes.instruments: Self-reported misophonia is mentioned, but the instrument is not named in the main text; details are in Appendix B, which was not retrieved. Other measures: an adapted Adult Hyperfocus Questionnaire, SWAN, SCQ, and sensory and anxiety questionnaires.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same sample as Dwyer, Sillas, Saron et al. (2024), the companion sensory paper ("This study's sample has been described more extensively elsewhere"). That paper may report the misophonia data in more detail.
codes.note: Misophonia comes up only in exploratory correlations ("self-reported hyperfocus was associated with self-reported misophonia", Suppl. Table B.7). The main text gives no count or proportion meeting any misophonia case definition. Appendix B and the supplement were not retrieved, so the reviewer should check them and the companion 2024 paper for cut-off counts.

codes.sample: 106 adult patients with hyperacusis and tinnitus (51 men, 55 women; aged 19-72, mean 45.2) seen at a tertiary referral ENT centre in Poland. They were recruited for hyperacusis/tinnitus, not misophonia. The initial group was 117 hyperacusis patients; analysis was limited to the 106 who also had tinnitus.
codes.instruments: Visual analogue scale for misophonia (0-100): "Are human-produced sounds (e.g., eating, breathing, chewing, sniffing) unpleasant for you?" Also a clinical interview, the HAQ, the Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ), STAI, THI and audiometry/ULL.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The misophonia VAS is reported only as correlations with the HAQ (weak, non-significant); it has no cut-off and no counts. The only count is in Section 3.1: "Three patients reported that sounds produced by humans (chewing, swallowing, sneezing, etc.) caused them discomfort" (3/106). This is a free-report trigger type, not a case definition. A reviewer should decide.

codes.sample: Turkish adults aged 18–65 from the general population who answered "Yes" to "Are environmental sounds disturbing for you?" and passed a hearing screening. N=257 volunteers: 204 study group, 53 control group. The size of the pool that was asked the question is not reported.
codes.instruments: Preliminary form with definitions of DST subclasses (hyperacusis, misophonia, phonophobia), on which participants marked which applied to them; newly developed Decreased Sound Tolerance Scale-Screening (DSTS-S), misophonia section (14 items, cut-off ≥4); Patient Interview Form; GHS-12.

case_definitions.definition: Self-endorsed misophonia definition on preliminary DST form (study group only)
case_definitions.quote: 40.1% of the 204 participants in the study group had hyperacusis, 16.6% had phonophobia, and 81.8% had misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Everyone recruited answered yes to being disturbed by environmental sounds, which is a sound-sensitivity selection. The unselected pool that was asked is not reported. How the 53 controls were defined is unclear. No counts are given for the DSTS-S cut-off of ≥4 (only ROC results). The reviewer may want to check whether the screening question counts as selection.

codes.sample: Case-control study in Italy: 11 adults with misophonia recruited through an online misophonia support group (Misofonia Italia on Facebook), and 44 sex-matched healthy controls recruited through local advertisements. Recruitment ran April 2018 to January 2020.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S, MQ (including the severity scale), Misophonia Activation Scale (MAS-1), MAQ, and a selection interview following Sanchez & da Silva. Other measures: Y-BOCS, HAM-A, HAM-D, STAI, RSA and SCL-90-R.
codes.note: Cases recruited via an online misophonia support group. The 44 controls were a matched comparison group, not a screened pool, and no screening counts are given. Misophonia scores appear only as group means ± SD (Table 2), so I3_no_counts would also apply. The 49% and 52% figures in the Discussion are cited from other studies.

codes.sample: 140 adults aged 18–45 (mean 29.98; 49 female, 91 male). 128 came from Prolific, a general online pool, pre-screened only for age, no hearing loss, no cognitive/psychiatric diagnosis and English fluency; not recruited for misophonia. 12 volunteers came from misophonia newsletters (soQuiet, Misophonia International), so they are a selected group. Online study, UC Berkeley.
codes.instruments: S-Five (25 items, total score 0–250). Cut-off ≥87 for clinically significant misophonia (Vitoratou et al.). The SSSQ, which includes one misophonia item, was also given but no case counts are reported for it.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total ≥87 (clinically significant misophonia), Prolific subsample only (unselected)
case_definitions.quote: Specifically, 18.75% of Prolific participants (N = 24) endorsed significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total ≥87, total mixed sample (includes 12 misophonia-newsletter volunteers; not for pooling)
case_definitions.quote: Based on the recommended cut‐off score of 87 or above on the S‐Five (Vitoratou et al., 2023), 25% of the total sample (N = 35) experienced clinically significant misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: No duplicate is apparent from this text. The study was pre-registered (OSF UCBG4) and may also appear as a thesis by the first author, V. K. Black (UC Berkeley).
codes.note: Use the Prolific subsample (24/128). The total of 35/140 includes 11/12 cases from the selected newsletter volunteers. The 128 are those left after exclusions: 142 Prolific participants completed the MAFT, and people with incomplete data were dropped. The pre-screen excluded psychiatric diagnosis and hearing loss, and required willingness to view distressing images.

codes.sample: Participants (number not stated; probably Augustana College students) did visual and auditory n-back tasks in a computer lab while a confederate made trigger sounds. The text does not say they were recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ), filled in after the tasks and used as a continuous covariate. Skin conductance was also recorded.
codes.possible_duplicate: None found.
codes.note: 2018 poster abstract. The MQ was used only as an ANCOVA covariate and in correlations. No sample size, cut-off or number/proportion of misophonia cases is given. Only the repository abstract page was retrieved, not the poster. If the reviewer can get the poster, they should check it for MQ cut-off counts; if any exist, this would become eligible or unclear.

codes.sample: 319 undergraduate students (176 female, 143 male) at Payame Noor University of Ahvaz, Iran, chosen by multi-stage random sampling (350 approached, 31 incomplete). Mean age 21.45 (SD 3.75). Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Persian Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al. 2014), including the severity item (1–15, where ≥7 means clinically significant). Also Y-BOCS, BAI-II and BDI-II.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified (postdoctoral project of K. Roushani; possibly overlaps with other Persian MQ papers by the same authors).
codes.note: Psychometric validation study. The methods give the MQ severity cut-off (p.4: score of 7 or higher = clinically significant), but the Results report only reliability, CFA and correlations. No number or % meeting the cut-off. Table bodies were not extracted; the titles of Tables 1–5 show only descriptives, reliability, fit indices and correlations. Check Table 1 in the PDF.

codes.sample: 15 volunteers aged 18–65 living in Antalya, Türkiye, analysed in an experiment on trigger-sound source. Inclusion required moderate or high MQ and A-MISO-S scores (80% female, mean age 29.53).
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (Turkish version), Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ, Turkish version), VAS discomfort ratings
codes.possible_duplicate: Based on Pelinsu Müfreze's master's thesis (supervised by Oğuzhan Herdi), Antalya Bilim University. The thesis may report the online screening pool.
codes.note: All analysed participants were selected for misophonia: "having moderate and high scores on the MQ and A-MISO-S" (p.2). The scales were completed online "for subject selection/acceptance", but the paper gives no number screened and no count of people meeting the criteria, so no prevalence can be derived. The thesis may report the screening pool.

codes.sample: US adults aged 18–64 recruited online through Prolific as part of a larger project on social cognition and mental health. 1,269 attempted and 1,175 were analysed (1,041 also did the task). The study description mentioned surveys on "mood, personality, and sensitivity to certain sounds", but participants were not selected for any diagnosis.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), with the Schröder et al. 2013 severity bands (0–4 subclinical, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 severe, 20–24 extreme). Other questionnaires: OCI-R, STAI, LSAS, SDS, EAT, AUDIT, BAPQ, AvPD-IS, ZAN-BPD, AES, SHS, UCLA-LS, ICAR.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S total ≥5 (clinically significant, mild or worse)
case_definitions.quote: 54.9% of participants had clinically significant symptoms (n = 645, total score: 5–24)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S total ≥10 (at least moderate)
case_definitions.quote: only 15.5% of participants had at least moderate symptoms (n = 182, total score: 10–24)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 5–9 (mild)
case_definitions.quote: 463 participants reported mild symptoms (39.4%)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 10–14 (moderate)
case_definitions.quote: 168 participants reported moderate symptoms (14.3%)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 15–19 (severe)
case_definitions.quote: 14 reported severe symptoms (1.2%)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 20–24 (extreme)
case_definitions.quote: 0 reported extreme symptoms (0%)

codes.possible_duplicate: Participants were part of "a larger online project examining social cognition and mental health" at Mount Sinai (Schiller/Gu labs). Other papers from that Prolific project, or a related thesis, may report the same A-MISO-S data.
codes.note: Recruitment was general (Prolific), not based on misophonia. However, the study ad mentioned "sensitivity to certain sounds", so some self-selection is possible. The A-MISO-S bands are consistent: 530+463+168+14=1175. The high/low Miso-OC quartile groups (n=260 each) are based on a combined misophonia–OC factor, not a misophonia-specific definition, so they are not listed as cases.

codes.sample: 19 community adults analysed (20 enrolled, 1 excluded for motion; 14 F, 5 M, mean age 25.6). They were recruited through social media, flyers and study websites as part of a larger longitudinal brain-development study at Ohio State. The authors state they were "not recruited (or excluded) for having particular misophonic triggers".
codes.instruments: Misophonia Activation Scale (MAS-1), Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ-2) and Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), combined into an equally weighted composite score from 0 to 100. OCI-R and DASS-21 were also given.

case_definitions.definition: Composite misophonia score >=20 out of 100 (post hoc cut-off copied from Kumar et al. 2021's group split)
case_definitions.quote: splitting our sample post hoc using a score of 20 as cutoff, resulting in seven individuals with higher misophonia scores (mean = 28.7, range = 20.5–37.3

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 'mild' misophonia band (score above 4; observed range 6–9)
case_definitions.quote: individuals in the "higher misophonia" group all scored above 4 on the A-MISO-S (Mean = 7.7, SD = 1.1, Range = 6–9), corresponding with "mild" misophonia, whereas individuals in the "lower misophonia" group all scored below 4

codes.possible_duplicate: Participants came from a larger ongoing longitudinal study (Saygin lab, Ohio State). They may overlap with other Hansen/Saygin misophonia reports, such as Hansen et al. 2021.
codes.note: Small fMRI study with an unselected sample, so the 7/19 split gives usable counts. Both definitions identify the same 7 people. The text is inconsistent at the A-MISO-S boundary: the lower group is "below 4" but its range is 0–4. Individual scores are in Supplementary Table 1, which was not retrieved.

codes.sample: 491 Portuguese-speaking adults aged 18-69 (80% female), a mixed convenience sample. They were recruited through social media (including the Facebook group 'Misofonia Sindrome' and an OCD group), Reddit, Twitter, mailing lists, contacts, and an online newspaper article about misophonia.
codes.instruments: European Portuguese S-Five (25 items) with the S-Five-T trigger checklist; A-MISO-S; MQ (MSYS, MEBS, MSES); an ad hoc self-identification item ('identified with misophonia'); PHQ-9, GAD-7, ASI-3

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported having misophonia (ad hoc self-identification item); a further 30% were unsure and 23% did not identify
case_definitions.quote: From the final sample, 47% reported having misophonia, 23% did not identify as having misophonia, and 30% were unsure if they had misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: No clear duplicate. This is one of the Vitoratou-group S-Five validation papers (UK, Mandarin, German), which used different samples. The earlier Portuguese interview study [23] (n=44) is a different sample.
codes.note: Recruitment was partly via misophonia channels (a misophonia Facebook group, a newspaper article on misophonia). No subsample from other channels is reported separately, so I1 vs E1 needs reviewer judgement. The only count is self-identification (47% of 491). No S-Five or A-MISO-S cut-off was applied.

codes.sample: Study-1 (Ch. 5): 91 adults (32 M, 55 F, 3 non-binary, 1 transgender; age 18-68), mostly recruited via Prolific as a general-population sample, plus a smaller group from the ASMR subreddit. No one was recruited for misophonia. Study-2: 47 ASMR-sensitive adults (selected for ASMR, not misophonia).
codes.instruments: Ad hoc items. Per-stimulus report (ASMR / misophonia / neither) for 24 auditory stimuli. Background item: 'believed to have previously experienced misophonia'. Novel MDCQ (adapted from MQ, A-MISO-S, MisoQuest, DMQ).
codes.possible_duplicate: The PhD thesis (Niven, UCL 2023) may overlap with a later Niven & Scott article on ASMR/misophonia prevalence and somatic distribution, or with a master's dissertation by the student who co-collected the data.
codes.note: The text stops in the Study-1 methods (~p. 227), before the results. The pages needed are missing: section 5.4.2 prevalence rates (p. 239), Table 2 (pp. 240-241), Table 5 (p. 251) and Study-2 Table 24 (p. 348). The abstract says misophonia was 'highly prevalent' but gives no numbers. The sample is likely eligible because recruitment was not based on misophonia. Retrieve the full text.

codes.sample: 49 community adults (42 female; mean age 27.02) from a larger Duke study on psychopathology and sensory processing. They were recruited through listservs and clinic flyers at an academic outpatient clinic that the authors say specialises in personality disorders. No diagnostic requirement; exclusions were age under 18 and current mania or psychosis.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), total score 0–68; also SCID-I, SCID-II, BDI-II and BAI

case_definitions.definition: High misophonia: MQ total score of 34 or higher (an ad hoc cut-off, meaning an average item score of at least 2)
case_definitions.location: Data Analytic Plan; Results, Self-Report section
case_definitions.quote: Independent samples t-tests indicated a significant difference in BDI and BAI scores between the high (n = 19) and low misophonia groups (n = 30)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same parent sample as McMahon et al. (2019), the larger sensory processing and psychopathology study. Cassiello-Robbins et al. (2020), on neuroticism and emotion regulation, may also use overlapping Duke data.
codes.note: Cut-off wording is inconsistent: 'below 34' = low, 'above 34' = high, but also 'this score, or higher'. The parent study was on sensory processing, but the authors call it a general community sample, not one selected for sound sensitivity. Recruitment at a personality disorder clinic may enrich psychopathology. The 38.8% is derived from 19/49.

codes.sample: 338 adults recruited via Prolific (232 British) and Prolific/social media (106 Finnish), aged 16–87, 218 female. Online survey on aversive musical experiences. Not recruited for misophonia. 16 of 354 excluded for poor data quality.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), 17 items, combined score only (range 17–85). Also AMES, ECS, TIPI, an ASMR item and a music-chills item.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Data are on OSF (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/VRNFA). The text does not mention any other report using this sample.
codes.note: The MQ is reported only as total-score means and SDs (Table 2, p.11: British 40.34 (10.75), Finnish 39.16 (11.81)), plus correlations, regressions and t-tests. The MQ Severity Scale and any cut-off or count of participants with misophonia are not reported. Raw data are on OSF, so a reviewer could derive counts there, but the report itself gives none.

codes.sample: N=263: 213 first-time adult psychiatric outpatients (18-65) at Çukurova University, Adana, Türkiye (2020-2021), plus 50 healthy volunteers (hospital staff and relatives). Nobody was recruited for misophonia. Psychotic disorders and hearing defects were excluded.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Interview Scale (Öz et al.) with the Öz diagnostic criteria, the Sound Disturbance Problems Form and the Misophonia Symptom List (MSL; 50 sounds). SCID-5/CV for psychiatric diagnoses. Also BAI, BDI, BIS and YBOCS.

case_definitions.definition: Disorder-level misophonia (Öz criteria: MSL moderate/very, plus an emotional/physical reaction, plus functional impairment), whole sample
case_definitions.quote: 60.1% (n=158) of the participants did not have any misophonia. 21.3% (n=56) of the participants had disorder-level misophonia, and 18.6% (n=49) had symptom-level misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Symptom-level misophonia (MSL moderate/very to at least 1 sound, without meeting the disorder-level criteria), whole sample
case_definitions.quote: 21.3% (n=56) of the participants had disorder-level misophonia, and 18.6% (n=49) had symptom-level misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Any misophonia (disorder-level plus symptom-level; sound sensitivity consistent with misophonia on the Sound Disturbance Problems Form), whole sample
case_definitions.quote: 39.9% (n=105) stated that they were disturbed by sound in line with misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Disorder-level misophonia, anxiety disorder subgroup (n=121 derived from Table 2: 56+65)
case_definitions.quote: Among the participants with anxiety disorder, 25.6% (n=31) had disorder-level misophonia, and 20.7% (n=25) had symptom-level misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Symptom-level misophonia, anxiety disorder subgroup
case_definitions.quote: Among the participants with anxiety disorder, 25.6% (n=31) had disorder-level misophonia, and 20.7% (n=25) had symptom-level misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Disorder-level / symptom-level misophonia, major depressive disorder subgroup (n=41 derived: 17+24)
case_definitions.quote: 9.8% (n=4) of the individuals diagnosed with major depressive disorder had disorder-level misophonia, and 31.7% (n=13) had symptom-level misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Disorder-level / symptom-level misophonia, OCD subgroup (n=29 derived: 12+17)
case_definitions.quote: 27.6% (n=8) of individuals diagnosed with OCD had disorder-level misophonia, and 13.8% (n=4) had symptom-level misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Disorder-level / symptom-level misophonia, healthy volunteers (n=50)
case_definitions.quote: 16% (n=8) of healthy individuals were diagnosed with disorder-level misophonia, and 2% (n=1) with symptom-level misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: None stated in the text. The study may come from the first author's psychiatry specialty thesis (Çukurova University), so check for a thesis version. It uses the Öz/Kılıç Ankara criteria but is a separate sample.
codes.note: I derived subgroup denominators from Table 2 (misophonia+ plus misophonia−); they match the printed percentages. People reporting hyperacusis (14), tinnitus (12) or phonophobia (4) were counted as non-misophonia. The sample is mostly mixed psychiatric patients. Smaller groups (ADHD, PTSD, tics, etc.) appear only in Table 2, as counts by misophonia status.

codes.sample: 59 adults aged 18–45 recruited from Carnegie Mellon University and the surrounding Pittsburgh area, paid or given course credit; 57 in the final sample. No recruitment criterion based on misophonia is reported.
codes.instruments: Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ), Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ) and S-Five, each scored with its published guidelines to classify participants as misophonic or non-misophonic. LDL audiometry was done only in the misophonic group.

case_definitions.definition: 'Misophonic' = clinical-level symptoms using the scoring guidelines of the DVMSQ, MQ and S-Five combined (exact rule for combining the scales not given)
case_definitions.quote: Our final sample size was 57 participants... Participants (N = 14) in the "misophonic" category reported symptoms that corresponded to clinical presentations of misophonia. Participants (N = 43) in the "non-misophonic" category

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The same lab (Heller, Oszczapinska) has other studies of sound pleasantness and misophonia (e.g., Heller & Smith 2022; Oszczapinska et al. 2024) that may overlap with this sample.
codes.note: Experimental pupillometry study. Recruitment method is not described (e.g., whether adverts targeted sound sensitivity). 14/57 (25%) is high and may mean an enriched sample, so please check. Why 59 dropped to 57 is not explained. The rule for combining the 3 scales is not stated.

codes.sample: Three samples, none recruited for misophonia: (1) Pilot study: 2751 UBC psychology undergraduates recruited via the Human Subject Pool (2028 F, 701 M). (2) Study 1: 650 UBC undergraduates (514 F, 124 M). (3) Study 2: 765 adults from MTurk after attention-check exclusions (244 F, 516 M), ages 18–93.
codes.instruments: An ad hoc yes/no misophonia item (pilot study and Study 2). The Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MpAQ/MAQ; Johnson/Dozier; 21 items scored 0–3), with a sum score of 2 or more counted as non-minimal sensitivity (Studies 1 and 2). Also the MkAQ (misokinesia) and STAI, which are not relevant here.

case_definitions.definition: Pilot: 'yes' to ad hoc misophonia item (strong negative feelings/thoughts/physical reactions to specific or repetitive sounds)
case_definitions.quote: for the misophonia sensitivity question, a total of 1406 students (or 51.1%) responded yes

case_definitions.definition: Pilot: yes to misophonia item, by sex (females / males)
case_definitions.quote: a total of 1118 females (or 55.1%) and 280 males (or 39.9%) responded yes to the misophonia sensitivity question

case_definitions.definition: Study 1: MpAQ sum score >= 2 (non-minimal misophonia sensitivity)
case_definitions.quote: a total of 460 students (or 70.8%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ

case_definitions.definition: Study 1: MpAQ sum >= 2 by sex
case_definitions.quote: a total of 366 females (or 71.2%) and 83 males (or 66.9%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ

case_definitions.definition: Study 2 (MTurk): 'yes' to ad hoc misophonia item
case_definitions.quote: for our misophonia question, a total of 325 participants (or 42.5%) responded yes

case_definitions.definition: Study 2: yes to misophonia item by sex
case_definitions.quote: a total of 120 females (or 49.2%) and 204 males (or 39.5%) responded yes to the misophonia question

case_definitions.definition: Study 2: MpAQ sum >= 2 by sex (total not reported)
case_definitions.quote: a total of 188 females (or 77.1%) and 397 males (or 76.9%) reported a sum score of 2 or more on the MpAQ

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Main focus is misokinesia, but misophonia is measured in unselected samples. The MpAQ ≥2 cut-off is very liberal, and the authors call the pilot item deliberately liberal. Study 2 gives no overall MpAQ ≥2 count, only counts by sex (5 non-binary/trans participants not included). In Study 2 the 'yes' counts by sex add to 324, against a total of 325. No page markers, so locations are section labels.

codes.sample: Phase 2: US adults aged 18–65 recruited via Amazon MTurk and not selected for misophonia. 800 were recruited and 424 passed the data integrity checks (54.5% male, mean age 37.7). Phase 1 had small samples of people with misophonia and their family members (n=10/10/10); these were selected samples and should be excluded.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; severity item ≥7), A-MISO-S (self-report version), MAS-I, MAQ, MCRS, MERS and the new Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ) candidate items.

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity/impairment item ≥7 (clinically significant misophonia; Wu et al., 2014)
case_definitions.location: Results (first paragraph); Convergence With Existing Misophonia Scales
case_definitions.quote: Sixty-seven participants (15.8%) reported "clinically significant symptoms" on the MQ (i.e., ≥ 7 on the impairment subscale

case_definitions.definition: MQ Emotions and Behaviors mean item score ≥2 AND MQ Severity ≥7 (conservative clinical criterion)
case_definitions.quote: modified to include individuals with an average item score ≥ 2 on the MQ Emotions and Behaviors Scale and ≥7 on the MQ Severity Scale (n = 21)

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity above the cut point of 10 (derived: 100% − 98.82% scoring up to that cut point); whether the boundary is ≥10 or >10 is unclear
case_definitions.location: Range for DMQ Impairment Scale Scores
case_definitions.quote: The cut point of 10 on the MQ severity scale ... corresponded with a mean item score of 3.17 on the DMQ Impairment scale (with 98.82% participants scoring up to this cut-point)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same Duke group (Rosenthal, Cassiello-Robbins et al.). Other Duke DMQ or MTurk papers may reuse this sample; check against Cassiello-Robbins et al. 2020/2021.
codes.note: No page markers, so locations are section labels. 84.20% scoring 0–6 on MQ severity matches 357/424. DMQ Symptoms cut-off (mean ≥1.8): number of cases not printed (≈57 derivable from sensitivity 1 / specificity 0.91 vs n=21). Table 3 trigger-frequency item (3.3% bothered >10 times/day) is not a misophonia case definition.

codes.sample: Dutch school pupils aged 8–18 from the general population, recruited through primary and secondary schools as a control group: initial n=256 child reports and n=59 parent reports. There was also a separate clinical sample of 95 youth referred for misophonia, which is selected and not usable for prevalence.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Screening List—Child and Youth, an 11-item final version with child and parent reports (cutoff ≥10 for child report, ≥9 for parent report, set by ROC analysis); AMISOS-Y

case_definitions.definition: Child-report Misophonia Screening List—Child and Youth total score ≥10 (ROC-derived cutoff), in the initial school control group
case_definitions.location: Results, Phase 2: Selection of Final Control Group; Table 1
case_definitions.quote: From the initial control group, 59 participants scored equal to or higher than the cutoff of 10 (indicating possible false negatives). They were therefore removed from further analyses, resulting in the final control group of N = 197 youth.

case_definitions.definition: Parent-report Misophonia Screening List—Child and Youth total score ≥9 (ROC-derived cutoff), in the initial school control group's parents
case_definitions.location: Results, Phase 2: Selection of Final Control Group; Table 1
case_definitions.quote: From the initial control group, 3 parents scored equal to or greater than the cutoff of 9, and were removed from further analyses

codes.possible_duplicate: The clinical sample comes from the RCT described in the trial design paper (ref [38], NL-OMON20775). The school control data may also appear in student theses or other reports by the Amsterdam UMC group.
codes.note: Cutoffs were set by ROC against the clinical sample plus these controls; not percentile-based. Control exclusions (misophonia treatment in past year, IQ<85, cannot read Dutch) may have removed some pupils before n=256, which the text calls 'participants without misophonia'. The 256 and 59 match Table 1's 'Initial control group' columns; 197+59=256; 59-3=56.

codes.sample: 100 online survey respondents (Sweden plus some international Reddit users; 78 women, 19 men). The first ~50 were recruited on purpose from misophonia Facebook/Reddit groups and forums. The rest came from convenience/snowball sharing (private Facebook, group chats, the Umeå department page) to reach people without misophonia.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc self-identification item ("ja, jag har misofoni" / sound oversensitivity / no / don't know). Items from the Wu et al. (2014) Misophonia Questionnaire, reported as means only. NSS-11 noise sensitivity scale.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identified misophonia on the ad hoc item 'ja, jag har misofoni' (pooled sample: purposive misophonia-forum recruits plus convenience sample)
case_definitions.quote: Enkäten besvarades av 100 respondenter. Det var 34 som hade misofoni, 32 som angav att de hade en ljudöverkänslighet, 27 som inte hade någon ljudöverkänslighet, och sju som inte visste

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified (Umeå University bachelor's thesis).
codes.note: About half the sample (the first 50 responses) came from misophonia forums, so 34/100 is not an unselected estimate. The convenience subsample (~50) would be eligible, but its counts are not reported separately (p.15: "Efter att 50 svar samlats in från dessa grupper..."). MQ items are reported only as means. The reviewer may prefer E1.

codes.sample: 200 University of Guilan students (BA/MA/PhD), 2024 (1403), convenience sample from an online survey shared in student WhatsApp/Telegram groups. Age 18–34 (mean 22.47 ± 4.32), 99 female / 101 male. Excluded: psychiatric medication, hospitalisation or trauma in the past 6 months, academic probation. Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), Persian version (Mehrabizadeh Honarmand & Roushani), total score 0–68, alpha 0.72 in this sample. Also BPAQ (aggression) and ASI-R (anxiety sensitivity).
codes.note: Eligible student sample measured with the MQ, but the paper reports only the MQ mean and SD (Table 1, p.5: about 30.25 ± 13.77, read from garbled RTL text), correlations and SEM paths. No cut-off, severity band or case count is given or can be derived. The 59.5% of 42 patients on p.2 is cited from Schröder 2013, not this sample's data.

codes.sample: 2095 undergraduate students at Wilfrid Laurier University (Canada), aged 18–60 (mean 20.34), recruited through the research participation system for course credit; 1,614 female, 436 male, 45 other. Not recruited on the basis of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ) Symptom Severity Composite (clinical cutoff: mean item score ≥1.8 / total ≥41.4). IHS for hyperacusis. DVMSQ and MQ were also administered but not reported here.

case_definitions.definition: DMQ Symptom Severity Composite: mean item score ≥1.8 or total ≥41.4 (clinical misophonia threshold, Rosenthal et al., 2021)
case_definitions.location: Results, 'Misophonia coping composite score' section; Table 3
case_definitions.quote: we analyzed the distribution of individuals who met the clinical cutoff (n = 378) on the DMQ across the social profiles ... Total | 378 | 1717

codes.possible_duplicate: The same survey (Wilfrid Laurier undergraduates; DVMSQ, MQ, DMQ, IHS, AASP, AQ) is probably also used in other papers from the Scheerer lab (e.g., Scheerer et al., 2024a,b,c) and in the 'future manuscripts' the authors mention. Check for overlap with those samples.
codes.note: The 18.0% prevalence is derived (378/2095); it is not printed. Table 3 also breaks clinical cases down by social profile: SA 58/662, GSD 98/361, VED 163/492, VEA 59/580. The DVMSQ and MQ were collected but their results are not reported here, so they may appear in companion papers.

codes.sample: Main study: N=665 adults (Prolific UK-representative general population, Prolific self-declared autistic, Cardiff University students; 231 autistic). Development cohorts N=774, 335, 227; retest N=191 and N=121; CFA N=561; convergent validity N=118 undergraduates (completed DMQ). None recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Cardiff Hypersensitivity Scale (CHYPS) auditory items, including a Misophonia subfactor (4-point frequency items); Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ, 15 trigger items) in the convergent-validity sample (N=118); GSQ; CATI.
codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with Price A. (2023) PhD thesis, Cardiff University (qualitative dataset and CHYPS development), and with Price et al. 2025 Vision Research (CHYPS-Visual).
codes.note: Psychometric/factor-analytic study. The Misophonia factor is reported only as loadings, reliability and correlations; the DMQ only for convergent validity. No cut-off or number/proportion with misophonia in the main text. Tables 1-5 and Supplement S14 (descriptives/quantiles) were not retrieved; a reviewer may want to check them, though quantiles alone give no case counts.

codes.sample: 249 adult completers of an online HMDS validation survey (146 non-completers). Recruited through researchers' networks, Facebook/Reddit groups, "online support groups, and various patient communities", flyers at Umeå University and in the city. The acknowledgements thank "hyperacusis and misophonia support groups". The sample spans more than 15 countries.
codes.instruments: Hyperacusis and Misophonia Discrimination Scale (HMDS; new, 63 items). One self-report status item for each condition (hyperacusis, misophonia, other): 'diagnosed by a professional' / 'not diagnosed, but I believe I have this condition' / 'I do not have this condition'.

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported misophonia only (diagnosed or believed), from the hearing-status item
case_definitions.quote: Self-reported hearing status ... Normal hearing 45 Hyperacusis 48 Misophonia 83 Both conditions 54 Only other auditory conditions 19

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported misophonia plus hyperacusis ('both conditions')
case_definitions.quote: Misophonia 83 Both conditions 54

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. Morales Gutiérrez (2023) is an earlier interview study used to develop the items; it appears to be a different sample.
codes.note: Recruitment targeted misophonia/hyperacusis support groups. Participants from unrelated groups and flyers are not reported as a separate subsample, and there is no unselected screened pool. So the 137/249 self-reported misophonia count reflects recruitment, not prevalence. HMDS has no cut-off. Recruitment was mixed, so the reviewer may prefer 'unclear'.

codes.sample: 278 Turkish-speaking adults aged 18-65 (66 male, 212 female), recruited through an online survey shared on LinkedIn, Instagram, Twitter and WhatsApp, Feb–Apr 2024. This included 29 students from a pilot. Recruitment was not based on misophonia. 78 (28.1%) reported a psychiatric disorder and 20 (7.2%) reported auditory problems.
codes.instruments: Turkish Sussex Misophonia Scale (SMS; Part I, 8 yes/no trigger items; Part II, 39 items scored 0-156), plus a 20-item short form (SMS-SF). Turkish Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ) with its severity scale, and DASS-21.
codes.note: Eligible unselected sample with misophonia measures (SMS, MQ). Only medians (SMS 25; MQ 31.5), reliability, factor analysis and correlations are reported. Methods describe the MQ severity cut-off for clinically significant misophonia, but the number meeting it is never reported. There are no Part I trigger counts either, so no cases or denominator can be derived.

codes.sample: Nationwide Indian survey (community outreach, social media, tertiary audiology centres): 10,980 identified, 480 excluded, 10,500 analysed. 10,000 normal-hearing adults (6,073 M, 3,927 F; age 39.3±4.7) and 500 adults with self-reported tinnitus (365 M, 135 F; age 42.6±6.9). Ages 18–50.
codes.instruments: Study-made general questionnaire (9 items: misophonia/tinnitus symptoms, used for screening); A-MISO-S and S-Five given to those who screened positive; THI and TCHSQ for tinnitus.

case_definitions.definition: Met criteria for misophonia (screening questionnaire; exact criteria not stated), normal-hearing group
case_definitions.quote: Among individuals with normal hearing, 26% (2,615 of 10,000) met the criteria for misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Comorbid misophonia in tinnitus group (same criteria)
case_definitions.quote: Within the tinnitus group, 17% (85 of 500) showed comorbid misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Severity bands among normal-hearing cases (mild/moderate/severe); counts must be derived from % of 2,615
case_definitions.quote: in the normal-hearing group, 66% of affected individuals reported mild symptoms, 24% moderate, and 10% severe.

case_definitions.definition: Severity bands among tinnitus participants with misophonia
case_definitions.quote: among tinnitus patients with misophonia, 33% had severe, 44% moderate, and 23% mild symptoms.

codes.possible_duplicate: Same research group (Prabhu, AIISH/Mysore) as Valsa et al. 2025 (adults in India), Aryal & Prabhu 2022, Patel et al. 2023 and Sujeeth et al. 2024. Overlap is not stated, but should be checked, especially with Valsa et al. 2025.
codes.note: Numbers don't add up; please check. 'Criteria' not defined. Only 200 cases had A-MISO-S data, so how severity was graded for 2,615 is unclear. Tinnitus without misophonia n=74, but 500-85=415. Mean age 39.3 overall but 24.8 in subgroups. Another 437/10,000 had subclinical sound sensitivity.

codes.sample: Oklahoma dataset: 777 university adults (from 1009 who consented, after exclusions), recruited from the Psychology department research pool and the general university population by mass email; data "collected for other purposes". Mean age 19.4, 74.6% female. Also the WAND general-population neuroimaging sample (N=162; 153 after QC), where misophonia was not measured directly.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al. 2014): total score (Symptoms + Emotions/Behaviors, 0–68) and the Severity Scale (0–15). Only in the WAND sample, MQ total was predicted from AASP items by a regression model; the AASP is not a misophonia-specific instrument.

case_definitions.definition: MQ total score above the cutoff of 30 (Möllmann et al. 2023), Oklahoma sample
case_definitions.quote: Participants ranged in their total MQ scores between zero and 63 (mean = 24.4), with 240 (31%) scoring above the cutoff of 30.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Severity Scale ≥7 ('clinical' misophonia), Oklahoma sample; 776 answered the severity item
case_definitions.quote: 99.9% (N = 776) responding to the single severity item... Self‐reported severity ranged from zero to 15 (mean = 4.4), with 147 (19%) falling above the cutoff of 7

case_definitions.definition: WAND sample: AASP-predicted MQ total above 30 (proxy, not a direct misophonia measure; reviewer to decide whether to include)
case_definitions.location: Results, Application of Model to WAND
case_definitions.quote: participants ranged in their predicted MQ scores between 8.9 and 45.1 (mean = 24.2), with 31 (19%) scoring above the cutoff of 30

codes.possible_duplicate: The Oklahoma dataset (University of Oklahoma, IRB#16450, N=777 students) was "collected for other purposes" and may overlap with other Oklahoma misophonia survey papers (e.g., Hansen et al.). Check before pooling.
codes.note: The eligible sample is Oklahoma: students not recruited for misophonia. The text does not say if recruitment mentioned misophonia. WAND figures (31/162 predicted ≥30; 29/153 'patients' after QC) come from AASP-based predictions, not a misophonia-specific measure, so likely not prevalence data. Severity item denominator is 776 because one person skipped it.
