codes.sample: 213 adults aged 18-62 (mean 25.7, 70.9% female), recruited online via Facebook, Instagram, Reddit and LinkedIn, Nov 2020 to Feb 2021. They were not recruited for misophonia, and the authors call them "nonclinical individuals" (p.10).
codes.instruments: New York Misophonia Scale (NYMS): emotional distress and behavioral reactions subscales, plus a total score from 0 to 164. Also used: ASI-3 (anxiety sensitivity) and DS-R (disgust).
codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with Barahmand U, Stalias-Mantzikos ME, Rotlevi E, Xiang Y. "Disgust and emotion dysregulation in misophonia" (Int J Ment Health Addict 2021; ref 53). It has the same authors, also uses the NYMS, and may share the same data collection.
codes.note: Misophonia was measured with the NYMS in an eligible non-clinical online sample (I1 and I2 met). However, the report gives only means, SDs, correlations and mediation results (Tables 2-4; e.g., NYMS total mean 59.20, SD 24.38). No cut-off, severity band or number/proportion of cases is reported or can be derived. The 20%/6% figures on p.1 are cited background prevalence, not data from this study.

codes.sample: 492 US adults recruited online (CloudResearch, Prolific, SPARK) by autism/ADHD status, not misophonia: 99 comparison (non-autistic, non-ADHD), 122 ADHD-only, 130 autistic-only, 141 autistic + ADHD.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc self-report item asking about current misophonia (self-identified or formally diagnosed) after a misophonia definition was shown; MIST-A Misophonia subscale T-scores (>60 elevated, >70 severe; no counts in main text); Core Discriminant Sounds (CDS-M) sound-rating task.

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported current misophonia (self-identified or diagnosed) after reading a definition: comparison group
case_definitions.quote: 17 misophonia (17.17%)

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported current misophonia after reading a definition: ADHD-only group
case_definitions.quote: 49 misophonia (40.16%)

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported current misophonia after reading a definition: autistic-only group
case_definitions.quote: 76 misophonia (58.46%)

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported current misophonia after reading a definition: autistic + ADHD group
case_definitions.quote: 98 misophonia (69.50%)

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported current misophonia, whole sample (derived by summing the four groups)
case_definitions.quote: This left a final sample of 492 participants (Table 1): 99 comparison ... 122 ADHD-only ... 130 autistic-only ... and 141 autistic + ADHD

codes.possible_duplicate: Same sample as Dwyer et al. (2024), which reports hyper-focus data ("The study sample and recruitment procedures have been described in more detail by Dwyer et al. (2024)").
codes.note: Recruited by autism/ADHD status (meets I1). Misophonia asked as a current self-identified/diagnosed condition, with a definition given (Table 1 note c). Counts printed per group; the total 240/492 is my own sum. MIST-A T>60/>70 cut-offs are described, but the main text gives no counts (Supplemental Appendix A may). Comparison group excluded people with autistic/ADHD relatives.

codes.sample: Case-control study of extended high-frequency audiometry in India. Participants came from a preliminary screening of 283 adults; 36 screened positive and 15 of them took part, plus 15 controls aged 18–54. The paper does not say how the 283 were recruited, and it does not say that recruitment was based on misophonia.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S, called the 'revised' scale in the paper), administered by a clinician, total score 0–28, given in English

case_definitions.definition: Identified as having misophonia on A-MISO-S screening. Stated grouping rule: an A-MISO-S score of 1–24 placed a participant in the misophonia group.
case_definitions.quote: A preliminary screening was done on 283 adults out of which 36 were identified to have misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: The study is part of the first author's doctoral thesis (Chalotra, Sumandeep Vidyapeeth). The same screening pool of 283 may appear in the thesis or in other papers by Chalotra et al. on misophonia.
codes.note: Odd cut-off: 'score 1–24' conflicts with the subclinical band of 0–4, and some cases in Table 1 score 2, so how the 36 were defined is unclear. No description of how the 283 were recruited or of the screening setting. Prevalence was derived by the reviewer and needs checking.

codes.sample: Cross-sectional survey (2013) of 1st- and 2nd-year medical students, Faculty of Medicine (Serbia, per funding statement); 1132 of ~1200 returned complete questionnaires (94%); 409 men, 723 women; age 21.4 ± 2.1. Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: 5 yes/no symptom items adapted from the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), with no intensity rating; nine proposed symptom-count criteria for 'high perceived misophonia'. Also Weinstein Noise Sensitivity Scale and Hamilton anxiety and depression scales.

case_definitions.definition: Criterion 9 (authors' proposed): at least 4 of 5 A-MISO-S-adapted symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Criterion 9 | At least four or more symptoms reported | 40 (9.8) | 62 (8.6) | 102 (9.0)

case_definitions.definition: Criterion 5: all 5 symptoms reported
case_definitions.quote: Criterion 5 | All five misophonia symptoms reported | 12 (2.9) | 19 (2.6) | 31 (2.7)

case_definitions.definition: Criterion 8: at least 3 of 5 symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Criterion 8 | At least three or more symptoms reported | 92 (22.5) | 156 (21.6) | 248 (21.9)

case_definitions.definition: Criterion 7: at least 2 of 5 symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Criterion 7 | At least two or more symptoms reported | 140 (34.2) | 248 (34.3) | 388 (34.3)

case_definitions.definition: Criterion 6: at least 1 of 5 symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Criterion 6 | At least one or more symptoms reported | 162 (39.6) | 313 (43.3) | 575 (50.8)

codes.possible_duplicate: Methods say the same 2013 medical-student survey was "described previously in detail" in ref. [15], an earlier publication on noise sensitivity, anxiety, depression and handedness in the same sample. Check whether that report also gave misophonia counts.
codes.note: Criterion 6 row in Table 4 is inconsistent: men/women (162/313) are copied from Symptom 1, but total 575 = 1132−557 and fits the other criteria (men should be 207). Table 2 gives single-symptom counts (e.g., Symptom 3: 115/1132, 10.2%). Items are yes/no only, not full A-MISO-S severity scoring; cut-offs not validated.

codes.sample: 342 adults aged 16 and over (224 women, 118 men) who regularly attended a medical psychology centre in Barcelona, Spain, in Sep–Dec 2019. 325 of them remained in Mar–Jun 2020. 98% were admitted for other psychological or psychosomatic problems; 2% came to be treated for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), cut-off >=5 for a misophonia diagnosis (M+). Other measures: LSB-50 symptom list (M+ group only) and the centre's 2RC consultation record.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S score >=5 (M+), whole sample, reference quarter Sep–Dec 2019
A-MISO-S >=5, women, Sep–Dec 2019
A-MISO-S >=5, men, Sep–Dec 2019
A-MISO-S >=5, participants remaining Mar–Jun 2020
case_definitions.location: Results, Phase II section; Table 1 Mar–Jun 2020
case_definitions.quote: the diagnosis was positive in 114 of the 325 participants (35% of the patients) and was similar for women (37%) than for men (31%)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S >=5, women, Mar–Jun 2020
A-MISO-S >=5, men, Mar–Jun 2020

codes.possible_duplicate: The 325 participants in 2020 are a subset of the 342 assessed in 2019, so the two prevalence figures overlap. I found no other publication from the same authors or centre described in this text.
codes.note: Clinical sample at a psychology centre, mostly attending for other conditions. 2% came for misophonia and the centre runs a misophonia programme, so prevalence may be inflated. The two periods overlap; prefer the baseline 119/342. A-MISO-S was given in a diagnostic battery before Aug 2019. The 'Making requests' row (M+ 111) does not match 119.

codes.sample: 119 adults aged 18–70 (mean 44.8 years; 79.0% female). All self-identified as having misophonia and were recruited through a BBC radio interview on misophonia into a participant pool used in earlier work (Andermane et al. 2023a). Participants with known hearing loss were excluded.
codes.instruments: Sussex Misophonia Scale (SMS; 48 triggers plus 39 Likert items, cut-off >50.5); a single-item hyperacusis screener (Fackrell scoping definition); the Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ; Khalfa 2002); and selected CORDS hyperacusis items (Williams et al. 2021).
codes.possible_duplicate: The sample was drawn from the participant pool in Andermane et al. 2023a (J Clin Psychol, symptom network model of misophonia) and is related to Andermane et al. 2023b (iScience).
codes.note: Every participant self-identified as misophonic ("All had self-identified as having misophonia"; recruited via a BBC radio interview on misophonia). No unselected screened pool is reported. The only counts given are hyperacusis prevalence within this misophonic sample (HQ >28: 36/119; >26: 47/119; screener: 66/119). The SMS cut-off of >50.5 is mentioned, but no count meeting it is reported.

codes.sample: 277 students (nursing, midwifery, EMS) at the Faculty of Nursing and Midwifery, Hamadan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, 2024. Proportional stratified random sampling from about 850 students; not recruited for misophonia. 48% male; mean age 22.95.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), Persian version (Mehrabizadeh Honarmand & Roushani, 2019), 17 items, with symptoms and emotions/behaviors subscales. Also the Internet Addiction Test (Young, 1998).
codes.note: The sample is eligible and misophonia was measured with the MQ. Misophonia results are only means/SDs (total 26.00 ± 12.59; subscales 12.22 ± 6.03, 13.77 ± 7.76), group comparisons (Table 3) and correlations (Table 4). No cut-off, severity band or case count. Counts are given only for internet addiction (25.6% at risk). Table 3 is abridged (full table on request).

codes.sample: Not determinable from the retrieved text. Only the front matter was retrieved: title pages, committee list and table of contents. The thesis is about youth with misophonia, apparently recruited through the Amsterdam UMC misophonia clinic or the RCT.
codes.instruments: Per table of contents: Misophonia Screening List - Child and Youth; AMISOS-Y (Dutch child- and parent-report versions). No details are in the retrieved text.
codes.possible_duplicate: PhD thesis (Rappoldt 2025) compiling: the RCT protocol (Contemp Clin Trials Commun 2023); the AMISOS-Y validation (Child Psychiatry Hum Dev 2024); and submitted papers on clinical characteristics, the RCT and cost of illness. Samples probably overlap.
codes.note: Only pages 1-8 (front matter, table of contents) were retrieved; no methods or results. The chapters suggest misophonia-selected samples (clinic, RCT, families), so likely E1. But Chapter 4 (validation) may include an unselected or control sample with counts above a cut-off. Full text of Chapters 3-4 is needed.

codes.sample: 283 adults aged 18–60 (193 female, 76 male, 14 non-binary), an internationally diverse sample recruited from online social media platforms and survey recruitment sites between November 2021 and January 2022. Eligibility: healthy adult aged 18–65 and proficient in English. The text does not say recruitment was based on misophonia; the authors call it a non-clinical sample.
codes.instruments: New York Misophonia Scale (NYMS; Part 1: 25 trigger items, scored 0–100; Part 2: 13 behavioural-reaction items, scored 0–42), State Mental Contamination Scale, Three-Domain Disgust Scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same authors and recruitment period as Stalias-Mantzikos et al., 'Early Maladaptive Schemas in Misophonia' (Clinical Psychologist); may be the same sample. Related: Barahmand et al. NYMS validation (J Psychiatr Pract 2023).
codes.note: Misophonia was measured with the NYMS in a sample not recruited for misophonia, but results are reported only as correlations (Table 2) and mediation estimates (Table 3). The report applies no NYMS cut-off and gives no number or proportion of participants with misophonia. The Limitations section says 'not every participant may be reflective of actually being misophonic', but gives no count.

codes.sample: 49 adults in Québec City, recruited mostly through a Université Laval research-participant mailing list and word of mouth; 3 came from a hyperacusis clinic (IRDPQ). After testing, participants were labelled as hyperacusis (n=20) or controls (n=29). Recruitment was not based on misophonia.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc screening question: "Generally, are you bothered/disgusted by specific sounds?" plus "If yes, which ones". Potential misophonia if the sounds named are known triggers (chewing, sniffing, repetitive sounds). Also used: HQ, WNSS, LDL, CDS tablet test.

case_definitions.definition: Potential misophonia: reports being bothered/disgusted by specific sounds, and the sounds named are known misophonia triggers (whole sample)
case_definitions.quote: Misophonia trigger sounds self- reported as annoying # (Y/ N) 10/8 10/15 ... # Missing values for the hyperacusis (n = 2) and control group (n = 4)

case_definitions.definition: Same screening definition, hyperacusis subgroup
case_definitions.quote: Misophonia trigger sounds self- reported as annoying # (Y/ N) 10/8

case_definitions.definition: Same screening definition, control subgroup
case_definitions.quote: Misophonia trigger sounds self- reported as annoying # (Y/ N) ... 10/15

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a new Québec sample; the earlier Enzler et al. 2021 studies are cited for comparison only.
codes.note: Hyperacusis case-control study, but groups were assigned after testing the whole pool of 49. Misophonia came from one crude ad hoc question ("potential misophonia"; no formal diagnoses). Percentages are derived and exclude 6 people with missing data. Reviewer should check whether the ads targeted people with sound sensitivity.

codes.sample: 123 adult regular patients of a medical psychology centre in Barcelona (78 women, 45 men; ages 18–87). Most came for depression, anxiety or other problems, and 2 came for misophonia. Of these, 82 with A-MISO-S-positive misophonia, plus their close relatives, entered a pre-post intervention study (Sept 2019–Mar 2020).
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), with the authors' own levels: 0 = 0-4 (none), 1 = 5-9 (mild), 2 = 10-14 (moderate), 3 = 15-19 (severe), 4 = 20-24 (extreme). Clinical anamnesis interview. Lexicometric associative-cards method.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S >=5 at pre-intervention (levels 1-4); derived from Table 1 Phase 1 bands
A-MISO-S >=5 at post-intervention (7 months later); Table 1 Phase 3 bands
case_definitions.quote: Level 0 (absence M+, 0-4) 41 [33.33] ... Level 1 (mild M+, 5-9) 5 [4.06] ... Level 2 37 [30.08] ... Level 3 31 [25.20] ... Level 4 9 [7.31]; forty-one (33.33%) of them ... were excluded because their diagnosis of misophonia was negative

codes.possible_duplicate: Same author, centre and clinic population as Ferrer-Torres & Giménez-Llort 2021a/2021b (Front Psychiatry). This preprint may also have been published later as a journal article.
codes.note: Borderline E1. The 123 were "people with clinical anamnesis suspicious of misophonia", picked by the clinician; the full clinic pool is not reported. The Methods call them regular patients, so please check. Counts conflict: Phase 1 bands give 52 negative but the text says 41 were excluded; Phase 3 bands total 123 though only 82 were retested; 11 of the 82 were negative at baseline.

codes.sample: 49 community adults, a transdiagnostic sample from a parent study on sensory processing dysfunction and mental health. They were recruited through online and newspaper postings and mental health provider referrals for a research program on emotion regulation, not for misophonia. 85.7% were female; mean age was 27.02. Setting: Duke University Medical Center, USA.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; symptom, emotions/behaviours and severity subscales); DERS; NEO-PI-3 Neuroticism; SCID-I
codes.possible_duplicate: Same parent sample as McMahon et al. (ref. 27), a study of self-reported sensory processing dysfunction and mental health problems in adults at Duke University.
codes.note: The sample was not selected for misophonia, and the MQ was used. Only MQ means and SDs are reported (impairment subscale M = 5.21, 'mild sound sensitivity, on average'), plus correlations and mediation results. No number or proportion meeting an MQ cut-off is given or can be derived. Table 1's MQ total score (97.35) seems to repeat the DERS value.

codes.sample: 322 undergraduate students from different courses at IFG, campus Goiânia (Brazil). Cross-sectional online survey (Google Forms). The text gives no sign that recruitment was based on misophonia.
codes.instruments: Self-declaration item on misophonia (answer options include yes / 'não sei' (don't know) / no); MisoQuest (scores 14–70, cut-off ≥61, Siepsiak et al. 2020).

case_definitions.definition: Self-declared misophonia (ad hoc self-identification item)
case_definitions.quote: Foram recrutados 322 estudantes, dos quais 56,5% se autodeclararam misofônicos.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest score ≥61 among students who self-declared misophonia
case_definitions.quote: 8,2% dos que se autodeclaram misofônicos tiveram diagnóstico confirmado pelo Misoquest... considera o score >= a 61 para o diagnóstico de misofonia

codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with any other report or thesis from the same IFG Goiânia PIVIC project (Cunha & Silva).
codes.note: Short conference abstract; Figure 1 (histograms) is not in the text. No raw counts printed. The self-declared share appears as both 56.5% and 56.8%. 99.7% of 'não sei'/'não' respondents scored <61, so a few may have scored ≥61. The overall MisoQuest prevalence out of 322 can't be worked out exactly. Check counts or contact the authors.

codes.sample: Children aged 6-15 (N = 171) and adults aged 18+ (N = 200), apparently not recruited for misophonia (UNLV Music Lab study; recruitment source not stated).
codes.instruments: Behavioural task: participants watched a 'Misophonia Video' and pressed the spacebar to show an emotional reaction ('# of times they pressed the spacebar while watching videos to indicate emotional reaction'). No misophonia questionnaire or interview is reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly linked to other UNLV Music Lab (Hannon, Mednicoff) misophonia/ASMR/frisson reports funded by the REAM Foundation.
codes.note: Undergraduate poster. Only correlations and trends are reported (misophonia rises with age, correlates with music training). No number or proportion meeting a misophonia case definition. Results figures may be missing, but the only measure is spacebar presses. E2 could also apply: no misophonia questionnaire, interview or diagnostic criteria.

codes.sample: Online sample of 140 adults aged 18-45 (49 F, 91 M; mean age 29.98). 128 came from Prolific, a general crowdsourcing pool screened for no hearing loss, no cognitive impairment and no self-reported current psychiatric diagnosis. The other 12 were volunteers from misophonia newsletters (soQuiet, Misophonia International). Only the Prolific subsample is unselected.
codes.instruments: S-Five (Selective Sound Sensitivity Syndrome Scale; cut-off ≥87 = clinically significant misophonia). SSSQ (6 items, includes 1 misophonia item; used only as a hyperacusis covariate, no misophonia counts given). Also DFlex, PTQ, RRS-B, ARS, SAD-T and the MAFT task.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total ≥87 (clinically significant misophonia), Prolific (unselected) subsample
case_definitions.quote: Specifically, 18.75% of Prolific participants (N = 24) endorsed significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total ≥87, total mixed sample (includes 12 misophonia-newsletter volunteers; not an unselected sample)
case_definitions.quote: Based on the recommended cut-off score of 87 or above on the S-Five (Vitoratou et al., 2023), 25% of the total sample (N = 35) experienced clinically significant misophonia

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total ≥87, newsletter volunteers (selected sample, recruited via misophonia communities)
case_definitions.quote: Out of the volunteers identified from misophonia-related newsletters, 91.67% (N = 11) endorsed significant misophonia

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a bioRxiv preprint (January 2025), so a later peer-reviewed journal version of the same sample may exist.
codes.note: Use the Prolific subsample: 24/128 (18.75%), S-Five ≥87. The 128 is my count (140 minus 12 volunteers, p.6). Do not use 35/140, which mixes in misophonia-selected volunteers. Prolific participants were 18-45 and excluded hearing loss and self-reported psychiatric diagnosis, which may bias the estimate.

codes.sample: 686 undergraduate instructors from six Florida state universities who completed an emailed Qualtrics survey (9,029 invited; 1,300 consented; 788 eligible).
codes.instruments: An ad hoc survey of instructors' awareness and attitudes: a yes/no item on knowing what misophonia is, an item on whether a student had disclosed misophonia, and 10 Likert items on willingness to provide accommodations. It does not assess the participants' own misophonia symptoms.
codes.note: This is an awareness/attitude survey. Misophonia was never measured in the participants themselves. The reported 18.4% (knew the definition) and 2.3% (17 instructors who had a student disclose misophonia) are not prevalence figures. The prevalence numbers in the text are cited from Wu et al. 2014 and Zhou et al. 2017. Could also be coded E2_no_misophonia_measure.

codes.sample: Preliminary sample of autistic (n=13 in Ch.1, 14 in Ch.2) and typically-developing comparison (n=17) adolescents aged 11–16, recruited from the community and research registries (UC Davis). They were not recruited for misophonia. DVMSQ data were available from 13 autistic and 16 comparison participants.
codes.instruments: Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ, self-report, slightly revised); MIST-A misophonia (anger/aggression) subscale; Core Discriminant Sounds psychoacoustic task (CDSMiso); plus BBCSS, SEQ-3.0, VADQ, LDLs.

case_definitions.definition: Meeting DVMSQ misophonia criteria (Williams et al. 2022, Table 2); derived count in comparison (non-autistic) group only: 16 with DVMSQ minus 15 not meeting = 1
case_definitions.quote: extracted in non-autistic participants not meeting the DVMSQ misophonia criteria as described in Table 2 of Williams et al. (2022); n=15. ... DVMSQ scores were available from 13 autistic and 16 comparison participants.

codes.possible_duplicate: PhD dissertation (Dwyer, UC Davis 2023) reporting preliminary data from an ongoing study. Later articles by Dwyer, Williams, Rivera et al. on autistic adolescents' auditory experiences may use the same or an expanded sample.
codes.note: The DVMSQ count is not stated directly. It is worked out as 16 comparison participants with DVMSQ data minus n=15 not meeting the criteria. The text is inconsistent: comparison CDS n is 17 in the text but 16 in Table 1.3. The autistic-group count is not reported. Supplementary Appendix A was not retrieved. The I3 evidence is borderline, so the reviewer should check the derivation.

codes.sample: Population-based household sample from Ankara city centre, Turkey (2015): residents aged >15 years in 300 randomly selected households (bus-stop sampling frame); final N = 541 (314 female, 227 male; mean age 43.5, range 15–88). Assessed face to face (15 by telephone) by trained interviewers.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Interview Schedule (MIS), a semi-structured interview developed for this study. It includes the Misophonia Checklist (MCL; 50 sounds + 'any others?', each rated 0–3) and items for the authors' proposed diagnostic criteria (trigger, intense emotion, coping strategies, interference).

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia diagnosis by the proposed criteria (≥1 MCL sound moderate/high + high anger/disgust/distress + ≥1 coping strategy often/always + ≥1 interference item yes)
case_definitions.location: Correlates of misophonia section; Table 1; Abstract
case_definitions.quote: Based on the proposed diagnostic criteria, the prevalence of misophonia in the study population (N = 541) was 12.8% (n = 69).

case_definitions.definition: At least one MCL misophonic sound rated as causing moderate or high distress (trigger criterion only)
case_definitions.quote: In all, 427 (78.9%) participants scored one or more MCL item as moderate or high.

codes.possible_duplicate: The MIS was developed by co-author G.O. for this study, so a related thesis or conference abstract by the same Hacettepe University group may report the same Ankara 2015 household sample. Check this.
codes.note: This is a representative general-population sample with an interview-based diagnosis, and the full text was available. Table 1 also gives a breakdown by age group (e.g., ages 15–24: 21/106 had misophonia). The primary estimate is 69/541. The 427/541 figure meets only the trigger criterion and is not a full diagnosis.

codes.sample: Adult OCD outpatients (18-50 y) at Sisli Hamidiye Etfal psychiatry clinic, Istanbul. They were assigned to groups with vs without misophonia using quotas (45 planned per group). 77 were analysed: 39 OCD+misophonia, 38 OCD only. 18 were excluded after assignment (6 depression, 12 incomplete tests).
codes.instruments: Clinical interview using Schröder et al. (2013) misophonia diagnostic criteria. No misophonia scale was used.

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia diagnosed with Schröder et al. 2013 criteria in OCD patients (quota-filled groups; not a prevalence estimate)
case_definitions.quote: A total of 77 patients (39 with OCD and misophonia, and 38 with OCD without misophonia) were included in the study.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Case-control design with quota sampling: "Once the planned number of patients was reached for one group, no further patients were included in that group". The number of OCD patients screened is not reported, so 39/77 reflects the quotas, not prevalence. Case-control studies count only with a reported screened pool. A reviewer might code this as E1 or I3.

codes.sample: University of Oklahoma students from the psychology research pool. They took an online survey, then attended in-person audiology and EEG sessions. 67 completed everything; the final analysed pool was 54 with valid EEG (mean age 18.96, 89% female). Participants reporting misophonia were given matched controls (case-control design).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014). Misophonia Severity Scale scores of 7 or more (on a 1–15 scale) defined the misophonia group. Participants were also asked about misophonia during the audiology workup.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Misophonia Severity Scale >=7 (clinically significant), in the in-person case-control sample
case_definitions.quote: Participants who had indicated experiencing misophonia had matched controls; 32% of the final participant pool had indicated experiencing misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: Part of a larger OU multisite project (Spectrum Characteristics Survey; Ethridge/Kimball lab). The survey sample may overlap with Norris et al. (2022), Frontiers in Neuroscience, 'Toward a Multidimensional Understanding of Misophonia Using Cluster-Based Phenotyping'.
codes.note: Not eligible: the sample was built as misophonia cases plus matched controls, so the 32% reflects the design, not prevalence. No misophonia counts are given for the unselected survey pool. Table 2 percentages imply 18 cases and 36 controls (18/54 = 33%, text says 32%). A reviewer could instead treat the sample as unselected volunteers and code it eligible.

codes.sample: 23andMe customers from the general population (N=80,607 genotyped participants of European ancestry who answered yes or no to the chewing-rage item). The sample was not recruited for misophonia. The paper is a secondary GWAS and genetic-correlation analysis of existing data.
codes.instruments: A single ad hoc self-report item from 23andMe: "Does the sound of other people chewing fill you with rage?" (yes/no). The authors use it as a proxy for misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Answered 'yes' to the single item "Does the sound of other people chewing fill you with rage?"
case_definitions.quote: N=80607 participants who reported either yes (N=17606) or no (N=63001) to the question: "Does the sound of other people chewing fill you with rage?" ... The prevalence of a positive answer to this question was 22%

codes.possible_duplicate: Same 23andMe sample and GWAS as Fayzullina et al. (2015), 23andMe White Paper 23-08, "Genetic Associations with Traits in 23andMe Customers". This preprint re-reports those counts. A later peer-reviewed version of this preprint may also exist (Smit et al.).
codes.note: Secondary analysis: the counts come from the Fayzullina et al. (2015) 23andMe GWAS. The case definition is one yes/no symptom item about chewing-induced rage, not full misophonia criteria. The authors say the 22% likely overestimates clinical prevalence. Only participants who answered yes or no were included. 23andMe participants may be more highly educated than the general population.

codes.sample: 196 occupational therapy (n=100) and audiology (n=96) students aged 17–28 at Istanbul Gelişim University, Turkey; questionnaires given face to face during lesson breaks; participation voluntary and not based on misophonia (p. 2–3).
codes.instruments: Turkish Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; subscales MQ1–MQ3, plus a 1–15 severity rating); Perceived Stress Scale (PSS); a demographic form with misophonia awareness and family-history items.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Eligible sample measured with the MQ, but only subscale means (e.g., MQ1 11.382), rank comparisons and correlations are given. No cut-off, severity band or count of participants with misophonia. The 8.2% (n=16) figure is family history of misophonia, and 39.3% (n=77) is knowing what misophonia is. Neither counts participants who have it.

codes.sample: 390 undergraduate students (nursing-midwifery, paramedical sciences, health) at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran, October 2020; stratified/systematic sampling from 1190 students; students with self-reported hearing-related diseases were excluded; 58.2% female.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al.), Persian version (Mehrabizade Honarmand & Roshani 2020); severity item ≥7 = misophonia. Also used: Maudsley OCI, BAI, BDI-II.

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity scale score of 7 or higher (clinically significant misophonia)
case_definitions.quote: Of the 390 participants in the study, 93 (23.8%) had experienced misophonia. ... Misophonia No | 297 (76.2) Yes | 93 (23.8)

codes.possible_duplicate: The acknowledgement says the study was part of Agrin Mohammadi's thesis (Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, grant 20828). If that thesis is in the set, it probably uses the same sample.
codes.note: The cut-off is 'a score of 7 or higher' on the MQ's final 1–15 severity item. Table 2's counts (93/390) agree with the abstract and Results text. The questionnaire went to students who were selected and contacted by phone; non-response is not reported.

codes.sample: Adults aged 18–60 recruited via Prolific (717 recruited, final analytic N = 341). Listed eligibility criteria: no hearing loss, no cognitive impairment, normal or corrected vision, native or bilingual English speaker. None mentions misophonia. Mean age 34.68; 50.76% male.
codes.instruments: S-Five (25 items; clinical cut-off ≥87, Vitoratou et al., 2023). Also an entry item on self-identified or diagnosed misophonia (no counts reported), plus SSSQ, SAD-T, IMQ, RFQ-8, QCAE, TAS-20, the Yoni task and MET.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total score ≥87 (clinically significant misophonia), full analytic sample
case_definitions.quote: yielding a final analytic sample of N = 341, including 146 below and 195 above cutoff threshold (≥87) (Vitoratou et al., 2023)

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total ≥87 among participants with mimicry (IMQ) data
case_definitions.quote: Mimicry data were available for 332 participants... Among participants with clinically elevated S-Five scores (≥87; N = 188), 77 (41.0%) endorsed mimicry

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The same team's earlier work (Black et al., 2025, N=140, similar tasks; Ash et al., 2023, mimicry) seems to use different samples.
codes.note: Paper says Prolific recruitment with no misophonia criterion, but cites the 'specificity of the target population', thanks SoQuiet and Duke CMER, and says 'Prolific participants then entered…', hinting at other sources. 57% scored ≥87, far above UK norms. Possible targeted recruitment: check OSF prereg (osf.io/vjkfx). Eligible (195/341) if the sample was unselected.

codes.sample: 549 students (285 F, 260 M, 4 undisclosed; mean age 23.2, SD 9.3): integrated high school technical (13-18 y), Adult and Youth Education and undergraduate programs, Federal Institute of Goias, Brazil. Recruited through class visits and course groups. Students with physical or intellectual limitations or known mental disorders were excluded. Cross-sectional online survey, Sept 2022 to Aug 2023.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (Brazilian Portuguese translation, 14 items, total score 14-70; cutoff ≥61)

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest total score ≥61 (Siepsiak et al. cutoff)
case_definitions.quote: A total of 549 students ... with scores ranging from 14 to 70 and a predefined cutoff value of 61 [14,22]. Considering this value, 4.5% of the participants were positive for misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Only the percentage is printed; derive the count from 4.5% × 549 (≈24.7, likely 25). The text has no page markers, so locations are given by section. The sample was not recruited on the basis of misophonia, but students were told the study's aims when invited. Students with known mental disorders were excluded. The Figure 2 histogram is referenced but not in the text.

codes.sample: 1,006 high school students from 6 high schools (8 classes each) in Kahta district, Adıyaman, Türkiye, Feb–Apr 2025; ~95% participation in selected classrooms; 67.6% female (n=680). Not recruited for misophonia. Excluded: chronic illness (e.g., epilepsy), foreign nationals.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al. 2014), Turkish adaptation (Deniz Sakarya & Çakmak): 17-item total (0–68) plus the single-item Misophonia Severity Scale (1–15), where ≥7 = clinically significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Misophonia Severity Scale ≥7 (clinically significant misophonia; equals moderate + severe + very severe bands)
case_definitions.quote: The remaining 16.7% (n = 168) reported no clinically significant misophonia symptoms. Overall, 49.7% of the participants (n = 500) were identified as having clinically significant levels of misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity band severe or very severe (derived: 89 + 52)
case_definitions.quote: 5.2% of the students (n = 52) reported very severe sound sensitivity, 8.8% (n = 89) reported severe sensitivity ... When cases with only severe or very severe sound sensitivity are considered in our sample, the prevalence drops to 14%

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity band very severe only
case_definitions.quote: 5.2% of the students (n = 52) reported very severe sound sensitivity

case_definitions.definition: Clinically significant misophonia (MQ severity ≥7), females
Clinically significant misophonia (MQ severity ≥7), males

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The authors (Kılıç FE) overlap with Kılıç C et al. 2021, but that study used a different population sample.
codes.note: The abstract wrongly says "children presenting to a public hospital"; the methods describe school sampling. How the 1–15 severity score maps to the bands is not stated. Clinically significant (500) = moderate + severe + very severe (359+89+52). 14% is approximate (141/1006). Table 4 also gives counts by grade.

codes.sample: 142 children and adolescents aged 10–14 (mean 11.72, SD 1.12; 65 female, 77 male) from Sussex, England. They are a subset (about 5%) of the MULTISENSE random school screening cohort: children whose parents agreed to further contact. They were not recruited for misophonia. Tested online at home, Nov 2020–Mar 2021.
codes.instruments: Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adolescents (SMS-Adolescent): 48 trigger items plus 39 Likert items, total score 0–156. Other measures (not misophonia): SCARED, OCI-CV, VSWQ-C, SWLS-C, creative self-concept.

case_definitions.definition: SMS-Adolescent total score at or above the sample's 90th percentile (score >=49; close to the adult cut-off of 50.5)
case_definitions.quote: to set the child threshold at the 90th percentile of total SMS-Adolescent scores. This threshold captured all children with a test-score of 49 or higher... Using this threshold score, we classified 15 children with misophonia... The remaining 127 children were designated controls

codes.possible_duplicate: Same Sussex research group as Rinaldi et al. 2021 (adult SMS), which is a different sample. The MULTISENSE cohort also appears in other reports (e.g., Simner et al. 2021). Other reports of SMS-Adolescent data from this cohort may exist.
codes.note: The cut-off was set at the 90th percentile of this sample's own scores, so the 10.6% is largely fixed by design rather than a true prevalence estimate. The sample is about 5% of the original random cohort (families who agreed to stay in touch), so self-selection is possible. Gender split of cases: 9 girls and 6 boys.

codes.sample: UK general-population sample recruited via Prolific and stratified by sex, age and ethnicity using census data (N = 772; aged 18+; mean age 46.4). A Pre-OK-SCIM interview subsample of 29 was drawn from across the S-Five deciles. A separate sample of people who self-identified with misophonia (n = 26 interviewed) was used only for ROC calibration.
codes.instruments: S-Five (25 items) and the S-Five-T trigger checklist; MQ (MSYS, MEBS, MSES); A-MISO-S (self-report); Pre-OK-SCIM semi-structured clinical interview (adapted Amsterdam UMC criteria); PHQ-9; GAD-7. Single items on awareness of the term and self-identification as having misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total >=87 (ROC-derived cut-off against Pre-OK-SCIM 'significant misophonia')
case_definitions.location: Results: Prevalence of misophonia in the UK population
case_definitions.quote: With 87 as the cut-off point on the S-Five, we found that 142 individuals out of 772 met the threshold for significant misophonia ... a percentage of 18.4%

case_definitions.definition: Pre-OK-SCIM interview: 'significant misophonia' (general-population interview subsample drawn from all S-Five deciles)
case_definitions.location: Results: Prevalence of misophonia in the UK population
case_definitions.quote: The Pre-OK-SCIM classified 14% (4 participants) of the general population sample and 81% (21 participants) of the misophonia sample as having 'significant misophonia'.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identifies as having misophonia (ad hoc item)
case_definitions.quote: Only 13.6% of the sample was aware of the term misophonia and 2.3% identify as having the disorder.

codes.possible_duplicate: Same S-Five study battery as Vitoratou et al. (S-Five development, misophonia sample) and Vitoratou et al. (S-Five-T trigger paper). The dataset is deposited at UK Data Service SN-856149. Later papers that analyse the same Prolific UK representative sample may overlap.
codes.note: Main estimate: 142/772 (18.4%). The interview subsample of 29 is not random: it was chosen from across the S-Five deciles, so 4/29 is not a prevalence estimate. For self-identification, the denominator is assumed to be 772; the count is not printed. MSES >=7 is described as a cut-off but no counts are given. The gender chi-square uses N = 768.

codes.sample: 94 analysed adult psychiatric inpatients with a current ICD-10 depression diagnosis (100 enrolled), recruited from wards in Kraków and Warsaw, Poland, for depression rather than misophonia. People with OCD, psychosis, bipolar depression, addiction or cognitive impairment were excluded. Ages 18–79.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, cut-off 61/70), plus a semi-structured face-to-face interview based on the Schröder et al. (2013) diagnostic criteria for misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Met misophonia criteria in both the face-to-face interview (Schröder criteria) and MisoQuest (≥61)
case_definitions.quote: Eight out of 94 subjects were diagnosed with misophonia (8.5%), meeting criteria for misophonia in both face-to-face interview and MisoQuest.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest score ≥61 of 70 (questionnaire alone)
case_definitions.quote: According to the assumed cutoff in MisoQuest (61 out of 70 points), 11 patients should be classified as having misophonia (11.7%).

case_definitions.definition: Interview diagnosis including mild misophonia (8 confirmed by both methods + 4 mild cases found only by interview)
case_definitions.quote: A total of 8.5% of patients met the criteria for misophonia. If we included the 4 cases with mild misophonia, with very limited impact on one's life, this would be 12.76%.

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The MisoQuest cut-off comes from an earlier MisoQuest validation study (2018), which used a different sample.
codes.note: No page markers, so locations are sections. The cut-off of 61 is mean minus 1 SD from an earlier, different sample, so not distribution-based. The 12 is derived; 12/94 = 12.77% (paper says 12.76%) and fits sensitivity 66.67% = 8/12. Patients were referred by their psychiatrists: a convenience sample, but not selected for misophonia.

codes.sample: Online cross-sectional survey of 450 adults in India (240 female, 210 male), aged 18-50 years, from various regions. All reported normal hearing. People with known auditory or visual disorders, cognitive impairment or hearing loss were excluded. Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: A yes/no screening question about reactions to auditory triggers, then the Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ; 21 items scored 0-3) for those who said yes. MAQ zones: Subclinical 0-11, Mild 12-24, Moderate 25-37, Severe 38-50, Extreme 51-63. The MkAQ (misokinesia) was also given.

case_definitions.definition: Misophonia present. The paper does not say which criterion was used (a yes on the screening question and/or an MAQ severity zone).
case_definitions.quote: The study found that 16.89% of participants experienced misophonia, highlighting its prevalence among Indian adults with normal hearing.

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The same research group published other Indian misophonia prevalence studies (Patel et al. 2023 college students; Yadav et al. 2024 Amity University students), but those appear to use different samples.
codes.note: The paper never states what counted as a case, and the MAQ severity bands are not reported. The number of cases has to be calculated from the percentage (about 76 of 450). There are internal inconsistencies: co-occurrence (8.89%) is higher than misokinesia prevalence (5.34%), and no sex-specific counts are given. Data quality is questionable.

codes.sample: 1,050 autistic adults (610 female, 427 male, 13 other; aged 16–85, M=46.8) from the Netherlands Autism Register. All were diagnosed by healthcare professionals using DSM-IV-TR/DSM-5 criteria. This is a clinical sample recruited for another condition (autism), not for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale-Revised (AMISOS-R); also AQ-28 and SPQ-Short (not misophonia measures).

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R score ≥21 (>20), the cut-off for moderate symptoms
case_definitions.quote: Total 1050 784 (75%) 266 (25%) ... In total, 25.3% scored >20 on the AMISOS-R.

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R score ≥24 (recalculated to match the Jakubovski threshold)
case_definitions.quote: For Jakobovski, we recalculated prevalences in the current data to scores of 24+ (141 cases)

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R ≥21, females only
AMISOS-R ≥21, males only

codes.possible_duplicate: The NAR cohort is also used in other NAR publications (e.g., Weiland et al. 2020 on the SPQ; Scheeren et al. 2022), but none of those are known to report misophonia. This is a medRxiv preprint, so a later peer-reviewed version of the same data may exist.
codes.note: Table 1 has internal inconsistencies. In the ethnicity rows the <21 and ≥21 columns look swapped (Dutch 302 vs 513). The co-occurring 'none' row does not add up (427+94=521 vs 512). The total row (784+266=1050) and the sex rows are consistent. The ≥24 denominator is assumed to be 1050, because the paper does not state it.

codes.sample: Undergraduate students from a psychology research pool at a large southwestern US university (original N = 343). The analysed dataset was a listwise-deleted subset (size not stated) with a 70/30 train/test split. The random forest training set had n = 148. Recruitment was not based on misophonia.
codes.instruments: Items labelled MQ (Misophonia Questionnaire) and S5 (probably S-Five), plus one binary self-report misophonia diagnosis variable (MQDX), used as the classification outcome.

case_definitions.definition: Self-report binary misophonia diagnosis variable (MQDX), training subset only
case_definitions.quote: OOB estimate of error rate: 0% ## Confusion matrix: ## 0 1 class.error ## 0 124 0 0 ## 1 0 24 0

codes.possible_duplicate: Same sample as Norris, Kimball, Nemri & Ethridge (2022), Frontiers in Neuroscience, doi:10.3389/fnins.2022.832516 (ref 15). That article probably reports MQ-based prevalence for the full sample and should be the preferred source.
codes.note: This is a methods tutorial reanalysing data from another study. The only count that can be derived is from the random forest training set: 24 of 148 coded MQDX = 1, i.e. with misophonia. The cut-off behind MQDX is not described. The text does not give the full analysed n or the test-set class counts. The reviewer may prefer to exclude this report as a secondary duplicate or as 'other'.

codes.sample: Community members from Oxford/Lafayette County/University of Mississippi, recruited for a larger misophonia study through flyers, ads, clinics and word of mouth. To be included, participants had to screen positive for misophonia. N = 67 met misophonia standards; 62 were analysed (M age 28.6; 82.1% female; 79.1% White).
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (cut-off ≥10); Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ); WSAS adapted to misophonia; structured interviews (DIAMOND, DIPD)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S total score ≥10 (clinical cut-off), within a sample already screened positive for misophonia
case_definitions.quote: On the A-MISO-S, 71.0% (n = 44) of the participants met the 10-score cutoff recommended for a clinical misophonia diagnosis

codes.possible_duplicate: The sample comes from Dixon lab's larger study at the University of Mississippi (Misophonia Research Fund grant). Other theses or articles from the HART Lab may use the same participants.
codes.note: Every participant had to screen positive for misophonia ("had to screen positive for misophonia"; "67 participants met the standards for misophonia"). The size of the unselected pool that was screened is not reported. So the A-MISO-S 44/62 count comes from an already-selected sample and cannot be used to estimate prevalence.

codes.sample: Convenience online survey of Turkish adults aged 18–65 recruited via social media, 26 July–30 August 2025 (n=86). The stated inclusion criteria required participants to have "self-reported at least a moderate level of misophonia symptoms". Participants were split into a misophonia group (n=35) and controls (n=51).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (Wu et al. 2014; the paper calls it "MisQuest"/"MisoQuest", but it is the MQ, Turkish version by Sakarya & Çakmak 2022). Cases were defined by a score of ≥7 on the 3 impairment items. Other measures: A/ASP, DES and DASS-21.

case_definitions.definition: MQ ("MisQuest") impairment items score ≥7
case_definitions.quote: a score ≥7 classified participants into the misophonia group (n=35), whereas scores <7 defined controls (n=51)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: An inclusion criterion requires "self-reported at least a moderate level of misophonia symptoms", so the whole sample was selected on misophonia. This conflicts with the 51 "healthy controls" (score <7) and with the general convenience recruitment, so the reviewer should check. If the criterion is an error, 35/86 meeting MQ ≥7 could be used.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative and theoretical essay that covers neuroanatomy, historical "cases" (Ming emperor, Danny Chan, Van Gogh) and the authors' treatment experience. The only prevalence figures are cited from other studies: 310 passers-by in a US city and 500 University of South Florida students.
codes.instruments: None administered. The Weinstein Noise Sensitivity Scale (Chinese version) is reproduced in Table 3 for reference only; it is not a misophonia measure and no data from it are reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: The cited figures (15.2% of 310 passers-by; 20% of 500 USF students) come from other primary studies, probably Wu et al. 2014 for the USF sample. Those studies should be assessed from their own reports.
codes.note: Despite the title, there are no methods, sample or original data. This is a narrative paper with secondary citations and anecdotes. Page 3 quotes secondary data: "随机抽样310 位路人……疑似恐音症倾向的路人居然高达15.2%" (of 310 randomly sampled passers-by, as many as 15.2% showed suspected misophonia tendencies). Check the reference list for the original studies.

codes.sample: Online cross-sectional survey, N=451 adults (mean age 36.5, 60.3% female). Recruited by emailing University of Surrey students and staff AND via patient support groups for tinnitus and sound intolerance. The two recruitment sources are not reported separately. 154 completed a retest.
codes.instruments: SSSQ2 (item 4 = misophonia), MisoQuest, AMISOS-R; also HIQ, TIQ, SAD-T, HHI

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest score indicating significant misophonia (cut-off not stated in text)
case_definitions.location: Section 3.1 Characteristics of the Study Population
case_definitions.quote: Based on scores for MisoQuest, 21.7% of patients (N = 98) had significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R severity band: mild misophonia
case_definitions.quote: 34.1% (N = 154) had a mild misophonia

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R severity band: moderate misophonia
case_definitions.quote: 35.5% (N = 160) had a moderate misophonia

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R severity band: severe to extreme misophonia
case_definitions.quote: 10.2% (N = 46) had a severe to extreme misophonia

case_definitions.definition: AMISOS-R: no misophonia (subclinical); complement of any misophonia band
case_definitions.quote: Based on scores for the AMISOS-A, 20.2% of patients (N = 91) had no misophonia (i.e., had sub-clinical symptoms)

codes.possible_duplicate: The same Surrey online survey (SSSQ2, MisoQuest, AMISOS-R, HIQ, TIQ, SAD-T, HHI; N≈451) may also be reported in other Aazh et al. papers, such as HIQ, MisoQuest or AMISOS-R validation studies or studies of misophonia and hyperacusis prevalence. Check for overlap.
codes.note: Counts and N=451 are given. But part of the sample came from sound-intolerance support groups (selection on sound sensitivity), not reported apart from university students/staff. Authors call the sample 'largely non-clinical'. Table 4 (SSSQ2 item 4 endorsement) not in retrieved text. 'AMISOS-A' in the text is presumably a typo for AMISOS-R.

codes.sample: 501 UK adults. 143 were self-declared misophonics from online communities, so this stream is excluded. 358 came from the general and student population (course credit; topic not disclosed beforehand). 29 of these could not be classified because of missing data, leaving 329 classifiable.
codes.instruments: Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adults (SMS-Adult; Part 2 has 39 Likert items, total 0-156, cut-off 50.5). Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), with Severity Scale >=7.

case_definitions.definition: SMS-Adult Part 2 total >50.5 (score >=51), general-population stream only
case_definitions.location: Table A2 title; Results (ROC) section; Discussion
case_definitions.quote: 45 People From the General Population Identified as Misophonic Using our SMS-Adult, and 284 Identified as Non-Misophonic

case_definitions.definition: SMS-Adult cut-off 50.5: specificity in the general-population controls (complement = positive rate)
case_definitions.location: Results: Establishing a Cutoff Threshold; Discussion
case_definitions.quote: successfully identifies 87.5% of misophonics while excluding 86.2% of controls ... Our 86% specificity means 14% of our general population sample were considered to have misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: These data may overlap with other Sussex SMS validation papers by the same group: Simner et al. 2021 and Rinaldi et al. 2023 (adults). Rinaldi et al. 2022 is the adolescent version.
codes.note: The 50.5 cut-off was set by ROC/Youden on this same sample (self-declared misophonics vs the general stream). It is sample-derived but not a percentile. MQ-defined cases (198/486) are given only for the pooled sample, which includes the misophonics, so they are not usable. 45/329 is from Table A2; footnote 5 reports 29 general-stream participants missing.

codes.sample: Two samples: (1) US general-population adults from Prolific, final n=1403, recruited for a survey advertised as being about "sensory sensitivities" (not misophonia). (2) Independent autistic adults from SPARK Research Match, final n=936, recruited for autism (another condition).
codes.instruments: Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ) with a criterion-based algorithm adapted from the Revised Amsterdam Criteria and the consensus definition. Also an abbreviated DMQ, IHS, and DSM-SP modified for phonophobia. Self-reported prior professional diagnosis of misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ algorithm: clinically significant misophonia (criteria A-F met) - Prolific general population
case_definitions.quote: a total of 102 individuals in the Prolific sample (7.3%, including 7 autistic adults) and 332 individuals in the SPARK sample (35.5%) met criteria for clinically significant misophonia

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ algorithm: clinically significant misophonia - SPARK autistic adults
case_definitions.quote: 35.5% (332/936) in a female-predominant sample of independent autistic adults recruited from the SPARK cohort

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ subclinical misophonia (criteria A-D met but not impairment F) - Prolific, additional to clinical cases
case_definitions.quote: Subclinical misophonia ... was present in an additional 144 adults in the Prolific sample (10.2%) and 97 adults in the SPARK sample (10.4%)

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ subclinical misophonia - SPARK autistic adults, additional to clinical cases
case_definitions.quote: 97 adults in the SPARK sample (10.4%)

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported previous professional diagnosis of misophonia - Prolific
case_definitions.quote: only 10 individuals in the Prolific sample (0.7%) and 21 individuals in the SPARK sample (2.2%) reported being previously diagnosed with misophonia by a professional

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported previous professional diagnosis of misophonia - SPARK
case_definitions.quote: 21 individuals in the SPARK sample (2.2%) reported being previously diagnosed with misophonia

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ screening item S1 positive (specific sounds extremely bothersome even if not loud) - Prolific
case_definitions.quote: 1478 of whom (Prolific: n = 833; SPARK: n = 645) affirmatively answered DVMSQ screening question S1

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ clinical misophonia by sex - SPARK females / males (counts from Table 3)
case_definitions.quote: clinically significant misophonia was present in slightly over one-third of our SPARK sample (44.2% of autistic females and 20.5% of autistic males)

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ clinical misophonia by sex - Prolific females / males (counts from Table 3)

codes.possible_duplicate: The SPARK sample overlaps heavily with Williams et al. (2022) ("A largely overlapping sample has previously been described elsewhere"). The Prolific sample (fall 2021, OSF y6edb) may also appear in other Williams/Woynaroski/Cascio papers on decreased sound tolerance.
codes.note: No page markers, so locations are sections and tables. SPARK S1-positive n is 645 in the text but 647 in Table 3. Prolific percentages by sex can be computed from Table 3. Authors say prevalence may be overestimated because the survey was advertised as being about "sensory sensitivities." The DVMSQ algorithm has not been validated against clinical interviews.

codes.sample: N = 214 treatment-seeking children and adolescents aged 10–21, recruited from inpatient and outpatient child and adolescent mental health services for any mental health problem at four sites in Germany and Austria (Nov 2022–Jan 2024). 211 were analysed for SMS-A Part 2: 3 reported no sounds and skipped it.
codes.instruments: Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adolescents (SMS-A), German translation (not validated). Part 1 is a checklist of repetitive sounds; Part 2 has 39 symptom items, with a cut-off of 49. The study also used self-generated items on age of onset, coping and setting.

case_definitions.definition: Probable misophonia: SMS-A Part 2 sum score at or above 49 (Results text says '> 49'; Measures says '49 or higher'; the group's minimum score is 49)
case_definitions.location: Results, 'Characteristics of repetitive sounds...'; Tables 1 and 4
case_definitions.quote: A sub-sample of n = 66 participants (31.28%) met the SMS-A cutoff criterion of > 49 indicating probable misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Reported at least one (misophonia-relevant) repetitive sound on the SMS-A Part 1 checklist. This is not a clinical case definition.
case_definitions.quote: Regarding (misophonia-relevant) repetitive sounds, n = 193 (90.19%) reported at least one sound (see Table 2).

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified in the text. Other reports from the same multi-centre project (for example, data from the Highly Sensitive Child Scale) may exist and could overlap with this sample.
codes.note: The SMS-A cut-off comes from the developers' external sample (90th percentile), not from this sample, so it is not distribution-based. 66/211 = 31.28% (the 211 = 66 + 145). Limitations section: two sites offered misophonia consultations, and about 10–15 participants may have been referred for misophonia. Selective referral is therefore possible, but the sample was not recruited for misophonia.

codes.sample: 499 Turkish university students aged 18–26 (mean 20.2, SD 1.6) from various universities, not recruited for misophonia. Data were collected online and on paper. 244 answered yes to a screening question; 60 randomly selected 'no' responders served as controls (n=304 analysed in phase 2).
codes.instruments: Ad hoc screening question on being disturbed by specific sounds (e.g., smacking, slurping, throat clearing); Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ), including the severity scale (1–15, ≥7 = clinical). Also THI, KHQ and DASP.

case_definitions.definition: Subjective misophonia: answered 'yes' to the screening question about being disturbed by specific trigger sounds
case_definitions.quote: A total of 244 students (48.8%) reported being sensitive to at least one specific sound, indicating subjective misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Clinical misophonia: screen-positive AND MQ severity score ≥7 (assessed only among the 244 screen-positives)
case_definitions.location: Results, second paragraph; Discussion; Conclusions; Abstract
case_definitions.quote: Of these participants, 163 were categorised as having subclinical misophonia and 81 as having clinical misophonia. This means that among those who reported misophonia symptoms, 26.6 per cent were in the clinical group

case_definitions.definition: Subclinical misophonia: screen-positive with MQ severity score <7
case_definitions.quote: 163 were categorised as having subclinical misophonia and 81 as having clinical misophonia ... 53.6 per cent in the subclinical group

codes.possible_duplicate: Acknowledgments: the study was partly presented as a preliminary study at Ulusal Otoloji Nörotoloji Kongresi & 14. Koklear Implantasyon Odyoloji Kongresi. A congress abstract may exist that reports the same sample.
codes.note: The reported percentages do not match the counts. 81/499 = 16.2%, but the paper says 19% (abstract and conclusions) and 19.2% (discussion). The 26.6% and 53.6% figures use 304 (244+60) as the denominator, not 244 (81/244 = 33.2%). Use the raw counts. The MQ severity cut-off was applied only to screen-positives.

codes.sample: US youth aged 8-17 from a deep-phenotyping study (Guzick et al. 2023). 102 had clinically significant misophonia (recruited for suspected misophonia, partly via misophonia social media; A-MISO-S ≥10). 94 had anxiety disorders (recruited for suspected anxiety; A-MISO-S ≤4 required). Screened: 112 with suspected misophonia, 140 with suspected anxiety.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (self-report, 5-item scoring); C-MAQ and P-MAQ; Misophonia Assessment Interview (MAI); MINI-KID; PROMIS Sleep Disturbance parent proxy; CBCL; MASC
codes.possible_duplicate: Reanalysis of the same dataset as Guzick et al. 2023 (pediatric misophonia vs. anxiety deep-phenotyping study); see also Cervin et al. 2023.
codes.note: Misophonia group was recruited for suspected misophonia. Anxiety group was recruited for another condition, but A-MISO-S ≤4 was required. Some of the 140 screened were excluded for "high A-MISO-S scores", but no number is given, so no prevalence can be derived (check Guzick 2023). The 30% figure is for sleep problems, not misophonia.

codes.sample: Exp 2: 142 adolescents aged 10–14 from the UK Multisense school cohort (22 junior schools in southern England, 99% uptake in 2016). They were re-tested between Nov 2020 and Mar 2021 and were not selected for misophonia. Exp 1: adults, a mix of self-declared misophonics from online forums and University of Sussex general-population volunteers; counts are not reported by stream.
codes.instruments: Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adolescents (SMS-A; child self-report, cut-off ≥49 out of 156, from Rinaldi et al. 2022). Adults: Sussex Misophonia Scale. Other measures: AQ, AQ-Adolescent, PERS, GSQ-P.

case_definitions.definition: SMS-A score ≥49 (out of 156); child self-report
case_definitions.quote: those scoring 49 or higher (out of 156) within the Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adolescents... The resultant misophonia group comprised 15 children... The remaining 127 children were designated controls

codes.possible_duplicate: The Exp 2 adolescents probably overlap with Rinaldi et al. 2022 (SMS-A validation, Multisense cohort) and other Multisense/misophonia-hub papers. The Exp 1 adults partly overlap with Simner et al. 2022 (attention-to-detail paper).
codes.note: Only Exp 2 is usable: 15/142 children (percentage derived). Exp 1 cannot be used: it pooled online-forum self-declared misophonics with students, dropped self-declared people below the cut-off, and gave no cases per stream. The Exp 2 children are a re-contacted subset of the original cohort.

codes.sample: Two German online convenience samples aged 16+. Recruitment was through social media and university mailing lists. The sampling frame included misophonia self-identification groups, general recruitment groups and hearing-disorder groups (tinnitus, hyperacusis). Study 1: N=639 analysed of 952 collected. Study 2: N=235 analysed of 322 recruited. Mostly female (86.2% and 85.1%).
codes.instruments: S-Five (German; total score ≥87 cut-off). BMQ-R (Jager et al. 2020 diagnostic criteria, scale mean >3; severe if >4). MisoQuest and S-Five-T were also given, but no cut-off counts are reported for them.

case_definitions.definition: Meets Jager et al. (2020) diagnostic criteria via BMQ-R (each criterion's scale mean >3), Study 1
case_definitions.quote: About half of the sample (47.5%) fulfilled the diagnostic criteria by Jager et al. (2020) (with 24.6% having severe symptoms) as classified by the BMQ-R.

case_definitions.definition: Severe misophonia via BMQ-R (each criterion's scale mean >4), Study 1
case_definitions.quote: (with 24.6% having severe symptoms) as classified by the BMQ-R

case_definitions.definition: Significant misophonia: S-Five total score ≥87, Study 1
case_definitions.quote: S-Five total score cut-off (i.e., total score of 87 or higher; cf. Vitoratou et al., 2022a), more than half of the sample (57.4%) had significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: Significant misophonia: S-Five total score ≥87, Study 2
case_definitions.quote: Significant misophonia as indicated by the S-Five total cut-off was observed for 58.3% of the sample.

codes.possible_duplicate: Study 1 was part of the larger BMQ-R validation study (Remmert et al., 2022, PLoS One), so it likely overlaps with that sample. This text is the Frontiers in Psychology 2022 version; the PsyArXiv preprint is the same report.
codes.note: Counts are there, but the sample is mixed: recruitment included misophonia groups, and the authors 'aimed at gathering data mainly from affected individuals'. No unselected subsample is reported separately, so the reviewer must judge I1. Case counts are not printed. The BMQ-R percentages may use a smaller denominator (N=609-616, Table 4).

codes.sample: Community volunteers recruited via a paid-participant study list at UBC (Canada), Feb–Jun 2022. 46 were recruited and 39 analysed (24 female, 1 gender non-conforming, 1 non-binary). Recruitment did not depend on sensitivity status.
codes.instruments: Misokinesia Assessment Questionnaire (MkAQ, 21 items). This measures sensitivity to seeing fidgeting movements (misokinesia). No misophonia-specific instrument was used.

case_definitions.definition: High misokinesia sensitivity (hiMKS): MkAQ sum score 3+ (misokinesia, not misophonia)
case_definitions.quote: participants having sum scores of 0–2 were labeled the “low misokinesia” group (loMKS; 15 women, 1 gender non-conforming...) and those with sum scores of 3+ were labeled “high misokinesia" group (hiMKS; 9 women, 1 non-binary

codes.possible_duplicate: Uses the same MkAQ grouping protocol as the authors' earlier misokinesia prevalence study (ref [2], Jaswal et al. 2021, Scientific Reports). This is a different, new ERP sample.
codes.note: The report only covers misokinesia, the visual sensitivity to fidgeting. It does not measure or define misophonia. Even for misokinesia, the sizes of the two groups are not stated; only their gender breakdowns are given. You could choose E2_no_misophonia_measure instead if misokinesia is counted as a related sensitivity measure. Either way, the report is not eligible.

codes.sample: Worldwide online survey (May–June 2020) of adults with tinnitus, from clinical and non-clinical populations. Recruited through patient organisations' social media and tinnitus clinics. 3,400 respondents; 2,980 eligible adults with tinnitus (mean age 58, 49% female).
codes.instruments: Self-reported yes/no presence of other hearing-related difficulties (hearing loss, hyperacusis, misophonia). This is an ad hoc misophonia item with no validated instrument. THI-S was used to measure tinnitus severity.

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported presence of misophonia (any combination: misophonia only, + hearing loss, + hyperacusis, + both); derived total = 26+18+46+54
case_definitions.quote: Presence of misophonia only 0 (0) 26 (3.3) 0 (0) ... hearing loss and misophonia 0 (0) 18 (2.3) 0 (0) ... hyperacusis and misophonia 0 (0) 46 (5.8) 0 (0) ... hearing loss, hyperacusis and misophonia 0 (0) 54 (6.7) 0 (0)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same survey sample as Beukes et al. (2020), 'Changes in Tinnitus Experiences During the COVID-19 Pandemic', Front Public Health 8:592878 (ref 27).
codes.note: Tinnitus is a non-misophonia clinical condition, so the sample qualifies. Misophonia was a single self-report item with no definition. Total derived from Table 1 rows; misophonia cases appear only in Cluster 2, whose rows sum to 795. The paper prints 54 (6.7), but 54/795 = 6.8%. Reviewer should confirm the item counts as an ad hoc misophonia measure.

codes.sample: German online convenience sample, N = 952 aged 16+, 86.7% female, mean age 33.85. Recruited via social media and university mailing lists, with "Specific groups of individuals identifying as having misophonia as well as unspecific groups" targeted. N = 621 completed the symptom part. Results are not reported by recruitment source.
codes.instruments: BMQ-R (General Sound Intolerance Symptoms (GSIS) screening scale plus 20 symptom scales), S-Five-E, MisoQuest (German translations), plus non-misophonia validation measures (AQ, DPSS-R, STICSA, BITe, DERS, NAQ, BEAQ, WHODAS 2.0, IPQ-MH)

case_definitions.definition: BMQ-R GSIS sum score >12 (≥13): the routing cut-off to the 'potentially affected' track. Only the complement (6.7% <13) is printed.
case_definitions.location: Results, General sound intolerance and sound classes; Procedure
case_definitions.quote: Only 6.7% of the participants had a GSIS sum score lower than 13 (chosen score for non-affected individuals), whereas more than half of the sample indicated the highest score of 20 (49.8%).

case_definitions.definition: BMQ-R GSIS maximum sum score of 20
case_definitions.location: Results, General sound intolerance and sound classes
case_definitions.quote: more than half of the sample indicated the highest score of 20 (49.8%)

codes.possible_duplicate: Its data are on OSF (doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9VFMS). The original BMQ study [ref 18] appears to use a different, earlier sample. Check for a thesis by the same Berlin group using this dataset.
codes.note: Scale-validation study. Recruitment was mixed and deliberately targeted self-identified misophonia groups; the authors say the sample "mainly comprised potentially affected individuals". No unselected subsample (e.g., students) is reported separately. GSIS proportions are not interpretable as prevalence. The reviewer may decide between E1 and eligible with high risk of bias.

codes.sample: fMRI case-control study at Duke (2020–2022). 112 adults had an in-person screening and 59 were scanned: 29 with misophonia (MQ criteria) and 30 non-misophonic clinical controls with high emotion dysregulation (DERS ≥89) and a DSM-5 disorder. Participants were recruited through ads, social media and medical-record outreach.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ): misophonia was defined as scoring ≥2 on both subscales and ≥7 on the severity scale. The Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ), DERS, ERQ, SCID-5 and SCID-5-PD were also used.
codes.possible_duplicate: These are baseline fMRI data from the parent neurostimulation trial NCT04348591. That trial's behavioural outcomes were reported in Neacsiu et al. 2024 (ref 32), so the sample is the same.
codes.note: Groups were recruited on purpose: one for misophonia ("self-reported significant misophonic severity (n = 29)") and one as non-misophonic clinical controls. No count of people meeting the MQ criterion in an unselected screened pool (e.g., the 112 screened) is given. Only a 4.6% prevalence from another study is cited (ref 8). Supplementary Table 1 lists DSM diagnoses only.

codes.sample: 40 normal-hearing participants recruited via Facebook announcements and a mailing list at a tinnitus/misophonia reference centre (Brazil): Misophonia Group n=10 (selected for misophonia), Tinnitus Control Group n=10 (selected for absence of misophonia), Asymptomatic Control Group n=20 (selected for no misophonia and no tinnitus).
codes.instruments: Clinical history of misophonia plus annoyance score ≥6 on a 0–10 Visual Analogue Scale (used only as a group inclusion criterion). Dichotic Sentence Identification test (outcome measure; not a misophonia measure).
codes.note: Case-control experiment. Groups were assigned in advance by misophonia/tinnitus status, and no unselected screened pool is reported. 43 subjects had audiometry only to check hearing thresholds. The 57% and 10% figures in the Discussion are cited from other studies (refs 13, 14), not this sample's data. Those cited studies could be checked for eligibility.

codes.sample: 151 recruited, 139 analysed after attention-check exclusions. Adults aged 17 or older from CloudResearch, the University of Western Ontario SONA pool, and online ads circulated to misophonia support groups (including the SoQuiet misophonia research pool). Counts are not broken down by recruitment source.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (English; cut-off ≥61), S-Five, S-Five-T trigger checklist, GAD-7, Sensory Hypersensitivity Scale

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest total score ≥61 (clinically significant misophonia), in the mixed sample that includes misophonia support-group recruits
case_definitions.quote: a sample of 139 participants was included in the analyses. Forty‐four participants met the MisoQuest cut‐off for clinically significant misophonia and the remaining 95 participants comprised the control group

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. A University of Western Ontario thesis on the same sample may exist; worth checking.
codes.note: Mixed sample: some came from unselected pools (CloudResearch, SONA), some from misophonia support groups. The 44/139 count is for the whole sample and is not split by source, so no count exists for the unselected part alone. E1 does not strictly apply. The reviewer could choose E1, or ask the authors for counts by source (raw data on OSF).

codes.sample: Study 3: 102 naive undergraduates (65 women, 33 men, 4 non-binary; ages 18-29) from the UC Santa Cruz psychology participant pool, not screened for misophonia. Severity data are reported for 101 participants. Study 1 (80 interviewees with misophonia) and Study 2 (34 raters, no MQ reported) give no eligible prevalence data.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014): Symptom Scale, Emotions and Behaviors Scale, and the single-item Misophonia Severity Scale (0/1-15).

case_definitions.definition: MQ Misophonia Severity Scale score of 7 or above (described as clinically significant misophonic reactions)
case_definitions.quote: For this scale, a score of 7 or above would constitute clinically significant misophonic reactions. There are 14 participants out of 101 (13.7% of the sample) that had misophonia severity scores of 7 or above.

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. Samermit et al. (2019) used a different, earlier sample. The 80 interviewees with misophonia will be used in later work, but they are a different, selected sample.
codes.note: Denominator mismatch: N=102, but the text gives 101, and 13.7% fits 14/102. The cut-off wording differs too: Methods says "above 7" on a 0-15 scale; Results says "7 or above" on a 1-15 scale. The Discussion repeats "14 ... severity score of 7 or higher". 4 participants scored 10-11, but this isn't a formal case definition.

codes.sample: 155 undergraduate students recruited through a university SONA research pool (Western University, Canada). Neurodevelopmental conditions were intentionally oversampled (self-reported ASD 9.7%, ADHD 46.5%). Recruitment was not based on misophonia. Age 17–59, mean 22.1; 69.7% female.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, total 14–70; clinical cut-off ≥61). Also AQ, AASP, MSCS, TAS-20, ASRS, RBQ-2A.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest total ≥ 61 (clinical cut-off), reported only within the LPA 'high neurodivergence expression' profile, which was derived partly from MisoQuest scores
case_definitions.quote: The high expression group demonstrated marked elevation compared to neurotypical norms: 43.8% met the clinical-cutoff for misophonia (MisoQuest score ≥ 61)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same author group as Raymond & Butler (2024, J Clin Psychol) on MisoQuest psychometrics in undergraduates. The sample could overlap or there could be a related thesis by K. E. Raymond. Check this.
codes.note: No whole-sample count for MisoQuest ≥61 (N=155). The only % given is for the high-expression profile (n=32), which was derived from MisoQuest itself. The moderate profile may also include cases, but no count is given. Contents of Tables 3 and 4 were lost in extraction. Raw data are said to be on OSF. Reviewer could accept this if subgroup data count.

codes.sample: 92 adult (>21 y) psychiatric outpatients at National University Hospital, Singapore, Feb 2017–Feb 2018 (98 invited, 93.9% response). They were not preselected for misophonia. Main diagnoses: depression 52.2%, schizophrenia 22.2%, anxiety disorders 12.2%.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), self-rated, given after a research assistant explained misophonia; DASS-21.
codes.note: Eligible sample ("not preselected" for misophonia), measured with A-MISO-S. The text reports A-MISO-S only as a continuous score in correlations and regressions; no cut-off, severity bands or case counts. Tables 1–3 were not in the retrieved text. Their descriptions suggest no counts, but the reviewer should check Table 1 for an A-MISO-S severity distribution.

codes.sample: 104 physiotherapy students at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador, Santo Domingo campus, chosen by simple random sampling in 2023. 97 of them reported previous headache.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc survey on headache history and the clinical signs that come with headache, plus observation and the DASS-21. No misophonia-specific instrument, interview or diagnostic criteria were used.

case_definitions.definition: 'Misofonía' reported as a symptom accompanying headache, among students with previous headache. This most likely means phonophobia during headache, not misophonia.
case_definitions.quote: la principal manifestación clínica asociada a la cefalea fue la fotofobia (26,8 %), seguida de la misofonía, las náuseas y vómitos (23,7 % en ambos casos).

codes.note: Migraine study. 'Misofonía' is listed with photophobia and nausea as a sign that comes with headache, so it almost certainly means phonophobia (ICHD migraine criteria), not misophonia. No misophonia-specific measure was used. If a reviewer rejects E2, the alternative reason is not_misophonia. The case count is not printed: 23 is my own calculation from 23.7% of 97.

codes.sample: Case-control fMRI study: 20 misophonic participants and 22 age- and sex-matched controls (Kumar et al., Current Biology 2017). The misophonic group was recruited because of misophonia. No unselected screened pool is reported.
