codes.instruments: Ratings of misophonic distress for trigger, unpleasant and neutral sounds made in the scanner (1-4 scale), plus the Body Consciousness Questionnaire. The main text does not describe a misophonia questionnaire used for screening; the supplementary questionnaire was not retrieved.
codes.possible_duplicate: This appears to be a Newcastle University repository copy of Kumar et al. (2017), Current Biology 27:1-7, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2016.12.048. The listed year of 2026 is the repository date, not the publication year.
codes.note: Page 2: "fMRI data were acquired in 20 misophonic and 22 age- and sex-matched controls". The groups are pre-defined in a case-control design, and no prevalence denominator or screening of an unselected pool is reported. The supplemental experimental procedures were not included in the retrieved text, but nothing in the main text suggests a screened pool.

codes.sample: 79 university students (50 female, 28 male, 1 other; mean age 21.94) at the University of Arkansas, paid participants in a Stroop experiment. Not recruited for misophonia. Four were excluded from the Stroop analyses (n=75).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; 17 items: sound sensitivity and emotional behaviors subscales; the severity-scale item was not reported). Also STAI state and Big 5 Neuroticism.
codes.note: The MQ was used only as a continuous score. The text reports only means, SDs and ranges (total MQ M=22.97, SD=11.32, range 2-57), plus correlations and regressions. No cut-off or MQ severity-scale count is given. Fig 1 shows score distributions, but no counts can be read from the text. The 19.9% quoted in the Introduction comes from Wu et al. 2014 [15], not from this sample.

codes.sample: 67 adults with misophonia plus their 67 partners (mean age 23.8±5.2), recruited from outpatient visits to psychiatrists/psychotherapists (n=28), gynecologists (n=16), ENT doctors (n=14) and urologists (n=9), Ukraine, 2016–2022. Controls: 67 couples of medical students/interns selected as having no misophonia. Pages 19–20.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S, 6 items); sexual quality of life measured with SQOL-F, FSFI, SQOL-M and IIEF.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same authors and clinical setting as Banyra O et al., 'Misophonia in urological patients: our experience of management', Archiv Psychiatr Res 2022;58(1):119-130 (ref. 30). That paper may overlap and should be checked on its own for a screened pool of urological patients.
codes.note: Participants were included because they had misophonia: 42 (62.7%) told the doctor themselves and 25 (37.3%) were asked after the doctor suspected it (p.19). No number of outpatients seen is given, so there is no denominator. Controls were picked as 'without misophonia'. Comorbidity counts (e.g., 38/67) describe cases only, not prevalence.

codes.sample: Exp 1: 65 adults aged 18-41 from Carnegie Mellon University and the surrounding area; recruitment basis not stated. Exp 2: 22 CMU students ("recruited from a general population"). Exp 3: 21 CMU students and faculty ("recruited from a general population"). All three were screened for misophonia.
codes.instruments: DVMSQ (criteria A-E), MQ Misophonia Severity Scale (≥7) and S-Five (≥87/250) in Exp 1; DVMSQ only in Exps 2 and 3.

case_definitions.definition: Exp 1: meets threshold on any of DVMSQ (A-E), MQ severity ≥7, or S-Five ≥87
case_definitions.quote: A subset of 26 participants scored at the clinically significant level on the DVMSQ, MQ, and/or S-Five, using the established clinical cutoffs for each scale

case_definitions.quote: 22 participants met the misophonia threshold on the DVMSQ, 19 on the MQ, and 8 on the S-Five

case_definitions.quote: As we recruited from a general population, all participants were included regardless of their DVMSQ score. One of the 22 participants was misophonic.

case_definitions.definition: Exp 3: misophonic on DVMSQ
case_definitions.quote: A new group of 21 participants ... As we recruited from a general population, all participants were included regardless of DVMSQ score. None of the participants were misophonic.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The stimuli come from Heller et al. (2025) and Samermit et al. (2022), but the samples appear to be new.
codes.note: Exps 2 and 3 are clearly unselected, so the report is eligible. Exp 1 does not say how participants were recruited. Its high rate (26/65, 40%) and the even split of 13 misophonic participants per order suggest possible enrichment for misophonia, so a reviewer should check the Exp 1 counts. The text has no page markers, so locations are section labels.

codes.sample: This was a convenience sample of 562 university students aged 18–30 (63.3% female, mean age 19.77) from the medicine, dentistry, nursing and psychology faculties at the University of Health Sciences, Turkey, recruited in classrooms in 2023. Of 579 recruited, 17 were excluded for age, self-reported ADHD or hearing loss. Hearing aids/impairment, ASD and ADHD were exclusion criteria.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ), Turkish version (Sakarya & Çakmak 2021); a score of ≥7 on the MQ Misophonia Severity Scale (1–15) was the case cut-off. Also used: DASS-21, BIS-11-SF and MOCI.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Misophonia Severity Scale score ≥7 (cut-off-defined elevated misophonia symptoms)
case_definitions.quote: Among the students who participated in the study, 92 individuals (16.4%) were identified as having elevated misophonia symptoms. Participants were divided into two groups: those with elevated misophonia symptoms (n = 92) and those without elevated misophonia symptoms (n = 470)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: This is an unselected student sample; nobody was recruited because of misophonia. Excluding students with ADHD, ASD or hearing impairment may slightly bias prevalence. Trigger and reaction frequencies are reported only within the MQ≥7 group (Supplementary Tables S1–S2, not retrieved), but they are not needed for the case count.

codes.sample: 343 undergraduate students at the University of Oklahoma, recruited through the psychology research participation pool for course credit (69.7% female, ages 18–36, mean 18.96). This is a non-clinical sample not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), with the MQ severity scale cut-off at 7 or more out of 10; S-Five (2018 unvalidated version), not used for case definition; also THI, Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile, BAPQ and SPQ-BRU.

case_definitions.definition: MQ Misophonia Severity Scale score of 7 or more (clinically relevant misophonia symptoms)
case_definitions.quote: Of 343 participants, 54 (15.6%) reported clinically relevant levels of misophonia symptoms indicated by self-reported scores of 7 or greater on the MQ Misophonia Severity Scale.

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity of 7 or more among participants answering yes to the tinnitus/ear-ringing screener (subsample)
case_definitions.quote: A total of 50.4% (N = 173) of participants reported experiencing ringing in the ears... Forty participants who qualified for misophonia reported experiencing tinnitus... The total incidence rate of co-occurrence of misophonia and tinnitus among all of those who reported tinnitus viascreener was 23.1%

codes.possible_duplicate: The authors are likely Norris, Kimball, Nemri and Ethridge (University of Oklahoma). The same Spectrum Characteristic Survey sample may also appear in a thesis or dissertation by the first author or in conference abstracts. Check for overlap.
codes.note: 54/343 works out to 15.7%, but the paper prints 15.6%. The cluster counts (31+22+1=54) match. The tinnitus subsample comes from a self-report ear-ringing screener. MQ and S-Five trigger frequency tables (Tables 3–4) are trigger endorsements, not misophonia case definitions.

codes.sample: 300 adults (149 male, 151 female; aged 18–50, mean 24.6) recruited online through Prolific from English-speaking countries; 60% students. People taking medication for depression, anxiety or low mood, and people with autism, were excluded. Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, English translation, total score 14–70). Developer cut-off is 61.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest total score above 61 (the developers' screening cut-off of 61)
case_definitions.quote: only 4 out of 300 participants (less than 2%) scored above 61 on the MisoQuest.

case_definitions.definition: Most-Misophonic group: top 20% of the sample's MisoQuest distribution (total score above 45)
case_definitions.quote: The resulting MM group (N = 66, 33 females, mean age: 24.0 SD = 5.9) included participants with a total score above 45 on the MisoQuest

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The Supplementary Material has a data-driven grouping of the same sample, but it was not retrieved here.
codes.note: The main prevalence figure is 4/300 above the 61-point cut-off. The text says "above 61", so it is unclear whether scores of exactly 61 were counted; worth checking against the OSF data. Excluding people on psychotropic medication and people with autism may push prevalence down. The top-20% group is defined from this sample's own distribution. Full text, no page markers.

codes.sample: 64 University of Florida students and community participants in an EEG/pupillometry experiment. They were prescreened with the Misophonia Symptom Scale (MSS) to include people with strong misophonia traits, then split into low-symptom (LMS, n=34) and high-symptom (HMS, n=30) groups. The size of the prescreening pool is not reported.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Symptom Scale (MSS) from the Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014). Also loudness discomfort levels (LDL) as a proxy for hyperacusis, and Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) ratings.

case_definitions.definition: High misophonia symptoms (HMS): MSS score >= 12 (LMS < 12). Applied to a sample already selected by prescreening.
case_definitions.quote: Total 64 34 30 ... reported for the MSS scores when participants scored low in misophonia symptoms (< 12, LMS), and high in misophonia symptoms (>= 12, HMS).

codes.possible_duplicate: The text is the bioRxiv preprint (doi 10.1101/2025.09.22.677819, posted 22 Sep 2025) of the 2026 Cerebral Cortex article. Both describe the same sample and should be treated as one record.
codes.note: Recruited via MSS prescreening "to include subjects who exhibit strong traits of misophonia symptoms" (p.7). Extreme-groups experiment; the screened pool is not reported (no number screened or meeting the criterion), so 30/64 is not prevalence. Group sizes differ: LDL results give LMS N=31, HMS N=29 (p.17), and 4 withdrew from that test.

codes.sample: 131 intensive care nurses (paediatric, neonatal and adult ICUs) at Sivas Cumhuriyet University Application and Research Hospital, Turkey. Recruited by stratified random sampling and voluntary participation, not on the basis of misophonia. Data collected 1–15 September 2023; 69.5% female, mean age 29.86.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Scale by Wu et al. 2014 (the MQ), Turkish version by Deniz Sakarya & Çakmak 2022: 17-item score (0–68) plus a 1–15 severity item, where 7 or above = clinically significant misophonia. Also used: Caring Behaviours Scale-24.

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity item (1–15 scale) score of 7 or above = clinically significant misophonia (Wu et al. 2014)
case_definitions.location: Discussion section (cut-off described in Methods, Misophonia Scale section)
case_definitions.quote: 58 of the participants scored 7 and above in the section of the misophonia scale that determines clinical severity. These findings indicate that the majority of the participants had misophonic sensitivity.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The count appears only in the Discussion, not in the Results or tables; the percentage was calculated by me. The authors call 58/131 a 'majority', but it is 44%. 58 is also the number of nurses with children (Table 1), so the reviewer should check that the figure is correct. The Methods say no forms were missing, so the denominator is taken as 131.

codes.sample: 101 probands with self-reported misophonia recruited "through various online organizations and support groups" (Dec 2023–Jun 2025), aged 8–64, 88% female. Their biological parents were also surveyed (84 mothers, 81 fathers). Parents were enrolled only because their child had misophonia, so this is a family-enriched sample, not an unselected one.
codes.instruments: Self-report item for misophonia ("Yes"/"Diagnosed by a clinician"/"Unsure"/"No"). Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ): Severity Score >41, Impairment Score >13, used for parents who answered "Unsure". Proband-reported family history.

case_definitions.definition: Mothers of probands: self-reported misophonia (Yes/Diagnosed by a clinician)
case_definitions.quote: Among parents who completed surveys (84 mothers and 81 fathers), 29 parents (24 mothers, five fathers) self-reported a diagnosis of misophonia

case_definitions.definition: Fathers of probands: self-reported misophonia, or 'Unsure' plus DMQ Severity >41 or Impairment >13
case_definitions.quote: 29 parents (24 mothers, five fathers) self-reported a diagnosis of misophonia, and 2 additional fathers reported "unsure" to misophonia and met the threshold values

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The sample is from an ongoing Yale genetics study of families (Fernandez/Olfson), so later reports from the same cohort are possible.
codes.note: All probands were recruited for self-identified misophonia (E1). Parents were enrolled only as relatives of affected probands, so their rates (mothers 24/84; fathers 7/81) show familial recurrence, not unselected prevalence. Listed in case a reviewer overrides. No unselected screened pool is reported. Proband counts above the DMQ >41 cut-off are not given (only mean 63.8).

codes.sample: Community adults (N = 66; 83.3% female; mean age about 28) from the Lafayette-Oxford-University region, Mississippi, USA. They were recruited for a larger misophonia characterisation project funded by the Misophonia Research Fund. Inclusion required an A-MISO-S score of 10 or more plus at least one trigger sound at screening.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S); Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; given but not reported); WSAS adapted to misophonia; PHQ-9

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S score of 10 or more (clinical cutoff)
case_definitions.quote: In terms of clinical cutoff (score ≥ 10), two-thirds of the sample reported clinical severity (n = 44, 66.7%), while the remaining endorsed subclinical levels of severity (n = 18, 27.3%).

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S severity bands: moderate (10–14), mild (5–9), severe (15–19), subclinical (0–4)
case_definitions.quote: moderate range (n = 29, 43.9%), followed by mild (n = 16, 24.2%), severe (n = 15, 22.7%), and subclinical (n = 2, 3%)

codes.possible_duplicate: This sample is part of a larger Misophonia Research Fund project run by L. J. Dixon (University of Mississippi). The same participants may appear in other Dixon lab publications.
codes.note: Recruitment was based on misophonia: screening required an A-MISO-S score of 10 or more plus a trigger sound. The thesis calls the sample "individuals with misophonia." It does not report how many were screened, so no unselected denominator exists. Band counts are listed only for reviewer checking; they describe a pre-selected sample. The A-MISO-S was given again at the session.

codes.sample: 936 cognitively able autistic adults (age 18–80, 63.0% assigned female at birth) from the SPARK cohort, recruited via SPARK Research Match in spring 2021. After data-quality exclusions, 936 of the original 1178 remained. The text does not say anyone was selected for sound sensitivity, so this counts as a clinical sample recruited for another condition (autism).
codes.instruments: DVMSQ screening algorithm (development version), used for the misophonia case definition. Abbreviated DMQ, used for dimensional scores only. Also given: IHS and DSM-Phono (hyperacusis and phonophobia measures).

case_definitions.definition: Clinically significant misophonia: meets all criteria of the DVMSQ screening algorithm
case_definitions.quote: 377 autistic adults (40.3% of the sample) met the criteria for hyperacusis, 332 (35.5%) met the criteria for misophonia, and 253 (27.0% of the whole sample) met criteria for both disorders simultaneously.

case_definitions.definition: Comorbid: meets DVMSQ misophonia criteria AND questionnaire-based hyperacusis criteria
case_definitions.quote: 253 (27.0% of the whole sample) met criteria for both disorders simultaneously.

codes.possible_duplicate: Dissertation Chapter 3. Same 936 SPARK adults as Chapter 2, the companion prevalence paper (part I). Complete overlap with the autistic sample in Williams, Cascio & Woynaroski 2022 (DVMSQ validation); more than 95% overlap with Williams et al. 2023 (PROMIS GH-10).
codes.note: Funded by the Misophonia Research Fund (project labelled DST), but recruitment came from SPARK's general autistic adult pool, with no stated selection for sound sensitivity. Reviewer should check the recruitment wording in Chapter 2. This report repeats Chapter 2's prevalence, so use only one of the two. DMQ impairment bands are mentioned but not reported.

codes.sample: 412 adults aged 18–68 recruited on Prolific, not on the basis of misophonia. The sample was deliberately enriched for autism and ADHD: 64 autism only, 57 ADHD only, 43 both, 248 neither. People with hearing impairment or neurological disease were excluded.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ): trigger checklist plus the 23-item Composite Symptoms Severity subscale (0–92). Also used: IHS (hyperacusis), Phonophobia Severity Scale, CATI, ASRS, ADC.

case_definitions.definition: Clinical misophonia: DMQ Composite Symptoms score ≥ 41.4, among participants with clinically significant hyperacusis (IHS total ≥ 56)
Clinical misophonia: DMQ Composite Symptoms score ≥ 41.4, among participants without clinically significant hyperacusis (IHS total < 56)

case_definitions.quote: we applied binary thresholds to identify participants with likely clinically significant hyperacusis (Total IHS ≥ 56...), misophonia (≥ 41.4 on the Composite Symptoms subscale

codes.possible_duplicate: No overlapping sample is reported. The same group (Igelström, Linköping) has related Prolific studies, e.g., Pieslinger et al. 2025 and Bang & Igelström 2024. Check whether any of these share participants.
codes.note: Hyperacusis group sizes are not printed; I back-calculated about 170 with and about 240 without. The total of 98/412 assumes no missing data, so please verify it. No misophonia counts are given by diagnosis group. The sample was enriched for autism and ADHD (about 40%), so the overall prevalence is not representative of the general population.

codes.sample: 185 adults in Australia (18–64 y; 145 female, 35 male, 5 non-binary). 148 (80%) were university students and the rest were members of the public. They were recruited through social media, SONA and campus flyers. Recruitment materials did not mention misophonia: "we wanted to ensure our sample was blind to the study's aims."

Some misokinesia percentages don't match their counts (female 17/145 printed as 14.8%). The misophonia figures checked all match. The sample is mostly female and self-selected through a general survey on sounds and visuals.

codes.sample: 300 adult US MTurk/CloudResearch participants recruited for an online misophonia screening (A-MISO-S). Not recruited for misophonia. Low (<4) and high (>10) scorers were invited to a main study (111 invited, 98 completed: 58 low, 40 high).
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (6 Likert items, summed score; subclinical <4, moderate >10). Also a single self-report item on experiencing misophonia (1–5), shown after a definition; no counts reported for this item.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S summed score >10 (moderate misophonia or above), among screened participants who also passed data-quality checks
case_definitions.quote: We recruited 300 participants for the initial misophonia screening... From this initial screening, 111 participants (low misophonia: n = 67; high misophonia: n = 44) were invited

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a PsyArXiv preprint; a later journal version of the same sample may exist. Data are on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/X2UDK).
codes.note: Check the denominator. The 44 scored >10 and passed the quality checks, but the number of the 300 who passed those checks is not reported, so 44/300 is a lower bound. Demographic matching adds some uncertainty about whether every valid >10 scorer was invited. OSF raw data could give exact counts. If the denominator is judged insufficient, use I3_no_counts.

codes.sample: 245 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers (adults 18-65; 63% male; 81% US residents), recruited in two waves: wave 1 had no misophonia-targeted advertising, while wave 2 'did have advertising that targets individuals with misophonia'. The prevalence reported pools both waves, and no per-wave counts are given.
codes.instruments: MisoQuest (14 items, 5-point Likert scale; cut-off ≥61 of 70 per Siepsiak et al., 2020b). Also an n-back working-memory task.

case_definitions.definition: MisoQuest score ≥61 (out of 70)
case_definitions.location: Results, Hypothesis One, p. 35 (cut-off on p. 32; N on p. 29)
case_definitions.quote: The MisoQuest misophonia rate in the sample was not found to be at the expected prevalence of 15-20%. The sample recorded a rate of 4.7% (n = 12).

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a master's thesis (Watson, FHSU 2022). Check for any later article or conference abstract from the same MTurk data.
codes.note: I1 concern: one of the two waves was deliberately aimed at people with misophonia, and the 4.7% figure combines both waves. The unselected wave 1 is not reported on its own. Denominator unclear: 4.7% of 245 is not 12, and 12/255 = 4.7%. The median split has no group counts. The reviewer needs to decide whether the mixed sample is acceptable.

codes.sample: Ch.2 Study 3: 897 English-speaking adults from Reddit ASMR forum (r/ASMR), 820 completed MAQ; recruited for ASMR interest, not misophonia. Other chapters (students n=187, n=100; ASMR Facebook/Reddit n=457) did not measure misophonia.
codes.instruments: 21-item modified Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ; Johnson, 2014; Dozier, 2015), Ch.2 Study 3 only.
codes.possible_duplicate: Ch.2 published as Roberts, Beath & Boag (2018), Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice, doi:10.1037/cns0000168 (same Study 3 MAQ data).

Text cut mid-Ch.6 discussion; rest is discussion and ethics appendices, unlikely to add counts.

codes.sample: Combined N=2807 US/international adults from 5 studies. Eligible subsamples: PROA general-population Prolific sample (n=1403); NDD sample of autistic/ADHD adults plus controls (n=478); AUT autistic adults (n=295). ClinDST (n=516) was recruited for DST, so it is excluded. LAB (n=115) was recruited with and without DST complaints.

AUT has 16 diagnosed cases; the other 279 are coded as missing, so 16/295 counts diagnoses only. LAB and the pooled general-population group involve selection on DST. ClinDST is excluded (E1).

codes.sample: 936 legally independent autistic adults aged 18–80 from the US SPARK cohort, recruited in Spring 2021 via SPARK Research Match. The study used a vague title and was not advertised as a sound-sensitivity study. 1271 consented and 936 were analysed (894 with no missing data); 63.0% were female. This is a clinical sample recruited for another condition (autism).

codes.possible_duplicate: Same SPARK sample as companion preprint 'DST Disorders... II: Demographic and Clinical Correlates' (Williams 2024, osf.io/syx9b). Overlaps with Williams' 2024 dissertation, Williams 2023 PROMIS Global-10 study and any published version.
codes.note: Autistic adults = clinical sample recruited for another condition. Main definition: DVMSQ caseness, 332/936. The p17 sex sentence has a typo ('Misophonia: Hyperacusis:'), but Table 2 confirms 261/590 F and 71/346 M. DMQ-IMP bands apply only within DVMSQ cases; counts not printed. Denominator for Table 1 percentages not stated.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a popular-science magazine article (The Synapse, student science magazine) that summarises other people's research on misokinesia.
codes.instruments: None administered. It only mentions a misokinesia sensitivity questionnaire from Jaswal and colleagues, cited secondhand.
codes.possible_duplicate: The cited figures (31.7% misophonia–misokinesia comorbidity; ~38% responding "yes" to misokinesia) come from Jaswal et al. (2021, Scientific Reports, UBC). That primary study should be assessed separately if it was retrieved.
codes.note: This is a narrative magazine/commentary piece with no original data. The prevalence figures are cited secondhand and are mostly about misokinesia, not misophonia: "nearly 38 percent of participants responded 'yes'"; "co-morbidity rate for misophonia and misokinesia is a staggering 31.7 percent." The full text was available (pp. 26–27).

codes.sample: Undergraduates at Wilfrid Laurier University, Canada, in an online survey advertised as about student quality of life, with no mention of sound tolerance. 3096 took part; 2080 remained after data-quality checks (435 male, 1600 female, 45 non-cisgendered; mean age 20.47). Because of a Qualtrics error, MQ severity data exist for only 1033 participants (n=1025 in Table 2).
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ): severity ≥7 plus Emotions & Behaviours mean ≥2. Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ): total ≥39. Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ): diagnostic algorithm giving clinical or subclinical. Also used: IHS (hyperacusis), AQ, MSCS.

case_definitions.definition: MQ: severity ≥7 and mean Emotions & Behaviours ≥2 (clinical misophonia)
case_definitions.quote: For the MQ, 12% (n = 128) of the sample met the clinical cut-off for misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: MQ clinical cut-off, by gender (women / men / non-cisgender)
case_definitions.quote: with 14% (n = 114) of women meeting cut-off, while 10% (n = 20) of men, and 25% (n = 6) of those with non-cisgender expression met the cut-off

case_definitions.definition: DMQ total ≥39 (severe symptoms = misophonia)
case_definitions.quote: For the DMQ, misophonia was reported in 18% (n = 374) of the sample.

case_definitions.definition: DMQ ≥39, by gender (women / men / non-cisgender)
case_definitions.quote: Prevalence according to DMQ was 21% (n = 328) among women, 6% (n = 24) among men, and 61% (n = 23) among non-cisgendered participants.

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ algorithm: clinical misophonia
case_definitions.quote: The DVMSQ detected clinical misophonia in 13% (n = 272) of the sample.

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ algorithm: subclinical misophonia
case_definitions.quote: 14% of the sample (n = 287) were suggested to have sub-clinical misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ clinical, by gender (women / men / non-cisgender)
case_definitions.quote: 14% of women (n = 230), 4% of men (n = 18), and 58% (n = 22) of non-cisgendered participants met criteria for clinical misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: DVMSQ clinical + subclinical combined (derived 272+287)
case_definitions.quote: this suggests that approximately 27% of post-secondary students are experiencing distress as a result of misophonia triggers

case_definitions.definition: Clinical misophonia on at least one of MQ, DMQ or DVMSQ
case_definitions.quote: 15% (n = 310) of the participants had clinically significant misophonia according to at least one of the MQ, DMQ, or DVMSQ

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a PsyArXiv preprint under review at PLOS ONE, so a journal version may exist. The same survey data (Oct 2023–Apr 2024) are also used in ref [35], Wickie, Van Esch & Scheerer, "Social success in a noisy world" (unpublished).
codes.note: Numbers disagree: MQ denominator unstated (128/1033≈12.4%); non-cis percentages imply n≈24 (MQ) and n≈38 (DMQ, DVMSQ), not 45. The "any measure" count (310) is below the DMQ count (374), which is impossible. Gender subtotals sum to 375 (DMQ) and 270 (DVMSQ), not the totals. Check the Supplementary Materials.

codes.sample: 96 college students at Texas State University (67 F, 29 M; mean age 20.91), recruited via ads, flyers and emails for a larger study on cognitive function and clinical correlates of misophonia. Only inclusion criteria: age 18-65, adequate vision, English fluency, no major neurological history. Groups were formed after testing from MQ scores.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014), including the MQ-3 single-item severity scale with clinical cutoff ≥7. Also MINI 7.0, DASS-21, STAI-6, I-7 and BFIS.

case_definitions.definition: MQ-3 (Misophonia Severity Scale) score >=7 = clinically significant misophonia (misophonia group); <=6 = control
case_definitions.quote: a score of 7 or more is considered clinical (misophonia group) and those with 6 or lower are seen as sub-clinical (control group)... Control (n=64) Misophonia (n=32) Entire Sample (N=96)

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a Master's thesis (Herrera, 2022; chair A. Abramovitch). The same sample may appear in a later journal article by Abramovitch/Herrera et al. on neuropsychological and clinical correlates of misophonia. Check for overlap.
codes.note: Recruitment was for a study about misophonia (p.18), so self-selection is possible, which may explain the high 33% rate. The group rule is ambiguous: 'Then, for our misophonia group, we used the upper quartile of the clinical group' (p.25). The group sizes still add up to N=96, and the control MQ-3 mean is 2.25 (SD 0.80). The reviewer should check whether 32/96 truly means MQ-3 >=7.

codes.sample: 638 undergraduate students aged 18–26 at Baskent University, Ankara, Turkey, sampled from faculties with weighting by faculty size. There were two subsamples: EFA N=420 and CFA N=218. The prevalence count is reported only for the CFA subsample (N=218; 62% female).
codes.instruments: Turkish version of the Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014). It has 17 scored items plus a severity item rated 1–15, where ≥7 means clinically significant misophonia.

case_definitions.definition: MQ severity scale (1–15) score ≥7 = clinically significant misophonia
case_definitions.location: Page 15, Internal consistency and discriminant validity section; Table 4
case_definitions.quote: 218 kişilik örneklemde 7 ve üzeri işaretleme yapanların oranı %38 (N =83) olarak bulunmuştur.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Other Turkish studies cited here (Öz, 2016 thesis; Alluşoğlu, 2020 thesis) are separate samples.
codes.note: The count is reported only for the CFA subsample (n=218). No count is given for the EFA subsample (n=420) or for the full 638. Table 4 also shows 135 without misophonia and 83 with. The paper is listed as 2020 (submission year), but it was published in 2022, Psikoloji Çalışmaları 42(1):231–255. The discussion again gives the rate as 38%.

codes.sample: Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 had separate, apparently unselected participant groups. The abstract calls them a "neurotypical population", probably university participants (UC Santa Cruz). No sample sizes appear in the retrieved text.
codes.instruments: None reported in the retrieved text. Sounds were rated for discomfort, unpleasantness and bodily sensations. The text does not show whether any misophonia questionnaire (e.g., MQ) was given.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is the supplementary material for Samermit, Saal & Davidenko (2019), "Cross-Sensory Stimuli Modulate Reactions to Aversive Sounds", Multisensory Research. The main article should be assessed as the primary record.
codes.note: Only the abstract and an empty "Supplementary Material" heading were retrieved; the supplement content is missing. The abstract does not say misophonia was measured (neurotypical sample; only implications for misophonia). If the full texts show no misophonia measure, exclude as E2/not_misophonia. Check the main article and supplement.

codes.sample: German online cross-sectional sample, aged 16 or older. Recruited via social media (Facebook, Instagram) and university mailing lists, from both "groups of individuals identifying as having misophonia" and "unspecific groups". Psychology students received course credit. N=952 completed the GSIS screening scale; 621 completed the symptom part; 86.7% female; mean age 33.85.
codes.instruments: Berlin Misophonia Questionnaire Revised (BMQ-R), including the GSIS screening scale (4 items, sum 0–20; >12 = 'potentially affected' track). Also S-Five-E, MisoQuest (German translation), AQ, DPSS-R, STICSA, BITe, DERS, NAQ, BEAQ, WHODAS 2.0 and IPQ-MH.

case_definitions.definition: BMQ-R GSIS sum score >12 (≥13), the pragmatic cut-off for the 'potentially affected' track. The derived complement is 93.3%.
case_definitions.location: Page 25 (Results, GSIS); cut-off on pp. 20–21; N on p. 24
case_definitions.quote: Only 6.7% of participants had/showed a GSIS sum score lower than 13 (chosen score for non-affected individuals), whereas more than half of the sample indicated the highest score of 20 (49.8%).

case_definitions.definition: BMQ-R GSIS maximum sum score of 20
case_definitions.quote: more than half of the sample indicated the highest score of 20 (49.8%)

codes.possible_duplicate: Probably the same sample as the peer-reviewed BMQ-R validation article by Remmert, Schmidt, Mussel & Eid (2022, PLOS ONE). The earlier BMQ version (Remmert 2017 B.Sc. thesis, ref 22) used a different, earlier sample.
codes.note: Mixed recruitment: misophonia self-identification groups pooled with unspecific groups and student lists. No unselected subsample is reported separately. Authors say the sample "mainly comprises potentially affected individuals". This is not strictly E1, but the proportions are heavily selection-biased. Reviewer to decide on E1. GSIS cut-off is pragmatic, not validated.

codes.sample: Study 1: 265 general Japanese adults recruited online through a crowdsourcing service (CrowdWorks) in November 2023 (128 men, 137 women; mean age 40.78, range 20–68). They were not recruited for misophonia. Study 2 (test–retest; 142 adults at T1 and 120 at T2, from Freeasy) reports no category counts.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S-J, the Japanese version of the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (6 items, 0–24), using Schröder et al. (2013) severity bands. Other measures: HQ, DPSS-R-J, J-PI32, DASS-21.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S-J total ≥5 (mild or worse; 'clinically significant misophonia')
case_definitions.quote: Overall, 76% of the 265 respondents had clinically significant misophonia (total score: 5–24), and the remaining 24% had subclinical misophonia (total score: 0–4).

case_definitions.quote: Mild (Total Score 5–9) 105（39.6） 55 50

case_definitions.quote: Moderate (Total Score 10–14) 83（31.3） ... Severe (Total Score 15–19) 11（4.2） ... Extreme (Total Score 20–24) 2（0.8） ... Note. n = 265.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S-J total ≥15 (severe or extreme)
case_definitions.quote: Severe (Total Score 15–19) 11（4.2） 7 4 Extreme (Total Score 20–24) 2（0.8） 0 2 Note. n = 265.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S-J total 20–24 (extreme band)
case_definitions.quote: Extreme (Total Score 20–24) 2（0.8） 0 2

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Note that the cited Japanese MQ studies (Itoi et al. 2025; Yamazawa & Midorikawa 2025; Tada et al. 2022) used different samples.
codes.note: Table 3 also gives severity-band counts by sex (e.g., ≥5: 94 of 128 men and 107 of 137 women, derived). This is a general-population convenience sample from a crowdsourcing service; the authors flag possible selection bias. The A-MISO-S was given to everyone, without a screening item for misophonia. Study 2's T1 sample (n=142) has no prevalence data.

codes.sample: 256 Mandarin-speaking adults aged 18+ (186 female; mean age 25; 63% students). Recruited by snowball sampling on Chinese social media (WeChat, Weibo, Douban), Twitter, Reddit and the KCL recruitment circular. The text does not say recruitment was based on misophonia.
codes.instruments: S-Five (Mandarin) and S-Five-T; A-MISO-S (self-report); MQ, including the severity item with a cut-off of ≥7 (n=118); ad hoc items on knowing the term misophonia and identifying as having it; PHQ-9; GAD-7.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identified as having misophonia (ad hoc yes/no item)
case_definitions.quote: 85 participants (33%) stated they were aware of the term misophonia and 41 (16%) identified as having misophonia.

codes.possible_duplicate: May share data with an MSc thesis by Jingxin Wang / Qiaochu Wang (KCL) or a later journal version of this S-Five Mandarin validation. Check other Vitoratou S-Five reports.
codes.note: Self-identification is the only countable case definition. The MQ severity cut-off (≥7) is described, but no count is reported for it; the S-Five gives only means. The advert's wording isn't described, so check whether it was framed around misophonia. If self-identification isn't accepted as a case definition, the paper becomes I3_no_counts.

codes.sample: 703 adults in an online survey (728 completed; 25 excluded for failing attention checks). 396 came from Prolific (general population) and 307 from misophonia support groups on social media (a selected sample). The groups were split by self-identification: 315 identified with misophonia and 388 did not or were unsure.
codes.instruments: S-Five (continuous severity and factor scores, with no cut-off applied) and an ad hoc item: 'Do you identify with having misophonia?' (yes/no/unsure). Other measures: ASI-3, BCQ, DPSS-R, GAD-7, LESS-II and PHQ-9.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identifies with having misophonia ('yes' to 'Do you identify with having misophonia?'), in the COMBINED sample (Prolific + misophonia support groups)
case_definitions.location: Page 2 Abstract; Page 13 Table 1; Pages 6-7 Results
case_definitions.quote: A sample of 703 individuals, 315 of whom identified with having misophonia

codes.possible_duplicate: Probably the preprint of Wang, Vitoratou, Uglik-Marucha & Gregory (2022), Frontiers in Psychology, 'Emotion processes predicting outbursts and functional impact in misophonia'. Its Prolific sample may overlap with other S-Five reports by Vitoratou et al.
codes.note: The Prolific subsample (n=396) would meet I1, but its count of self-identified misophonia is not reported separately. The only count, 315/703, includes 307 people recruited from misophonia support groups, so it is not a prevalence estimate. The S-Five is reported only as medians and IQRs. Check the published version for source-specific counts.

codes.sample: Planned sample: 1000+ self-referred misophonics (recruited via BBC Radio 4 publicity, misophonia-hub.org) and ~200 normative controls (students, acquaintances, Prolific/Testable), aged 18-70. No data reported.
codes.instruments: Sussex Misophonia Scale (cut-off 50.5/156); bespoke hearing questionnaire with a misophonia self-report item; trigger list (51 triggers); plus AQ, GSQ, ASI-3, MAIA, OCI, POEM, pattern glare test, sound rating task
codes.possible_duplicate: This is the pre-registration for the Sussex 'Profiling Misophonia in Adults' study (Ward, Rinaldi, Simner et al.). Any later results paper may report SMS cut-off rates in the normative control group and should be assessed on its own.
codes.note: Pre-registered method and analysis plan with no results (p.1: "Pre-registered Method and Analysis Plan"; p.3: "This data has not been analysed"). The plan includes classifying controls with the SMS cut-off of 50.5, but no counts are given. Controls who believe they have misophonia are asked not to take part, so the control sample is partly selected.

codes.sample: Not reported in the retrieved text. The file holds only the DVMSQ v1.5 questionnaire and its scoring instructions. It gives no participants, recruitment details or results.
codes.instruments: Duke-Vanderbilt Misophonia Screening Questionnaire (DVMSQ v1.5): a screening item (S1), 18 Likert items, and a theory-based diagnostic algorithm (criteria A–F) defining clinically significant and sub-clinical misophonia.
codes.possible_duplicate: This file is probably the instrument supplement to the DVMSQ validation by Williams et al. (2022), possibly published in Frontiers in Psychology. Check the full validation paper, which may report algorithm-based case counts.
codes.note: The PDF has only the questionnaire, scoring rules and the algorithm (clinically significant = A–F; sub-clinical = A–D without F). No methods, sample or results, so I1 and I3 can't be checked. Retrieve the full validation report. If this record is only the instrument, exclude it under E4_design (no data).

codes.sample: 44 Portuguese adults (≥18 y), recruited for a study of depressive symptoms, not misophonia: 20 primary healthcare patients (Aveiro) invited by their family physician and 24 psychiatric outpatients (Coimbra). 82% female; mean age 48. Data collected Oct–Nov 2018.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), translated into Portuguese and given by the researcher within a structured clinical interview (cut-off ≥5 = clinically significant; bands 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 severe, 20–24 extreme). HAM-D 17 for depressive symptoms.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥5 (clinically significant misophonic symptoms), total sample
case_definitions.quote: The prevalence of clinically significant misophonic symptoms of the sample is 25% (n=11).

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥5, primary healthcare subsample
case_definitions.quote: Of people from primary healthcare group, 25% (n=5) show clinically significant depressive symptoms and 25% (n=5) reveal clinically significant misophonic symptoms.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥5, psychiatric outpatient subsample
case_definitions.quote: of people from psychiatric outpatient setting, 54% (n=13) show clinically significant depressive symptoms and 25% (n=6) present clinically significant misophonic symptoms

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S moderate band 10–14 (≥10; no severe/extreme cases), total sample

codes.possible_duplicate: The consent form names a shared study ("Misofonia - a relação com sintomas depressivos, mecanismos de coping e impacto na vida diária") with co-investigator Cláudia Marina Cruz. Her companion master's thesis (on coping and impact) probably uses the same 44 participants.
codes.note: This is a master's thesis (MIM) from Coimbra, dated Feb 2019 on the cover. The sample was not selected for misophonia, but participants were told what misophonia is before the interview. The A-MISO-S ≥5 cut-off is not validated. Subgroups by depression status are also reported: 5/26 (19%) without and 6/18 (33%) with clinically significant depressive symptoms (Table VI, p.14–15).

codes.sample: 44 adult Portuguese patients, quasi-random sample of people attending consultations in primary care (Aveiro, n=20) and secondary psychiatric care (Coimbra, n=24), Oct–Nov 2018. They were not recruited for misophonia. Mean age 48.4; 81.8% female.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (Portuguese translation, completed by the interviewer in a structured clinical interview; bands 0-4 subclinical, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate). Items adapted from MAQ, MCR, MER and MIS were asked only of people scoring ≥5.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥5 (significant misophonic symptoms), whole sample
case_definitions.quote: since the presence of significant misophonic symptoms was only considered if the A-MISO-S score was ≥5 ... 11 patients with significant symptoms were found (25% of the sample).

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S 5-9 (mild), whole sample (3 primary + 5 secondary)
A-MISO-S 10-14 (moderate), whole sample (2 primary + 1 secondary)
A-MISO-S ≥5, primary care subsample
case_definitions.quote: 5 patients with significant symptoms were found in primary healthcare (25% of the primary healthcare patients)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥5, secondary (psychiatric) care subsample
case_definitions.quote: 6 in secondary healthcare (25% of the secondary healthcare participants)

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S severe (15-19) or extreme (20-24)
case_definitions.quote: No patients with severe or extreme misophonic symptoms were found.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S >0 and <5 (negative reactions, subclinical)
case_definitions.quote: Negative reactions to certain sounds (scores>0 and <5) were found in 11 (25%) participants.

codes.possible_duplicate: Master's thesis (cover dated Feb 2019). It thanks co-researcher Sandra Assunção, and the interview form covers misophonia and depressive symptoms. A companion thesis may use the same 44-patient sample.
codes.note: Sample came from clinics for other reasons, so it is eligible as a clinical/primary-care sample. A-MISO-S was given by an interviewer rather than self-completed. The two care settings are reported separately in Table III. Table III percentages are calculated out of all 44 participants, not out of each setting.

codes.sample: Survey data (n = 1,881) from the authors' study of functional impairment in misophonia (Möllmann et al., 2023). This OSF file does not say how participants were recruited or whether they were selected for misophonia.
codes.instruments: AMISOS (Amsterdam Misophonia Scale), AMISOS-R, MAQ (Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire), MQ (sumscore, severity scale and Emotions & Behaviors subscale), and MSL (named in the README).
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a supplement to Möllmann A, Heinrichs N, Illies L, Potthast N, Kley H (2023). The central role of symptom severity and associated characteristics for functional impairment in misophonia. Front Psychiatry 14:1112472, doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1112472. It uses the same n = 1,881 sample.
codes.note: OSF supplement with ROC tables only (sensitivity, specificity, Youden, LR+/LR- per sumscore). It gives no count meeting any cutoff and no count positive on the reference standard (functional impairment), so prevalence can't be derived. Recruitment isn't described. Screen the linked Frontiers article separately; it may report counts.

codes.sample: German online survey (bachelor thesis, FU Berlin, 2017). Main study N=494, analysed N=490 (85.9% women, ages 15-66). Recruited via >25 Facebook groups (tinnitus and misophonia groups, anxiety/depression groups, psychology/survey groups), the website misophonie-aktuell.de and FU psychology students. Separate pilot (n=32) included only self-described sound-sensitive people.
codes.instruments: Berliner Misophonie Fragebogen (BMF; early version of the BMQ). Groups were formed from the 4-item sound-intolerance score (GI-S, MA1-MA4, range 0-20) plus a hyperacusis item (HA2). Validation measures: GÜF, STAXI-2, FEEL-E.

case_definitions.definition: 'Potentielle Misophonie': GI-S (4 sound-intolerance items, 0-20) score of 19 or 20; people with hyperacusis (HA2 'no') assigned elsewhere
case_definitions.quote: Personen, die einen GI-S von 19 oder 20 aufwiesen, wurden zur Gruppe „Potentielle Misophonie“ gezählt. ... Potentielle Misophonie 267 54.5

case_definitions.definition: 'Grenzbereich' (borderline): GI-S score 13-18, described as heightened sound intolerance and potential misophonia
case_definitions.quote: Alle Personen mit Werten zwischen 13 und 18 wurden zur Gruppe „Grenzbereich“ zugeordnet ... Grenzbereich 150 30.6

codes.possible_duplicate: Bachelor thesis by Nico Remmert (2017), posted on OSF in 2021. It may share data or authors with Remmert et al.'s later BMQ / BMQ-R validation papers (Schmidt, Mussel, Eid). Check for overlapping samples.
codes.note: Recruitment was mixed: partly misophonia/tinnitus groups and a misophonia website, partly psychology/survey groups and anxiety/depression groups. No unselected subsample is reported with its own counts. Author (p.59): sample 'hauptsächlich Menschen ... die sich selbst als betroffen ansehen'. Case definition uses generic sound-intolerance items. Reviewer to decide between E1 and eligible.

codes.sample: 395 Spanish-speaking adults who were interviewed. The title and abstract describe them as "adults with suspected misophonia". How they were recruited (general pool or selected for misophonia) cannot be told from the retrieved text.
codes.instruments: A new self-perception questionnaire with 4 blocks: auditory triggers, visual triggers, emotional closeness to the person making the sound, and impact on daily life. Items are on misophonia triggers. No cut-off or case definition is visible in the retrieved text.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a SAGE/Authorea preprint (doi:10.31124/advance.24878439.v1). There may be a later peer-reviewed version from the same authors (Castillo Fierro, Muñoz Quezada, Lucero Mondaca).
codes.note: Only the preprint wrapper was retrieved: the abstract and Appendix 2 (item KMO/alpha values). The main manuscript, Tables 1–4 and Appendix 1 are hosted files on Authorea and are missing. Without them we cannot see recruitment (wording such as "suspected misophonia" suggests a possibly selected sample, i.e. E1) or any counts. Get the main manuscript file.

codes.sample: Nationally representative probability-based sample of U.S. adults from Ipsos KnowledgePanel (N = 4005). The sample was not recruited for misophonia. The analysed groups were a misophonia group (n = 185) and a symptom-free control group (n = 1644).
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S; cut-off ≥10) and the Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ) Severity Scale (cut-off ≥7). Both were used together to define cases.

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S ≥10 AND MQ Severity Scale ≥7 (clinical cut-offs on both measures)
case_definitions.quote: Participants were drawn from a large, nationally representative sample of U.S. adults (N = 4005). In this study, the misophonia group (n = 185) included participants who met the clinical cutoff on both the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (≥10 [A-MISO-S]...) and the Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ) Severity Scale (≥7

codes.possible_duplicate: Same KnowledgePanel dataset as Dixon et al., 2024 (J Psychopathol Clin Sci, 'Prevalence, phenomenology, and impact of misophonia...US adults'), which reported 4.6%. The text says 'see Dixon et al., 2024 for full details'.
codes.note: This report gives no prevalence figure of its own. The percentage is derived from n = 185 out of N = 4005, and it matches the 4.6% the paper cites from Dixon et al., 2024. All analyses used weights, but it is unclear whether n = 185 is weighted or unweighted. The prevalence estimate should come from Dixon et al., 2024. A-MISO-S ≤4 together with MQ ≤3 defines the controls, not cases.

codes.sample: Japanese adults, online survey. Control group of 500 recruited via an Internet research service (iBRIDGE), gender-matched (90% female); 387 analysed after excluding people with mental/physical disease and invalid responders. There was also a separate self-identified misophonia group (n=63 analysed), which is not eligible.
codes.instruments: Japanese Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ-J): Symptom Scale, Emotions and Behaviors Scale, Severity Scale (1–15); cut-off ≥7 on the Severity Scale (Wu et al., 2014). Also GSQ, HQ, OCI-R, STAI, BDI-II, WSAS.

case_definitions.definition: MQ-J Misophonia Severity Scale ≥7 (clinically significant misophonia symptoms), control (non-misophonia) group
case_definitions.quote: Based on this criterion, 58 (92 %) misophonic and 103 (23 %) control participants were classified as having significant misophonia symptoms.

case_definitions.definition: MQ-J Severity Scale ≥7 among control-pool participants excluded for physical or mental illness
case_definitions.quote: of the 63 control group participants with physical or mental illnesses who were excluded, 25 (39.6 %) scored 7 or higher.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Tada et al. (2022), which also used the MQ in a Japanese sample, is cited as a different study.
codes.note: Denominators don't agree: 103/387 = 26.6%, not 23%. 103/448 (Table 1 N, which includes the misophonia group) = 23%. Table 4 control rows add up to about 386. 113 controls were excluded, but only 63 are described as ill. Do not count the self-identified misophonia group's 58/63. Controls were gender-matched to a mostly female group.

codes.sample: 15 parents of autistic children aged 6–17 (USA), recruited via word of mouth, community outreach and autism organizations. Prior misophonia/hyperacusis/phonophobia diagnosis was not required. Excluded: children with ODD, schizophrenia or OCD. Data collected Nov 2022–Mar 2023.
codes.instruments: Qualitative focus group and individual interviews guided by PMHQ-2 items (Appendix B), used as discussion prompts and not scored; online survey with demographics, including parent-reported child diagnosis. Content analysis was used to build the I-DST inventory.

case_definitions.definition: Parent-reported existing formal misophonia diagnosis of the child (demographic item, not a misophonia assessment)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same project and procedures as Carson et al. (2025), the PMHQ study in the International Journal of Audiology. The survey and interview data were also used to develop the PMHQ-4 (in review), so the sample may overlap.
codes.note: Qualitative content-analysis study. The n (%) counts are for themes only, not misophonia cases, and there is no scored misophonia measure or interview diagnosis. The only figure is a parent-reported prior diagnosis, 0/15 (Table 1). If the reviewer accepts that as an ad hoc case definition, this autism sample could be reconsidered. Alternative reason: E2/I3.

codes.sample: 200 adolescents aged 12–18 (123 female, 77 male) who attended a child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient clinic in Ankara, Türkiye, April 2024–April 2025. They were recruited as clinic attendees, not for misophonia. Exclusions: diagnosed ASD, psychosis, neurological disease, IQ ≤80, ENT conditions, uncorrected hearing impairment. 96% had a psychiatric diagnosis.

The self-report AMISOS-R cut-off is ≥11. ASD was excluded. Unrelated inconsistency: the text says female sex was more common in the Misophonia (+) group, but the regression gives OR 0.41 for female sex.

codes.sample: 77 children and adolescents aged 0-18 (mean age 11.17±4.26; 53.2% male) referred to a child psychiatry clinic in Istanbul through the KORDEP COVID-19 telepsychiatry support line, May 2020 to February 2021. This is a clinical sample seeking general mental-health help, not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Clinician telephone psychiatric interview. The K-SADS-PL-T does not cover misophonia, so it was screened with 'appropriate clinical questions' in the interview. CGI-S and CGAS were also used. No named misophonia scale and no explicit diagnostic criteria are given.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Misophonia was diagnosed over the phone using unspecified 'clinical questions' (p.3), not a validated tool or stated criteria. Check that this meets I2 as a clinical interview. Table 1 percentages use n=77. Small inconsistency: 81.6% (n=62) had any diagnosis, but Table 1 gives 20+41=61. Children under 6 were assessed from parent report only.

codes.sample: 30 normal-hearing adults aged 18–30 recruited by purposive sampling: 15 diagnosed with misophonia (12 F, 3 M) and 15 controls (9 F, 6 M). Case-control ABR study at AIISH, Mysore, India. No unselected screened pool is reported.
codes.instruments: Schröder et al. diagnostic criteria; MisoQuest; Revised Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (RAMISO-S) for severity (0–10 none, 11–20 mild, 21–30 moderate, 31–40 severe); THI and MKHQ used to exclude tinnitus/hyperacusis
codes.possible_duplicate: Same authors/institute run other misophonia ABR/evoked-potential studies (e.g., Aryal & Prabhu 2023 J Otol; 2024 Aud Vestib Res; Madappally et al. 2025). Recruitment pools could overlap, but none is clearly the same sample.
codes.note: Case-control design with purposive sampling. The misophonia group was chosen because it had misophonia: "only those scoring 21 or higher were included" (p.3). The severity split (10 moderate, 5 severe; p.3) applies only within this selected group. No screening denominator is given, so prevalence cannot be derived. Controls were not reported as screened from an unselected pool.

codes.sample: 495 students from Iranian public universities / medical sciences faculties (Tehran, Beheshti, Iran, Allameh Tabatabai), recruited by convenience sampling; not recruited for misophonia. Table 1: 380 female (78.4%), 84 male (17.3%); mean age 24.10±6.01.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ, Wu et al., 2014), including a severity scale with a stated cut-off of 7; also the Sheehan Disability Scale, ASP-A, DPSS-R, MAACL-R and the Attention Control Scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a preprint (Authorea, 2023). Check whether a peer-reviewed article by Ghorbani, Mazaheri Asadi, Ashouri et al. reports the same 495-student sample, possibly with prevalence counts.
codes.note: Eligible sample, misophonia measured with the MQ. The Measures section (p.3) names a cut-off of 7 ("at least moderate sensitivity to sound"), but no number or percentage meeting it is reported. Table 1 is demographics only; Table 2 has only correlations and means/SDs (MQ total 29.75, SD 13.92). Results are SEM path coefficients.

codes.sample: 845 undergraduate students at the University of Nevada, Reno, recruited for an online survey about sensory sensitivities (April 2022–March 2023). 7 were screened out for epilepsy or seizures and 169 were excluded for neurological/psychiatric conditions or medication, leaving 669 analysed (465 F, 187 M, 15 non-binary, 2 not stated; mean age 20.1). A separate NIRS study had 9 participants.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (Schröder et al., 2013), with 6 items scored 0–4 and summed (range 0–24); Khalfa Hyperacusis Questionnaire (14 items); Functional Hearing Questionnaire (8 items); adapted online Pattern Glare Test.
codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly overlaps with other Haigh lab UNR student survey samples (e.g., Haigh et al., 2022/2023, Frontiers in Psychology; Torrens et al., 2024). The overlap is not confirmed.
codes.note: The sample is eligible and the A-MISO-S was given, but it is reported only as a summed score used in Spearman correlations (rs(667)=.11) and a Figure 1A scatterplot. No cut-off, severity band or count is reported; the prevalence figures on p.3 are cited from other studies. Raw data are on OSF (osf.io/s9eyv), so counts may be derivable there.

codes.sample: Case-control experiment (TEOAE contralateral suppression). From a prior survey of Mysore University students, 40 people with misophonia symptoms were invited; 10 subclinical were excluded, leaving 30 cases (15 mild, 15 moderate-severe). 15 controls without misophonia were recruited separately. N=55 enrolled, 45 analysed.
codes.instruments: Revised Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (Revised A-MISO-S / RAMISO-S; 0-10 subclinical, 11-20 mild, 21-30 moderate-severe, 31-40 severe-extreme); misophonia assessment questionnaire in the screening survey; Kannada THI; LDL testing.

case_definitions.definition: Revised A-MISO-S score ≥11 (mild or worse) among people invited because of misophonia symptoms (selected sample, not a prevalence denominator)
case_definitions.quote: Out of the initial 40 participants invited to the study, ten individuals who exhibited subclinical symptoms with a score lower than ten on the Revised Amsterdam misophonia scale were excluded

codes.possible_duplicate: The screening survey of Mysore University students is probably the one in Aryal & Prabhu 2022, Neuroscience Research Notes 5(4):161 (ref 3, prevalence 23.28%). The same pool may also underlie other Aryal & Prabhu 2023-2024 experimental papers (auditory brainstem, cortical functioning).
codes.note: The participants analysed were invited because they had misophonia symptoms in a prior survey. This report does not give the size of the screened survey pool or how many people in it met any criterion, so prevalence cannot be worked out from it. The 30/40 count is within a sample already selected for misophonia. The reviewer should get the prevalence data from the 2022 survey article instead.

codes.sample: 606 young adults in Canada (726 took part, 606 had complete questionnaires), aged 18–32. 77.1% women, 64.4% university students. Recruited through flyers on Dalhousie University campuses, social media and email; people with confirmed neuropsychiatric disorders were excluded. Recruitment was not based on misophonia.

codes.note: No case counts are printed; percentages refer to N=606. Mild+ is 24.50% in most places but 24.60% (CI 21.3–28.2) in 2.4.1. Table 3 has n=139 with misophonia (22.9% of 606), 49 with hyperacusis (vs ~52) and 71 with tinnitus (vs 77), so it does not match. Fig. 1F (severity bands) has no values in the extracted text. Check it.

codes.sample: Phase 2: US adult community sample recruited through Amazon MTurk (ages 18–65, English fluency, US residence). No misophonia-based selection. Of 800 recruited, 424 passed the data-integrity checks and were analysed (54.5% male, mean age 37.7). The Phase 1 interview and feedback samples (n=10+10+10) were selected for misophonia and are excluded.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ, including the severity/impairment item), A-MISO-S (given as self-report), MAS-I, MAQ, MCRS, MERS, and the DMQ candidate items (sound type, trigger frequency, subscales).

codes.possible_duplicate: Listed as a 2024 unpublished report, but the text is the published Rosenthal et al. 2021, Front Psychol 12:709928, so likely the same report. The MTurk sample may overlap with other Duke-group community studies (Cassiello-Robbins 2020/2021); not confirmed.
codes.note: The main estimate is MQ severity ≥7: 67/424. Table 3 also gives the self-reported frequency of being bothered by sounds (e.g., >10 times/day 3.3%), but this is not a case definition. The DMQ symptoms cut-point (mean item score ≥1.8) was derived in this sample, but the number scoring above it is not reported. The A-MISO-S severity bands were given, but no counts are reported for them.

codes.sample: 201 undergraduate nursing students at Larestan University of Medical Sciences, Iran (convenience sample; 244 recruited from 310 dormitory residents; 12 excluded as incomplete, 21 as multivariate outliers); 131 female, 70 male; mean age 21.75 ± 2.15. Data collected Nov 2023–Jan 2024. Not recruited on the basis of misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014; Persian version), DASS-21, Y-BOCS, Buss-Perry Aggression Questionnaire
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Note: the related Yektatalab et al. 2022 prevalence study (Shiraz University of Medical Sciences) is cited but uses a different sample.
codes.note: The MQ was used only as a continuous score: "we used the total score dimensionally without applying a clinical cutoff" (p.4). Only the mean and SD (41.204 ± 7.460; Table 2), correlations and mediation coefficients are reported. No number or proportion meeting any misophonia case definition is given or can be derived.

codes.sample: Undergraduate psychology students at Wilfrid Laurier University, Canada (Sept 2023–Apr 2024). Recruitment was framed as a quality-of-life study and did not mention DST. Initial n=3096; final N=2095 after data-integrity exclusions (Mage 21.7; 1615 female, 436 male, 44 non-cis). DMQ SS completed by n=1699; IHS by n=1968.

codes.note: Table 1 % seem to use N=2095 (165/2095=7.9%, 325/2095=15.5%, 206/2095=9.8%), but only 1699 completed the DMQ (325/1699=19.1%). DVMSQ denominator not reported. Sub-clinical DVMSQ count not given. Table 1 swaps the male/female counts. Supplementary materials (not retrieved) may give fuller counts.

codes.sample: Pakistani college/university students aged 16–25. The abstract says 2,021 were recruited. 12 were excluded on PSYRATS screening for psychotic symptoms, leaving N = 2000 who completed the Urdu Duke Misophonia Scale. People with hearing disability, medical or psychological history, cognitive deficits or substance abuse were excluded. The paper describes sampling as both random and convenience.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Scale / Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (Rosenthal et al., 2021), Urdu translation, including a trigger-frequency item. PSYRATS was used for screening; OCI-R and ASI-3 were also given.

codes.possible_duplicate: The same N = 2000 / n = 428 sample was probably also used in the same authors' Urdu DMS validation paper ('to establish the reliability and validity of the scale') and possibly in a misophonia–OCD paper. Check other papers by Qurrah-tul-ain and Gul.
codes.note: The criterion used to classify the 428 is never stated. Sample sizes conflict: 2,021 recruited minus 12 = 2,009, not 2,000. Sampling is called both random and convenience. It is unclear whether the 196 frequency-based cases came from the 428 or all 2000; the reviewer should check before choosing a denominator.

codes.sample: Turkish medical students aged 18-28 at Süleyman Demirel University, Isparta. 500 were given the scales, 12 declined and 43 were excluded (psychiatric disorder, psychotropic medication or hearing problems). Analysed n=445 (249 female, 196 male). The sample was not recruited for misophonia.

Table 2 gives single trigger-item answers (e.g., eating sounds 276/445), but these are not case definitions.

codes.sample: 25 undergraduates (mean age 19.6, 96% female), described as nonclinical but "prescreened for elevated misophonia symptoms"

codes.note: Conference abstract (full text is the abstract). Page 1: "All participants were prescreened for elevated misophonia symptoms." The analysed sample was selected for misophonia. The abstract gives no size for the screened pool and no number meeting a criterion. Only correlations are reported. If the prescreening data were available elsewhere, the study might become eligible.

codes.sample: Consecutive adult psychiatric inpatients (dementia excluded) screened at admission, Klinik für Psychiatrie, Psychosomatik und Psychotherapie Bamberg, Germany, 16 Dec 2019–6 Mar 2020. n=194 screened (109 F, 85 M; age 18–87, mean 46.7). Mostly affective (F3) and substance-use (F1) disorders. Of the 46 who screened positive, 27 completed the MAQ.

codes.possible_duplicate: Medical dissertation (Loch, Regensburg 2021). No journal article is cited in the text, but any later publication from the Bamberg psychiatric inpatient sample (Hajak, Trapp) may report the same data.
codes.note: The primary prevalence estimate is 46/194 (23.7%). Only 27 of the 46 screen-positives completed the MAQ, so MAQ bands do not use the full screened denominator. Participation in screening was voluntary; the number of admissions offered the screening form is not reported. 3 patients with dementia were excluded after the fact. The screening tool is a non-validated adaptation.

codes.sample: 74 adults (35 in Exp 1, 5 excluded; 44 in Exp 2), Amsterdam. No separate counts for the unselected (student) subsample.
