codes.sample: 47 patients diagnosed with OCD by DSM-5 criteria (29 women, 18 men; mean age 29.57 ± 10.9), Çukurova University Faculty of Medicine, Adana, Turkey. Clinical sample recruited for OCD, not for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Symptom List (Mizofoni Belirti Listesi, MBL); Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3; Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (BİFÖ); Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale
codes.possible_duplicate: Conference abstract (61st National Psychiatry Congress, 2025, SB-003); described as a preliminary study, so a later full article on the same OCD sample may exist.
codes.note: Eligible sample (OCD patients) and a misophonia-specific measure (MBL). However, only the mean total score is reported ("MBL toplam puanı 108,08 ± 32,47") plus correlations. No cut-off, severity band or number/proportion of misophonia cases is given. This is a conference abstract only; check any full article for counts.

codes.sample: 122 adults at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York: 46 typically developing (TD), 42 with autism (ASD) and 34 with misophonia. The misophonia group was recruited for misophonia. The ASD and TD groups were not recruited for misophonia, so they are eligible subsamples (ASD is a clinical sample recruited for another condition).
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale (A-MISO-S), completed by all participants. Also BAPQ, LSAS avoidance items and ADOS-2.
codes.possible_duplicate: The misophonia group probably comes from the Mount Sinai misophonia research programme (Gu, Schiller, Foss-Feig; funded by the Misophonia Research Fund). Participants may overlap with other papers from this group, e.g., Banker et al. 2025, Nat Mental Health.
codes.note: Page 4 says all participants completed the A-MISO-S. However, the main text and Table 1 give no A-MISO-S scores, no cut-off counts, and no misophonia counts for the ASD or TD groups; A-MISO-S results are not reported at all. Supplemental Materials (inclusion criteria, recruitment) were not retrieved. Check them for A-MISO-S counts in the ASD/TD groups, which would change the decision.

codes.sample: 112 parents (one per child) from a child psychiatry outpatient clinic, Diyarbakır, Türkiye: 56 parents of children with ASD and 56 parents of typically developing children who were assessed at the clinic. Recruitment was not based on misophonia. Parents with hearing loss, ASD, ID, bipolar, psychotic disorder or dementia were excluded.
codes.instruments: AMISOS-R (Turkish version, Cakiroglu et al. 2022). Severity bands: 0–10 normal/subthreshold, 11–20 mild, 21–30 moderate, 31–40 severe. Also AQ and CARS.
codes.possible_duplicate: Presented as a poster at the 9th National Adolescent Health Congress (April 25–26, 2025, Diyarbakır). A congress abstract may exist.
codes.note: AMISOS-R bands are defined (p.3). Table 4 (p.5) compares AQ across subclinical, mild, moderate and severe groups but gives no n or % per band. Only means, medians and correlations are reported. Trigger % (throat sounds 55.4% vs 26.8%) are not case definitions. Subscale means hint at about 4 severe and 9 moderate, but this is not exact. Consider asking the authors for band counts.

codes.sample: 30 chronic outpatients with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder (diagnosis confirmed by SCID) and 28 demographically matched healthy volunteers, USA (Maryland). Recruited for an MRI study, not for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014): symptoms, emotional behavior, and self-reported sound sensitivity (SRSS). Also the Sensory Processing Scale, Aberrant Salience Inventory, and TEPS.

case_definitions.definition: At least one MQ Emotional Behavior item rated 4 ('always') in response to a misophonia trigger sound; SZ group
case_definitions.quote: four participants with SZ gave at least one item from the MQ Emotional Behavior section a rating of 4, meaning that they "always" engage in the respective avoidant/emotional behavior

case_definitions.definition: At least one MQ Emotional Behavior item rated 4 ('always'); healthy volunteer group
case_definitions.quote: This was true for no HVs. In general, these results indicate that while very few participants exhibited true misophonia

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is the PMC author manuscript of Schizophr Res 2024;274:329-336.
codes.note: Borderline. The only count uses an item-frequency definition (any Emotional Behavior item rated 'always'). This is not a standard MQ cut-off, and the authors do not explicitly call it a case definition. The standard SRSS ≥7 cut-off is not reported as counts; only means are given (SZ 4.741, HV 2.478). The reviewer should confirm whether the item-based definition is acceptable.

codes.sample: 117 adults aged 18–70 with tinnitus (56 male, 61 female) seen at the Department of Audiology, All India Institute of Speech and Hearing, Mysuru, India. This is a clinical sample recruited for tinnitus, not for misophonia. People with comorbid hyperacusis or misophonia were excluded.
codes.instruments: Amsterdam Misophonia Scale-Revised (AMISOS-R) was used to identify people with misophonia. Other measures: Khalfa hyperacusis questionnaire, Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI), pure-tone audiometry, speech identification scores, and two open-ended questions (PQ and LEQ).
codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly related to Manchaiah, Nisha, Prabhu et al. 2022 (Acta Otolaryngol, tinnitus consequences at the same institute), but there is no clear evidence that the sample overlaps.
codes.note: AMISOS-R was used only to screen out misophonia (p.3: "individuals suffering from other co-morbidities, such as hyperacusis and misophonia, were excluded"). The paper gives no number screened or excluded and no cut-off, so no prevalence can be derived. Contacting the authors might yield the screening counts.

codes.sample: 348 adolescent psychiatric outpatients aged 12–18 (56% female) seen at a private psychiatric centre in Türkiye, January–July 2023. They had non-psychotic disorders (anxiety, ADHD, depression, OCD spectrum, etc.); ASD, psychosis, bipolar disorder and ID were excluded. Recruitment was not based on misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonic Symptom Checklist (MCL; Öz & Kılıç; 50 sounds, 4-point Likert, total score 0–150), self-reported by the adolescents. Also used: MOCI, AQ-Adolescent (parent-rated) and CPRS-48 (parent-rated).
codes.possible_duplicate: Same lead author (Herdi) as Çolak et al. 2021, J Obsessive Compuls Relat Disord (adult non-psychotic outpatients). That is a different sample, so it is probably not a duplicate.
codes.note: The sample is eligible (outpatients recruited for other conditions) and misophonia was measured with the MCL. However, the paper reports MCL results only as a median (41, range 2–124), Mann-Whitney comparisons, correlations and regression (p.4). It gives no cut-off, severity bands, or number or proportion of participants with misophonia.

codes.sample: 133 adults: 70 Trabzon 112 Emergency Call Center workers exposed to noise at least 8 h/day, aged 18-60, without hearing loss, plus 63 volunteer academicians at Avrasya University as controls (80 women, 53 men). Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Turkish Decreased Sound Tolerance Scale – Screening (ASTÖ-T; Alluşoğlu & Aksoy), with a 14-item misophonia subscale scored 0-3 per item; stated misophonia threshold is a subscale total of 4 or more.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The study was funded as a TÜBİTAK 2209-A undergraduate project; a related student report may exist.
codes.note: Misophonia cut-off of 4 or more is defined (p.4: "mizofoni için ise 4 veya üzerinde"). Tables 1, 3–5 give only n, mean, min, max, median and p; no count or % at or above the cut-off is given or derivable. Table 2 (loud music) is missing from the extracted text; check the PDF to confirm it also has no counts.

codes.sample: Study 3: 102 naive undergraduates (65 women, 33 men, 4 non-binary; ages 18–29) from the University of California, Santa Cruz Psychology participant pool, not screened for misophonia. Study 1 interviewed 80 people recruited because they had misophonia (selected sample, not usable here). Study 2 (N=34) did not give the MQ.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Questionnaire (MQ; Wu et al., 2014): Symptom Scale, Emotions and Behaviors Scale (Sensitivity Score 0–68), and the Misophonia Severity Scale (single item, 0/1–15).

case_definitions.definition: MQ Misophonia Severity Scale score of 7 or above ('clinically significant misophonic reactions')
case_definitions.quote: For this scale, a score of 7 or above would constitute clinically significant misophonic reactions. There are 14 participants out of 101 (13.7% of the sample) that had misophonia severity scores of 7 or above.

codes.possible_duplicate: The record is listed as an OSF item (osf.io/3ysfh, the database/data repository). The retrieved text is the Frontiers in Psychology article (Samermit et al., 2022, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2022.890829). They likely describe the same Study 3 sample, so check for a duplicate record.
codes.note: The denominator doesn't add up: 14/101 is 13.9%, but 14/102 is 13.7%, and Study 3 had N=102. The t-test is also reported as t101. The cut-off is described two ways: 'above 7' on p.3 and '7 or above' on p.9. The Discussion (p.11) repeats '14 of the participants had a severity score of 7 or higher'. The 80 interviewees in Study 1 were selected for misophonia and are excluded.

codes.sample: UK general-population adults (≥18) recruited via Prolific, stratified by sex, age and ethnicity using UK census data; N = 772 (396 women, 372 men, 4 non-binary/other; mean age 46.4). Interview subsample: 29 from this general sample, chosen from every 10th-tile of the S-Five distribution, plus 26 from a self-identified misophonia sample.
codes.instruments: S-Five (25 items) with S-Five-T trigger checklist; MQ (MSYS, MEBS, MSES); A-MISO-S; a semi-structured clinician interview (Pre-OK-SCIM) adapted from the Amsterdam UMC revised criteria; PHQ-9; GAD-7.

case_definitions.definition: S-Five total score ≥87 (out of 250), a cut-off from ROC analysis against the Pre-OK-SCIM interview ('significant misophonia')
case_definitions.location: Page 10, Prevalence of misophonia in the UK population
case_definitions.quote: With 87 as the cut-off point on the S-Five, we found that 142 individuals out of 772 met the threshold for significant misophonia in our UK representative sample. Therefore, we estimated that a percentage of 18.4%

case_definitions.definition: Pre-OK-SCIM interview outcome 'significant misophonia' in the general-population interview subsample (chosen across S-Five deciles, so not a random subsample)
case_definitions.location: Page 10, Prevalence of misophonia in the UK population
case_definitions.quote: The Pre-OK-SCIM classified 14% (4 participants) of the general population sample and 81% (21 participants) of the misophonia sample as having 'significant misophonia'.

case_definitions.definition: Self-identifies as having misophonia (ad hoc item); only a percentage is printed, n not given
case_definitions.quote: Only 13.6% of the sample was aware of the term misophonia and 2.3% identify as having the disorder.

codes.possible_duplicate: The record is the UK Data Service dataset (10.5255/UKDA-SN-856149), but the text is the PLOS ONE 2023 article (e0282777). Both cover the same sample. The 2021 Audiology IRT paper may share data.
codes.note: Primary estimate: 142/772 (18.4%). The interview subsample was deliberately spread across S-Five deciles, so 4/29 is not a representative prevalence. The 2.3% self-identification count is derived, not printed (0.023×772 ≈ 18). The MSES ≥7 cut-off is described, but no counts are reported. Not all participants completed the MQ (n=376) or A-MISO-S (n=396), and no cut-off counts are given for either.

codes.sample: Main sample: N = 175 adults recruited via Prolific (general population; exclusions: hearing aids, self-reported hearing loss, neurological, psychotic disorder). It was enriched with 28 autistic participants, giving 147 non-autistic and 28 autistic. Not recruited for misophonia. Pilot sample: N = 520 Prolific adults who completed only the GSQ and BAPQ, with no misophonia measure.
codes.instruments: Duke Misophonia Questionnaire (DMQ): Symptom Severity subscale (2 items accidentally left out; reframed as 'when intensely bothered by a sound or sounds'), Trigger subscale (14 yes/no items) and Coping subscales. Also BAPQ, SSQ, and the GSQ auditory items (pilot sample only).
codes.possible_duplicate: The pilot sample (N = 520) is pooled from Bang & Igelström 2023, Autism 27(7):2158–2172. It has no misophonia measure. No duplicate is apparent for the main DMQ sample (N = 175).
codes.note: DMQ is given only as median ± MAD by group (Table 1, p.4), plus regressions (Table 2) and trigger logistic regressions (Supp. Table S9, not retrieved). No DMQ cut-off, band or case count. The authors say results are not evidence of clinical misophonia (p.10). The supplement could be checked, but trigger endorsement would not be a case definition.

codes.sample: 42 individuals with bipolar affective disorder in remission and 46 healthy controls (N=88; 51 male, 58.0%); Tokat Gaziosmanpaşa University, Türkiye. Bipolar group recruited for another condition; controls non-clinical.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Symptom List (likely the Turkish version of the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale or the Misophonia Questionnaire symptom list); OCPD screening scale; Mood Dysregulation Scale; Beck Depression Inventory.
codes.possible_duplicate: Conference abstract (OP-25, Psychiatric Association of Türkiye Annual Meeting 2026). A later full article from the same group (Bak, Eser, Güneysu, Aydın, Ünal Demir) may report this sample with prevalence counts.
codes.note: Full abstract retrieved. Misophonia is reported only as group means (0.74±0.66 vs 0.57±0.31), plus correlations and regression. No cut-off, case count or proportion is reported. Any full-length publication should be checked for counts by cut-off.

codes.sample: 597 Indian high school students aged 14–16 (269 female, 328 male) with no history of psychological or otological problems and no medication use. Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Misophonia Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ; Johnson, revised by Dozier 2013): 21 items scored 0–3. Bands: Sub-clinical <10, Mild 11–21, Moderate 22–42, Severe 43–63. Self-administered with help from parents or caregivers.

case_definitions.definition: MAQ mild or above (score ≥11); the headline prevalence (mild+moderate+severe)
case_definitions.quote: approximately 34.67% of the participants exhibiting symptoms of this disorder ... Mild Misophonia 62 47 109 Moderate Misophonia 50 44 94 Severe Misophonia 02 02 4 Total 328 269 597

case_definitions.definition: MAQ moderate or above (score ≥22); the authors' stated definition of misophonia
case_definitions.quote: individuals with moderate and above degrees were considered as individuals with misophonia ... Moderate Misophonia 50 44 94 Severe Misophonia 02 02 4 Total 328 269 597

case_definitions.definition: MAQ severe (score 43–63). The printed 1.93% is a share of the 207 cases, not of 597.
case_definitions.quote: Severe Misophonia 02 02 4 Total 328 269 597

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The same group (Prabhu) published studies of Indian college students (Patel et al. 2022; Aryal & Prabhu 2022), but those are different samples.
codes.note: The printed 34.67% counts mild cases too, yet the Method says only moderate and above count as misophonia; mild is only 'at risk'. Band percentages (52.65/45.41/1.93%) use the 207 cases as the denominator, not 597. A score of exactly 10 falls in no band. Table 1 gives counts by sex.

codes.sample: US youth aged 8–17 recruited online. Misophonia group: 112 recruited with suspected misophonia, 102 analysed (selected sample). Anxiety comparison group: 140 recruited with suspected anxiety disorders and screened with the A-MISO-S, with 94 analysed. The anxiety group was recruited for another condition.
codes.instruments: A-MISO-S (child report; ≥10 = at least moderate misophonia; ≤4 = subclinical), Misophonia Assessment Interview (MAI; misophonia group only), C-MAQ and P-MAQ, MINI-KID

case_definitions.definition: A-MISO-S score above subclinical level (>4), which excluded children from the anxiety group; screened pool of youth recruited with suspected anxiety disorders
case_definitions.quote: of the 140 in the anxiety group, 94 were included. Reasons for exclusion in the anxiety group included: MASC score below the clinical cutoff, n = 26 (19%), A-MISO-S score too high, 9 (6%)

codes.possible_duplicate: The same Baylor youth sample is probably used in Cervin et al. (2022, psychometric evaluation of child and parent misophonia measures) and possibly in Smith et al. (2022, J Affect Disord 316:76–82).
codes.note: Borderline. The misophonia sample (n=102) is selected (E1). Eligibility rests only on the anxiety-group screen: 9/140 had A-MISO-S >4. Caveats: unclear whether all 140 completed the A-MISO-S or exclusions were sequential, so the denominator is uncertain; recruitment used 'misophonia/anxiety-focused' pages; the cut-off is >4, not ≥10. The reviewer may prefer E1.
